/*
The same engine, a completely different genome.

A life-like rule is a TABLE: which neighbour counts cause a birth, which cause survival. At a
radius-2 neighbourhood that is 24 birth bits and 25 survival bits, a fixed-length bit string, and
therefore a genome two parents can be recombined across. Field had exactly one other two-parent
crossover before this (afield.lang.morpho.MorphoGenerator); LifeRuleGenome.crossover is uniform
crossover over the rule table and it is real recombination, not a graft.

Radius 2 rather than the classic Moore 8 is a deliberate choice and it is the most useful thing
in this box. At radius 1 the space is 2^17 rules, and a few hundred INDEPENDENT draws land close
to the optimum on their own -- the first version of this demo measured evolution winning by 3%
for exactly that reason. A control arm that nearly wins is telling you the problem is easy, not
that the search is good. At radius 2 the space is 2^49 and the margin is 27%.
*/

val ops = LifeRuleGenome(radius = 2)
val soups = listOf(
    randomSoup(48, 48, density = 0.35, seed = 101L),
    randomSoup(48, 48, density = 0.12, seed = 202L),
)

/*
"Alive but not saturated, and still changing" -- activity times a Gaussian band on density.
Each factor alone is trivially gamed. A rule that fills the grid and stays filled scores 1 on
density and 0 on activity; a rule that flickers every cell scores ~1 on activity and ~0 on the
band; an extinct rule scores the floor. Only the product is large for a rule that keeps a
moderate population AND keeps rearranging it, which is what everybody means by an interesting
rule and what nobody can state by looking.
*/
val objective = caEdgeOfChaosObjective(soups, warmup = 20, scored = 30)
val budget = 400

val control = PopulationSearch.random(ops, objective, budget, seed = 7L, label = "random")

/*
LEXICASE, because this objective genuinely has a case structure: one case per soup. A rule that
holds together on one initial condition and collapses on the other is exactly what a
tournament's average hides, and lexicase never averages.
*/
val evolved = PopulationSearch.evolve(
    ops,
    objective,
    budget,
    seed = 7L,
    mu = 8,
    lambda = 16,
    selection = Selection.LEXICASE,
    crossoverRate = 0.3,
    immigrantRate = 0.1,
    label = "evolve",
)

println(control.summary())
println(evolved.summary())
println()
println(
    "margin %.4f  (%.1f%% above the control)"
        .format(
            evolved.bestFitness - control.bestFitness,
            100.0 * (evolved.bestFitness / control.bestFitness - 1.0),
        ),
)
println("recombined ${evolved.recombined} children by uniform crossover over the rule table")
println()
println("evolved rule ${lifeRuleSignature(evolved.best!!.genome)}")
println("control rule ${lifeRuleSignature(control.best!!.genome)}")
println()
println("The first record holders score BELOW the control: the control is the best of 400")
println("independent draws, so a population starts under it and has to climb past it.")
println()
println("Try Selection.TOURNAMENT above and compare. Try LifeRuleGenome() with no radius argument")
println("and watch the margin collapse -- that is the easy problem, and it is worth seeing.")

val panels = mutableListOf<Pair<String, Img>>()
panels +=
    "rnd %.3f".format(control.bestFitness) to
        caRun(soups[0], control.best!!.genome, 20, 30).finalGrid.toImg(2).upscaleNearest(3)
val picks =
    evolved.improvements.indices.toList().let { idx ->
        if (idx.size <= 5) idx else (1..5).map { (it * idx.size / 5) - 1 }
    }
for (i in picks) {
    val imp = evolved.improvements[i]
    panels +=
        "g%d %.3f".format(imp.generation, imp.fitness) to
            caRun(soups[0], imp.genome, 20, 30).finalGrid.toImg(2).upscaleNearest(3)
}
showImg(
    montage(panels, columns = 3, cellSide = 200),
    caption =
        "the control's best, then each successive record holder, all on the same soup -- the\n        early ones score BELOW the control, which is what overtaking looks like",
)

/*
Illuminate the rule space instead of optimising it.

MAP-Elites keeps the best rule found in each cell of a grid over the BEHAVIOUR space -- here
(density, activity), the same two numbers caEdgeOfChaosObjective already reports as its
Evaluation.behaviour. What comes out is not one answer but a map of "the best rule that behaves
like THIS", which is the contact sheet below.

This is the figure worth looking at. Top left is sparse and nearly dead; bottom right is dense
and noisy; and somewhere in the middle band are the rules that hold structure while still moving.
*/

val ops = LifeRuleGenome(radius = 2)
val soups = listOf(randomSoup(48, 48, density = 0.35, seed = 303L))
val objective = caEdgeOfChaosObjective(soups, warmup = 20, scored = 25)
val bins = listOf(6, 6)
val axes = listOf(0.0..1.0, 0.0..0.6)
val budget = 600

val archive = PopulationSearch.mapElites(ops, objective, budget, axes, bins, seed = 31L, initial = 40)
println(archive)
println("off-grid (clamped to an edge cell): ${archive.offGridCandidates} of $budget")
println()

/*
The control arm for a quality-diversity claim is the same budget of independent draws, binned
identically and reduced to the best genome per cell. Comparing against a single best random rule
would be the wrong control, because MAP-Elites is not trying to find one good rule.
*/
val controlCells = HashMap<List<Int>, Double>()
val rng = kotlin.random.Random(31L)
repeat(budget) {
    val e = objective.evaluate(ops.random(rng))
    val cell =
        axes.indices.map { d ->
            (((e.behaviour[d] - axes[d].start) / (axes[d].endInclusive - axes[d].start)) * bins[d])
                .toInt()
                .coerceIn(0, bins[d] - 1)
        }
    val incumbent = controlCells[cell]
    if (incumbent == null || e.fitness > incumbent) controlCells[cell] = e.fitness
}
val controlQd = controlCells.values.sum()
println("random-sampled archive: ${controlCells.size}/${archive.cells} cells, QD %.3f".format(controlQd))
println("illuminated archive:    ${archive.elites.size}/${archive.cells} cells, QD %.3f".format(archive.qdScore))
println()
println("Quality, not coverage, is the claim. Random sampling spreads over a descriptor space for")
println("free -- that is what random means -- while MAP-Elites reaches a new cell only when a")
println("mutation moves a descriptor across a bin boundary. What illumination buys is the quality")
println("held in each cell it does occupy.")

val panels =
    archive.elites.entries.sortedWith(compareBy({ it.key[0] }, { it.key[1] })).map { (cell, elite) ->
        "%d%d %.2f".format(cell[0], cell[1], elite.fitness) to
            caRun(soups[0], elite.genome, 20, 25).finalGrid.toImg(2).upscaleNearest(3)
    }
showImg(
    montage(panels, columns = 6, cellSide = 150),
    caption = "one panel per occupied cell; the label is (density bin)(activity bin) and the score",
)

A wall in alife_script is a line SEGMENT, and a segment has no thickness. So the obvious
collision test — "does the agent's new position overlap a wall" — is false for any step big
enough to step over it, at any speed at all. The collision here is swept: it solves for the
first moment of contact along the step, not for where the step happened to land.

Three agents, one wall, three answers to "what now".
*/

val w = ScriptWorld(width = 200.0, height = 200.0, seed = 1L, wrap = false)
/*
A room as well as the barrier, so a BOUNCE agent has something to come back off. The arena
edge is NOT a wall — ScriptWorld.confine just clamps there — so without this the bouncer
parks in a corner and the trail says nothing.
*/
w.addPolygon(12.0, 12.0, 188.0, 12.0, 188.0, 188.0, 12.0, 188.0, name = "room")
w.addWall(120.0, 30.0, 120.0, 170.0, name = "barrier")

listOf(WallResponse.SLIDE, WallResponse.BOUNCE, WallResponse.STOP).forEachIndexed { i, r ->
    w.spawn(
        25.0,
        60.0 + i * 25.0,
        maxSpeed = 90.0,
        radius = 2.0,
        steerResponse = 1.0,
        vx = 90.0,
        vy = 16.0,
        wallResponse = r,
        restitution = 0.9,
        tag = r.name,
    ) {
        moveFor(8.0) { keepVelocity() }
    }
}
w.run(420)

w.actors.forEach {
    println(
        "%-7s %3d contact(s), ended at %6.1f, %6.1f"
            .format(
                it.tag,
                it.wallContacts,
                it.position.x,
                it.position.y,
            ),
    )
}
println()
println("90 units/s at 60 Hz is 1.5 units per step against a radius of 2 — no tunnelling risk.")
println("Raise maxSpeed and vx to 900 and every number above stays sane; that is the whole")
println("point of solving for the contact instead of testing the endpoint.")

    *(w.obstacleFLines() + w.trailFLines()).toTypedArray(),

    w = 440.0,
    h = 440.0,

wall. Set it to 1.0 and the trail is a billiard. SLIDE is the default because it is the only
one of the three that lets an agent still get somewhere while touching something.
*/

before:
/*
seek() points at the goal and pushes. That is correct and cheap when there is a straight line,
and when there is a barrier in the way it presses into the barrier for as long as you let it.
No amount of avoidWalls() fixes that: avoidance is local, and the decision to go the OTHER way
round a wall is not. route() plans — a radius-aware A* through the world's walls, smoothed
against the same swept test the physics uses, then followed waypoint by waypoint.

The maze is an S. The first barrier is open only at the BOTTOM, the second only at the TOP, so
no fixed "always turn left" solves it. Both arms run avoidWalls at the same weight: this is
routing against the best local steering available, not routing against nothing.
*/

val GOAL_X = 175.0
val GOAL_Y = 100.0
val STEPS = 1800 // 30 s at 60 Hz
val SEEDS = listOf(1L, 2L, 3L, 4L)
val PER_SEED = 8

fun maze(seed: Long, routed: Boolean): ScriptWorld {
    val w = ScriptWorld(width = 200.0, height = 200.0, seed = seed, wrap = false)
    w.addWall(70.0, 45.0, 70.0, 200.0, name = "open at the bottom")
    w.addWall(130.0, 0.0, 130.0, 155.0, name = "open at the top")
    val jitter = kotlin.random.Random(seed) // same jitter in both arms: same start positions
    repeat(PER_SEED) {
        w.spawn(
            18.0 + jitter.nextDouble(-8.0, 8.0),
            100.0 + jitter.nextDouble(-28.0, 28.0),
            maxSpeed = 35.0,
            radius = 1.2,
            steerResponse = 0.3,
            tag = if (routed) "routed" else "direct",
        ) {
            val goal = point(GOAL_X, GOAL_Y) // R3c: this now works inside moveUntil too
            moveUntil(maxSeconds = STEPS / 60.0, speed = 35.0, until = { near(goal, 6.0) }) {
                if (routed) route(goal, clearance = 3.5) else seek(goal)
                avoidWalls(clearance = 3.0, weight = 0.6)
                separate(range = 4.0, weight = 0.4)
            }
            rest(2.0)
        }
    }
    return w
}

val curves = LinkedHashMap<String, List<Double>>()
val shown = LinkedHashMap<String, ScriptWorld>()
for (routed in listOf(true, false)) {
    val name = if (routed) "routed" else "direct"
    val cumulative = MutableList(STEPS) { 0.0 }
    var population = 0
    var travel = 0.0
    for (s in SEEDS) {
        val w = maze(s, routed)
        val done = mutableSetOf<Int>()
        repeat(STEPS) { t ->
            w.step()
            for (a in w.actors) if (a.id !in done && a.distanceTo(GOAL_X, GOAL_Y) <= 6.0) done += a.id
            cumulative[t] = cumulative[t] + done.size
        }
        population += w.actors.size
        travel += w.totalPathLength()
        if (s == SEEDS.first()) shown[name] = w
    }
    curves[name] = cumulative.map { it / population }
    println(
        "%-7s arrived %.3f of %d   mean travel %.1f"
            .format(
                name,
                cumulative.last() / population,
                population,
                travel / population,
            ),
    )
}
println()
println("Both arms travel — the second column is the non-degeneracy check. A margin over a")
println("control that never left home would mean nothing.")

showSignals(
    "routed" to curves["routed"]!!,
    "direct" to curves["direct"]!!,
    channel = "arrivals",
    title = "fraction arrived, ${SEEDS.size} seeds x $PER_SEED agents per arm",
    yTitle = "of 1",
)

/*
Try this: change `route(goal, clearance = 3.5)` to `clearance = 0.5`. The route still gets
there, but it plans 1.7 units from every corner — inside the reach of the avoidWalls term the
same agent is running — and the two terms then disagree all the way round each corner. The
arrival curve sags. Plan outside your own avoidance range.
*/

name: certified_envelope
description: |

  signal viewer's 0.02 s samples: box 1 draws the sampled min/max envelope the function workbench draws, and the
  glitch is not in it (missed by 0.4956 in its bin). Box 2 draws the same viewer with the opt-in certified band
  (certifiedSignalChannel), which reaches the glitch's true height, because it bounds every value in each bin by
  interval arithmetic over the FnFormulas table instead of sampling. Box 3 is certifiedRange (the global max, its
  witness x and a proven bound 1e-9 above it) and three yes/no claims. Box 4 is what refuses - a fn { } lambda,
  by name - and the workbench's 'holds exactly 1 for 30 seconds' claim proven exactly on a formula-built event.
  Box 5 is the workbench's own worked example, rewritten from formula ops bit for bit, with its claims
  certified: every plateau exactly 1 (PROVEN), >= 0 (PROVEN), and <= 1 REFUTED by 4 ulps at 284.99994 s.

      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          One hour: a slow 40-second swing, plus a glitch 10 ms wide at 1234.57 s — exactly halfway
          between two of the viewer's 0.02 s samples. Built from Functions ops rather than a
          fn { } lambda, so every node has a formula. Box 2 needs that.
          */
          val signal = with(Functions) {
              sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45) + gaussian(1234.57, 0.002, 0.5, Functions.Domain.ALL)
          }

          // The sampled envelope, drawn the way the function workbench draws it: min and max per bin.
          val viewer = SignalViewer(listOf(SignalChannel("x", signal::eval)), 0.0, 3600.0)
          displaySignal(
              viewer,
              "main",
              SignalViewerOptions(label = "sampled envelope only", viewKey = "certified_envelope:sampled"),
          )

          // The same query the plot makes, read back as numbers. Bin 342 holds the glitch.
          val bins = viewer.window(0.0, 3600.0, 1000).lanes[0].current
          val bin = (1234.57 / 3.6).toInt()

              "numbers",
              Table(listOf("what", "value"), title = "what the sampled plot can see")
                  .row("f(1234.57), the glitch's peak", signal(1234.57))

          behind it in amber, a certified bound per bin: every value the function takes in the bin
          lies inside, whether or not a sample landed on it. Nothing here is sampled more finely.

          // witness, and at most the proven bound. The same for the minimum.

          val max = range.max!!
          val min = range.min!!
          display(
              "range",
              Table(

                      title = "certifiedRange(0, 3600): certified = ${range.certified}",

                  .row("min", min.value, min.witness, min.bound, min.enclosures)
                  .role("at x", CellRole.ACCENT),

              signal.certifiedNeverExceeds(0.8, 0.0, 3600.0),
              signal.certifiedReaches(0.75, 0.0, 3600.0),
          )
          display(

              Table(listOf("claim", "verdict", "witness x"))
                  .rows(claims.map { listOf(it.claim, it.kind.name, it.witness) })
                  .roleBy("verdict") { if (it == "PROVEN") CellRole.OK else CellRole.WARN },

  - create:
      box: limits
      name: "4 - What refuses, and an exact hold"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1800.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*

          lambdas: one opaque node each, so there is nothing for an interval walk to read. It refuses by
          name rather than guess.
          */
          val lambdaChannel = with(Functions) { fn(0.0..3600.0, "x") { t -> 0.45 + 0.2 * kotlin.math.sin(t) } }
          val refused = lambdaChannel.enclose(0.0, 3600.0)

          // The workbench's claim that an event holds exactly 1 for 30 seconds, rebuilt from formula ops:
          // rise 185..285, hold to 315, fall to 415, over the moving background.
          val held = with(Functions) {
              val one = c(1.0, Functions.Domain.ALL)
              val background = sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45)
              val envelope =
                  smoothStep(185.0, 285.0, Functions.Domain.ALL) * (one - smoothStep(315.0, 415.0, Functions.Domain.ALL))
              one - (one - background) * (one - envelope)
          }
          val checks = listOf(
              held.certifiedEquals(1.0, 285.0, 315.0),
              held.certifiedEquals(1.0, 284.0, 315.0),
              held.certifiedNeverExceeds(1.0, 0.0, 3600.0, slack = 1e-12),
          )
          display(
              "limits",
              Table(listOf("question", "answer"), title = "refusals and exact holds")
                  .row("enclose the lambda channel", "certified = ${refused.certified}: ${refused.refusal}")
                  .rows(checks.map { listOf(it.claim, it.kind.name + (it.witness?.let { w -> " at x = $w" } ?: "")) })
                  .role("answer", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: workbench
      name: "5 - The worked example, certified"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 2120.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          The function workbench's worked example (public/docs/assets/function_conversation/final.kt),
          twice. `lambda` is its channel code, verbatim: one fn { } per channel, which the interval walk
          refuses. `formula` is the same function from formula-bearing ops. The only construct that needed
          a lambda was the piecewise event selection; here it is exact 0/1 `step` indicators, with every
          product and sum in the lambda's order, so the two agree bit for bit.
          */
          val events = listOf(
              StudyEvent("e1", 185.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e2", 785.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e3", 1425.0, 200.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e5", 2585.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e6", 3185.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
          )
          val names = listOf("x", "y", "z")

          fun smooth01(value: Double): Double {
              val u = value.coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
              return u * u * u * (10.0 + u * (-15.0 + 6.0 * u))
          }
          fun backgroundOf(seconds: Double, channel: Int): Double {
              val drift = 2.0 * PI / 3.0 * kotlin.math.sin(2.0 * PI * seconds / 100.0)
              val phase = 2.0 * PI * seconds / 40.0 + (channel - 1) * drift
              return 0.45 + 0.20 * kotlin.math.sin(phase) + 0.04 * kotlin.math.sin(2.0 * PI * seconds / 230.0)
          }
          fun shoulderOf(base: Double, age: Double, span: Double): Double {
              val u = (age / span).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
              val cycles = 0.06 * age + 0.5 * (0.80 - 0.06) * age * age / span
              val pulse = 0.5 - 0.5 * kotlin.math.cos(2.0 * PI * cycles)
              val strength = smooth01(u)
              val pulsed = (1.0 - strength) * base + strength * (0.25 + (1.0 - 0.25) * pulse)
              val merge = smooth01((u - (1.0 - 0.20)) / 0.20)
              return (1.0 - merge) * pulsed + merge
          }
          fun lambda(index: Int, name: String) = with(Functions) {
              fn(0.0..3600.0, name) { seconds ->
                  val base = backgroundOf(seconds, index)
                  val event = events.firstOrNull { seconds >= it.start && seconds <= it.end }
                  when {
                      event == null -> base
                      seconds < event.plateauStart -> {
                          val age = seconds - event.start
                          val lag = if (event.id == "e3" && name == "y" && age < 180.0) {
                              val u = age / 180.0
                              val v = 1.0 - u
                              6.0 * 64.0 * u * u * u * v * v * v
                          } else 0.0
                          shoulderOf(base, age - lag, event.rise)
                      }
                      seconds <= event.plateauEnd -> 1.0
                      else -> shoulderOf(base, event.end - seconds, event.fall)
                  }
              }
          }

          fun formula(index: Int, name: String) = with(Functions) {
              val all = Functions.Domain.ALL
              fun k(v: Double) = c(v, all)
              val t = identity(all)
              val one = k(1.0)
              fun sinOf(p: Functions.Fn) = sin(frequency = k(0.0), phase = p) // sin(0*x + p) is sin(p), exactly
              fun cosOf(p: Functions.Fn) = cos(frequency = k(0.0), phase = p)
              fun smooth(v: Functions.Fn): Functions.Fn {
                  val u = v.clamp(0.0, 1.0)
                  return u * u * u * (k(10.0) + u * (k(-15.0) + k(6.0) * u))
              }
              val drift = k(2.0 * PI / 3.0) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(100.0))
              val base =
                  k(0.45) +
                      k(0.20) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(40.0) + k((index - 1).toDouble()) * drift) +
                      k(0.04) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(230.0))
              fun shoulder(age: Functions.Fn, span: Double): Functions.Fn {
                  val u = (age / k(span)).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
                  val cycles = k(0.06) * age + k(0.5 * (0.80 - 0.06)) * age * age / k(span)
                  val pulse = k(0.5) - k(0.5) * cosOf(k(2.0 * PI) * cycles)
                  val strength = smooth(u)
                  val pulsed = (one - strength) * base + strength * (k(0.25) + k(1.0 - 0.25) * pulse)
                  val merge = smooth((u - k(1.0 - 0.20)) / k(0.20))
                  return (one - merge) * pulsed + merge
              }
              fun from(a: Double) = step(a, all) // exactly [x >= a]; [x <= b] is 1 - from(nextUp(b))
              var sum: Functions.Fn = k(0.0) * t
              var inside: Functions.Fn = k(0.0)
              for (e in events) {
                  val age = t - k(e.start)
                  val local = if (e.id == "e3" && name == "y") {
                      val u = age / k(180.0)
                      val v = one - u
                      age - (k(180.0) - age).sign().clamp(0.0, 1.0) * (k(6.0 * 64.0) * u * u * u * v * v * v)
                  } else age
                  sum =
                      sum +
                          ((from(e.start) - from(e.plateauStart)) * shoulder(local, e.rise) +
                              (from(e.plateauStart) - from(Math.nextUp(e.plateauEnd))) * one +
                              (from(Math.nextUp(e.plateauEnd)) - from(Math.nextUp(e.end))) * shoulder(k(e.end) - t, e.fall))
                  inside = inside + (from(e.start) - from(Math.nextUp(e.end)))
              }
              sum + (one - inside) * base
          }

          val rows = mutableListOf<List<Any?>>()
          for ((i, name) in names.withIndex()) {
              val l = lambda(i, name)
              val f = formula(i, name)
              val grid = (0..72_000).map { it * 0.05 }
              val mismatches = grid.count { l(it).toRawBits() != f(it).toRawBits() }
              val holds = events.count { f.certifiedEquals(1.0, it.plateauStart, it.plateauEnd).proven }
              val above = f.certifiedNeverExceeds(1.0, 0.0, 3600.0)
              val witness = above.witness!!
              rows +=
                  listOf(
                      name,
                      "${FnIntervals.unsupportedOps(l)} / ${FnIntervals.unsupportedOps(f)}",
                      "$mismatches of ${grid.size}",
                      "$holds of ${events.size} PROVEN",
                      f.certifiedNeverBelow(0.0, 0.0, 3600.0).kind.name,
                      "${above.kind} at $witness: lambda ${l(witness)}",
                  )
          }
          display(
              "claims",
              Table(
                      listOf("ch", "refused ops (lambda / formula)", "bit mismatches", "== 1 on plateau", ">= 0", "<= 1"),
                      title = "the worked example's claims, on its formula rewrite",
                  )
                  .rows(rows)
                  .role("<= 1", CellRole.WARN),
          )

          // How far above 1: certifiedRange's proven bound is the certificate for <= 1 + 1e-9 (x only; ~11 s).
          val xMax = formula(0, "x").certifiedRange(0.0, 3600.0, tolerance = 9e-10).max!!
          display(
              "max",
              Table(listOf("what", "value"), title = "channel x, the whole hour")
                  .row("max reached", xMax.value.toString())
                  .row("at x", xMax.witness.toString())
                  .row("proven bound", xMax.bound.toString())
                  .row("enclosures", xMax.enclosures)
                  .role("value", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )

name: chart_clip
description: >

  figure with `clip = false` — which is the behaviour that shipped `sharp_edge.png` on
  `public/docs/tetgen.md` — a long note wrapping and not wrapping, and the numbers behind both,
  read off the drawn geometry rather than described.

  Open the document and run box 2. The plot becomes a stamp in one corner of an empty rectangle.
  The switch is the single word `clip` on the line the box points at, and the box prints the
  bounds that make the difference: a panel fits the geometry's OWN bounds, so anything outside the
  declared frame does not get cropped, it shrinks everything else.

  This transcript is what built `dev_docs/agents/demos/chart_clip/metadata.edn`; re-running it
  rebuilds that document. See `dev_docs/chart_clip_and_note.md`.
operations:
  - create:
      box: clip_on
      name: 1 - The corner, clipped
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 440.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          A magnified corner of a body far larger than the window — the shape of figure that
          finds this bug, because it is the one that needs an explicit domain. The outline is
          2 x 3; the window is 0.24 x 0.24 around one of its corners.
          */
          val outline = listOf(
              -1.0 to -1.5,
              1.0 to -1.5,
              1.0 to 1.5,
              -1.0 to 1.5,
              -1.0 to -1.5,
          )

          val c =
              Chart(title = "one corner of a 2 x 3 outline", xLabel = "x", yLabel = "y")
                  .line("outline", outline.map { it.first }, outline.map { it.second })
          c.width = 780.0
          c.height = 440.0
          c.xDomain = 0.82 to 1.06
          c.yDomain = 1.32 to 1.56

          showChart(c)

          /*
          `plotRect` is the rectangle the axes bound, and the one mark geometry is clipped to.
          `toFLines()` is the whole figure in pixels, and its union bounds are exactly what
          `linesToHTML` publishes to the panel. Everything is inside the 780 x 440 asked for.
          */
          val ps = c.toFLines().flatMap { l -> l.nodes.mapNotNull { it.toOrNull } }
          println("plotRect: " + c.plotRect())
          println(
              "drawn:    %.0f,%.0f %.0fx%.0f"
                  .format(
                      ps.minOf { it.x },
                      ps.minOf { it.y },
                      ps.maxOf { it.x } - ps.minOf { it.x },
                      ps.maxOf { it.y } - ps.minOf { it.y },
                  ),
          )
  - create:

    kernel = GpKernels.matern(1.5, doubleArrayOf(0.55, 0.8)),
    noiseStd = 0.04,
)

            -1.2 + 2.4 * (i / side) / (side - 1),
        )
    }

before:
/*
Type a λ-term, get its normal form. `LambdaTerms.normalise` is the whole pipeline in one call:
parse the text, compile it to an interaction net, reduce the net until nothing fires, read a term
back out. Nothing here needs a GPU, a network or any setup.
*/

val run = LambdaTerms.normalise("(\\m n f x. m f (n f x)) (\\f x. f x) (\\f x. f (f x))")
println("add one two  =  ${run.printed}")
println("${run.steps} reactions, ${run.fans} fans compiled, ${run.remainingNodes} agents left standing")
println("oracle agrees: " + LambdaTerms.alphaEquivalent(run.result, LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder(run.term)))

/*
That last line is the only reason to trust the one above it. `referenceNormalOrder` is an ordinary
capture-avoiding substitution evaluator with no nets and no sharing anywhere in it — it exists in
order to disagree with the net, and the readback is compared to it with `alphaEquivalent`, not with
`==`, because a readback invents its own binder names.
*/

println()
println("term                                       normal form                   steps  fans  agents")
listOf(
        "\\x. x",
        "(\\x y z. x z (y z)) (\\x y. x) (\\x y. x)",
        "(\\n f x. f (n f x)) (\\f x. f (f x))",
        "(\\m n f. m (n f)) (\\f x. f (f x)) (\\f x. f (f (f x)))",
        "(\\f x. f (f (f x))) (\\f x. f (f x))",
        "(\\n f x. n (\\g h. h (g f)) (\\u. x) (\\u. u)) (\\f x. f (f (f x)))",
        "(\\x. x x) (\\y. ((\\x. x) (\\x. x)) y)",
        "(\\x y. x) (\\x. x) ((\\m n f. m (n f)) (\\f x. f (f x)) (\\f x. f (f (f x))))",
    )
    .forEach { source ->
        val each = LambdaTerms.normalise(source)
        val ok = LambdaTerms.alphaEquivalent(each.result, LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder(each.term))
        println(
            source.take(40).padEnd(42) +
                each.printed.take(28).padEnd(30) +
                "%5d %5d %7d".format(each.steps, each.fans, each.remainingNodes) +
                (if (ok) "" else "   ORACLE DISAGREES"),
        )
    }

/*
Read the `agents` column against the `normal form` column on the exponentiation row — `three two`,
which is 2^3. The net is left standing at 10 agents; the term it reads back as needs 11 nodes (one
ROOT, two LAM, eight APP). The net is SMALLER than its own answer, because it stayed shared: the
unfolding happened in the readback, not in the reduction. A fan in a normal form is not a node of
the term, it is a bracket on the path through it, which is what `Lambda.FAN_LABEL` is for.

Do not read that as a general claim. `mul two three` finishes at 10 agents against a 9-node term
and `mul three three` comes out even. Which way it goes depends on the term.
*/

println()
println("what the compiler builds, for `\\f. \\y. f (f y)`:")
val compiled = LambdaTerms.compile(LambdaTerms.parse("\\f. \\y. f (f y)"))
println("  " + compiled.net.nodes.groupingBy { it.type.name }.eachCount().toSortedMap())
println("  ${compiled.fans} fan(s) for the variable used twice, ${compiled.erasers} eraser(s) for unused binders")

/*
Try it: put a term of your own in the list. `\x. x x` applied to itself diverges, and the net will
too — `normalise` takes a `maxSteps` and `run.finished` is false when it ran out, which is all
a reducer can report about a term that has no normal form.
*/

before:
/*
The whole corpus against the oracle, and then against four schedulers. This is the box that says
whether any of the rest is true: `readback(reduce(compile(t)))` against an ordinary
capture-avoiding normal-order evaluator, for every named term, printed rather than summarised.
*/

val corpus = LambdaTerms.corpus()
val orders = listOf(
    ActivationOrder.FIRST_FOUND,
    ActivationOrder.LEFTMOST_BY_ID,
    ActivationOrder.RIGHTMOST_BY_ID,
    ActivationOrder.HIGHEST_PAIR_ENERGY,
)
println("${corpus.size} named closed terms, ${orders.size} schedulers")
println()

println("                        steps  fans  agents  normal form")
var netTotal = 0
val disagreed = mutableListOf<String>()
val notConfluent = mutableListOf<String>()

corpus.forEach { (name, source) ->
    val term = LambdaTerms.parse(source)
    val oracleKey = LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder(term))
    val keys = orders.associateWith { LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.normalise(term, order = it).result) }
    val run = LambdaTerms.normalise(term)
    netTotal += run.steps
    if (keys.getValue(ActivationOrder.FIRST_FOUND) != oracleKey) disagreed += name
    if (keys.values.toSet().size != 1) notConfluent += name
    println(
        name.padEnd(22) + "%6d %5d %7d".format(run.steps, run.fans, run.remainingNodes) + "  " + run.printed.take(46),
    )
}

println()
println(
    "agreed with the oracle : ${corpus.size - disagreed.size} of ${corpus.size}" +
        if (disagreed.isEmpty()) "" else "   DISAGREED: $disagreed",
)
println(
    "confluent across ${orders.size} schedulers: ${corpus.size - notConfluent.size} of ${corpus.size}" +
        if (notConfluent.isEmpty()) "" else "   NOT CONFLUENT: $notConfluent",
)
println("net reactions          : $netTotal over ${corpus.size} terms at FIRST_FOUND")

/*
Two things that number is not. It is not comparable to a β-step count — a net reaction is any rule
firing, β or duplication or erasure or a fan meeting, so the two are different units. And it is not
the word "optimal": there are no brackets and no croissants here, so the sharing is correct but
nothing bounds how many times a fan may be copied.
*/

println()
println("and the pieces on their own:")
println(
    "  parse -> format round-trips exactly: " +
        corpus.values.all { LambdaTerms.parse(LambdaTerms.format(LambdaTerms.parse(it))) == LambdaTerms.parse(it) },
)
println(
    "  every corpus term is closed: " +
        corpus.values.all { LambdaTerms.freeVariablesOf(LambdaTerms.parse(it)).isEmpty() },
)
println("  de Bruijn key of Church two: " + LambdaTerms.deBruijnKey(LambdaTerms.parse("\\f x. f (f x)")))
println(
    "  substitution avoids capture: " +
        LambdaTerms.format(LambdaTerms.substitute(LambdaTerms.parse("\\y. x y"), "x", LambdaTerms.parse("y"))),
)

/*
Try it: add a term to `LambdaTerms.corpus()` in `src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/lambdaterms.kt`.
`stdlib.lambda-terms.smoke` asserts the corpus by the SET OF ITS NAMES, so a new entry fails that
test until you name it there too — which is the point. A corpus that can shrink is not a corpus.
*/

before:
name: keyframe_key_discovery
description: >
  The keyframe browser, and whether it can show you your own keys.

  Three boxes, no GPU, no window: a KeyframeScope needs neither, and each box writes its key directory
  into a fresh temp dir so nothing lands in this document.

    1. kf_before_after  — six keys named `a b c d d2 d3`, the shapes a real session actually produced,
                   browsed twice in one box. The top panel uses `pattern = "??"`, which was the last
                   pattern that session tried; it shows two of the six and now says so, with a button
                   that widens it in one click. The bottom panel uses the default. The printed numbers
                   are the whole story: the old default `**/*.json` found **zero** of these six,
                   because `saveKey` writes the path it is handed and appends no extension, so
                   `capture().save("d3".path)` produces a file called `d3`. `?` is exactly one
                   character and `??` exactly two, so no single-length glob spans `a b c d` and
                   `d2 d3` — and `{?,??}` always did, with nothing anywhere saying so.
    2. kf_junk_vs_damage — four good keys, two files that were never keys, and one key Field wrote and
                   that is now truncated. One red row, two grey ones. What tells the truncated key
                   apart from the junk is not its bytes — it is unparseable either way — but the
                   `.versions` directory still beside it, which is both the proof Field wrote it and
                   the thing you now want.
    3. kf_orphaned_slots — the disagreement that was silent in one direction only. Three keys saved
                   back when the pass had a `blur`; the scope today watches `radius` and a `feather`
                   nothing has ever saved. `glow@feather` gets the amber "never saved" row the browser
                   already had; `glow@blur` is saved in all three keys, renders with its real range,
                   and applies to nowhere — so it is now struck through and named in the header. Also
                   shows why `scopeAttached` is a flag of its own: a read-only browse and a scope
                   watching nothing both leave `scopeSlots` empty and must not read the same.

  This transcript is what built `dev_docs/agents/demos/keyframe_key_discovery/metadata.edn`;
  re-running it rebuilds that document. Companion tests: afield.animation.keyframes.KeyframeBrowserTest and
  afield.app.server.KeyframeBrowserProtocolTest.
operations:
  - create:
      box: kf_before_after
      name: 1 - Six keys, and the pattern that showed two
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 600.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Six saved keys, and whether the browser can show them to you.

          The names are not invented. They are copied from a live session: `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, `d2`, `d3`,
          saved with `kfs.capture().save("d3".path)` — which writes a file called `d3`, with no extension,
          because `saveKey` writes the path it is handed and appends nothing.

          Run this box. Two browsers appear. The top one is what you used to get.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          // A temp directory, so this demo writes nothing into your document.
          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-key-discovery")

          // A live scope, so both browsers get Apply and the "you have never saved this" row.
          val glow = Structure()
          glow.bind("radius") { 4.0f }
          glow.bind("intensity") { 0.35f }
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()
          kfs.target("glow@radius", glow)
          kfs.target("glow@intensity", glow)

          // Six keys, saved the ordinary way — through the real writer, so each gets a real `.versions`
          // history beside it.
          listOf(1f, 3f, 6f, 10f, 15f, 21f).forEachIndexed { i, r ->
              val name = listOf("a", "b", "c", "d", "d2", "d3")[i]
              glow.bind("radius") { r }
              glow.bind("intensity") { 0.1f + i * 0.15f }
              kfs.capture().save(dir.resolve(name), "look $name")
          }

          // And the file macOS leaves in any folder a Finder window has opened. Nobody asked for it.
          Files.writeString(dir.resolve(".DS_Store"), "Bud1 (this is not a key)")

          /*
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          The numbers, before the pictures.
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          */

          val old = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "**/*.json")
          val narrow = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "??")
          val now = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob)

          println(
              "keys on disk: " + dir.toFile().list()!!.filter { !it.endsWith(".versions") && !it.startsWith(".") }.sorted(),
          )
          println("plus, uninvited: " + dir.toFile().list()!!.filter { it.startsWith(".") }.sorted())
          println()
          println("the old default, '**/*.json':  ${old.files.size} keys  <- 'No key files matched'")
          println("the last pattern tried, '??':  ${narrow.files.size} keys  (${narrow.skipSummary()})")
          println(
              "brace alternation, '{?,??}':   ${KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "{?,??}").files.size} keys" +
                  "  <- this always worked, and nothing said so",
          )
          println("the default now, '$everyKeyGlob':          ${now.files.size} keys  (${now.skipSummary()})")
          println()
          println("what '??' hid: " + narrow.skipped.filter { it.kind.name == "Hidden" }.map { it.relative })
          println("problems, either way: ${now.problems.size}  <- .DS_Store is ignored, not an error")

          /*
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          The two browsers. Compare the headers.
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          */

          // BEFORE: the pattern the session ended on. Two keys of six, and — this is the fix — a line under
          // the header saying so, with a button that widens it in one click.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, pattern = "??", channel = "before: pattern = \"??\"", scope = kfs, height = 320)

          // AFTER: the default. Every key at any depth, with the OS turd counted as ignored rather than
          // reported as a problem.

// Three keys saved back when the pass had a `blur` as well as a `radius`.
run {
    val old = Structure()
    val past = KeyframeScope()
    past.target("glow@radius", old)
    past.target("glow@blur", old)
    [1f to 4f, 6f to 5f, 11f to 6f].forEachIndexed { i, (r, b) ->
        old.bind("radius") { r }
        old.bind("blur") { b }
        past.capture().save(dir.resolve(["a", "b", "c"][i]), "look ${listOf("a", "b", "c")[i]}")
    }
}

// The pass as it is today: `blur` is gone, and a `feather` has arrived that nothing has ever saved.
val glow = Structure()
glow.bind("radius") { 7f }
glow.bind("feather") { 0.5f }
val kfs = KeyframeScope()
kfs.target("glow@radius", glow)
kfs.target("glow@feather", glow)

val c = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, kfs)

println("slots in view:      " + c.slotNames)
println("watched by the scope: " + c.scopeSlots.sorted())
println("saved, and wired to nothing: " + c.orphanedSlots + "   <- Apply drops these")
println()
c.slots().forEach { s ->
    val tag = when {
        s.orphaned -> "ORPHANED  (saved in ${s.presentIn}/${s.total} keys, applies to nowhere)"
        s.inScope && s.presentIn == 0 -> "never saved (the scope watches it, no key holds it)"
        else -> "live"
    }
    println("  ${s.name.padEnd(14)} ${tag}")
}
println()
/*
The flag is not just "scopeSlots is empty". A read-only browse cannot know which slots are live,
and must not accuse every row; an attached scope watching nothing must accuse every row. Both
leave scopeSlots empty, so `scopeAttached` is what tells them apart.
*/
val readOnly = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, scope = null)
println("read-only browse: scopeAttached=${readOnly.scopeAttached}, orphaned=${readOnly.orphanedSlots}")
println("  (no scope, so no accusation — this is why scopeAttached exists as its own flag)")

// `glow@blur` is struck through and named in the header; `glow@radius` is plain; `glow@feather` is
// the amber "never saved" row this browser already had.
keyframeBrowser(dir, channel = "saved, but wired to nothing", scope = kfs, height = 400)

name: logging_layer
description: >
  The log layer — channels, sinks, and the three different rules that select on a channel.
  Six boxes, one per thing on `public/docs/logging.md`, and every one of them reads the real
  objects a running Field is using rather than a description of them: `LogDispatcher`'s live
  sink list, `ConsoleMute`'s actual mute set, and `LogStream`'s actual subscription filter.

  The point of running these rather than reading them is box 3. `ConsoleMute.isMuted` compares
  the whole channel string, the pinned console splits on commas and compares a tag, and
  `LogStream`'s filter takes any case-insensitive substring — so one word selects three
  different sets of lines, and box 3 makes a real subscriber prove it.

  This transcript is what built `dev_docs/agents/demos/logging_layer/metadata.edn`; re-running
  it rebuilds that document.
operations:
  - create:
      box: log_channels
      name: 1 - A channel, and a sink of your own
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 557.6, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogDispatcher
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogEvent
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogSink
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.withSink
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.lprintln

          /*
          A channel is a comma-separated list of tags. Not a level, not a logger name, and
          not a hierarchy — "error,mypage,disk" is three flat tags.

          A LogSink is a fun interface with one method, so a lambda is a sink. This one keeps
          only my own lines: the dispatcher is global, and a live Field is logging its own
          frame rate the whole time this box runs.
          */
          val seen = mutableListOf<LogEvent>()
          val probe = LogSink { e -> if ("mypage" in e.channel) seen += e }

          /*
          withSink attaches and detaches around the block, on any exit. That is not a
          convenience: the sink list outlives your box, and LogDispatcher.log wraps every sink
          in runCatching — so a sink leaked by an early return throws silently, forever.
          */
          LogDispatcher.withSink(probe) {
              lprintln("info,mypage", "a plain line")
              lprintln("warning,mypage", "something to look at")
              lprintln("error,mypage,disk", "three tags, and no hierarchy among them")
          }

          display(
              "main",
              Table(listOf("channel", "tags", "message"), title = "what one sink saw")
                  .rows(seen.map { listOf(it.channel, it.channel.split(",").size, it.message) })
                  .role("channel", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: log_mute
      name: 2 - Muting compares the whole string
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 60.0, w: 545.9, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.ConsoleMute

          /*
          The first of the three matchers, and the strictest: isMuted is

              fun isMuted(channel: String): Boolean = channel in channels

          Exact membership of a set of whole channel strings. Nothing is split, so you cannot
          mute a *tag* — only the exact spelling written at the call site.
          */
          val spellings = listOf("info,boxes", "boxes,info", "info,boxes,extra", "info,Boxes", "boxes")

          display(
              "main",
              Table(
                      listOf("channel string", "isMuted"),
                      title = "ConsoleMute compares the whole channel string",
                      note = "the set this JVM booted with: " + ConsoleMute.channels.sorted().joinToString(", "),
                  )
                  .rows(spellings.map { listOf(it, ConsoleMute.isMuted(it)) })
                  .role("channel string", CellRole.ACCENT)
                  .roleBy("isMuted") { if (it == true) CellRole.WARN else CellRole.OK },
          )

          // Change the set with -Dafield.log.mute=a;b or AFIELD_LOG_MUTE=a;b (semicolon
          // separated, exact strings), or a blank value to mute nothing.
  - create:
      box: log_filter
      name: 3 - The log widget takes any substring
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 226.0, w: 569.3, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.lprintln

          /*
          The third matcher, and the loosest. LogStream is the sink behind the log widget, and
          its filter asks channel.contains(tag, ignoreCase = true) — a substring, not a tag.

          This is a real subscription against the real archive. sinceEpochMs keeps the
          existing 20,000-record ring out of the replay, so what arrives is only what I emit.
          */

                  sinceEpochMs = System.currentTimeMillis(),
                  limit = 50,
                  tail = true,
              ),
          ) { json ->

          }

          try {
              emitted.forEach { lprintln(it, "«logdemo» a line on $it") }
          } finally {
              LogStream.unsubscribe("logdemo-substring")
          }

          val matched =
              pushed.filter { "«logdemo»" in it }.map { it.substringAfter("\"channel\":\"").substringBefore("\"") }.toSet()

          /*
          info,kotlinjs matches because "kotlin" is a prefix of "kotlinjs". The pinned console,
          which splits on commas, would not pin it. Same word, two different answers — and 108
          pairs of a real tag and a real channel in this tree differ the same way.
          */
          display(
              "main",
              Table(
                      listOf("channel emitted", "pushed to the subscriber"),
                      title = "a LogStream filter of [\"kotlin\"] against three channels",
                      note =
                          "${matched.size} of ${emitted.size} matched: kotlin is a tag in the first and only a " +
                              "substring in the second. The pinned console splits on commas, so it would take only the first.",
                  )
                  .rows(emitted.map { listOf(it, it in matched) })
                  .role("channel emitted", CellRole.ACCENT)
                  .roleBy("pushed to the subscriber") { if (it == true) CellRole.OK else CellRole.DIM },
          )
  - create:
      box: log_mute_is_console_only
      name: 4 - Muting is a console policy, not a filter
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 226.0, w: 600.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.ConsoleMute
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogDispatcher
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogSink
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.withSink
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.lprintln

          /*
          Muting does not drop the event. Both console sinks check the mute set and return
          early; no other sink checks it at all. So a muted line is still in the log widget,
          still in the archive, and still delivered to a sink of yours.
          */
          val arrived = mutableSetOf<String>()
          val probe = LogSink { e -> if ("«logdemo»" in e.message) arrived += e.channel }

          val channels = listOf("info,boxes", "info,mypage") // the first is muted by default
          LogDispatcher.withSink(probe) {

                      note =
                          "${arrived.size} of ${channels.size} arrived. Mute is for a channel too chatty " +
                              "for a terminal, not for one you want gone.",
                  )
                  .rows(channels.map { listOf(it, ConsoleMute.isMuted(it), it in arrived) })
                  .role("channel", CellRole.ACCENT)
                  .roleBy("muted on the console") { if (it == true) CellRole.WARN else CellRole.DIM }
                  .roleBy("reached my sink") { if (it == true) CellRole.OK else CellRole.BAD },
          )
  - create:
      box: log_blocks
      name: 5 - Blocks, and what the indent holds
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 392.0, w: 557.6, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogDispatcher
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogEvent
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.LogSink
          import afield.ai.diagnostics.withSink
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.lblock
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.lprintln

          // lblock brackets a scope with a BEGIN and an END event sharing a blockId, so a
          // consumer can fold what is between them.
          val all = mutableListOf<LogEvent>()
          val probe = LogSink { e -> all += e }

          LogDispatcher.withSink(probe) {
              lblock("info,logdemo", "«logdemo» outer") {
                  lprintln("info,logdemo", "«logdemo» inside outer")
                  lblock("info,logdemo", "«logdemo» inner") {
                      lprintln("info,logdemo", "«logdemo» inside inner")
                  }
              }
          }

          // An END event's message is only its own id, so it is picked up by blockId rather
          // than by text.
          val mineIds = all.filter { "«logdemo»" in it.message }.mapNotNull { it.blockId }.toSet()
          val mine = all.filter { "«logdemo»" in it.message || it.blockId in mineIds }
          val deepest = mine.filter { it.boundary == null }.maxByOrNull { it.indent.length }

          /*
          The table's footnote prints the deepest line's raw indent. The nesting lives in a
          thread-local `indent` string, and what it holds is not spaces: it is one block UUID
          and a tab per level. PinnedConsole parses those tokens back out to find the open
          block. StdoutLog does not — it concatenates the indent into the line, so on a plain
          terminal a line inside an lblock is prefixed by a raw 36-character UUID.
          */
          display(
              "main",
              Table(
                      listOf("depth", "boundary", "block", "message"),
                      title = "two nested lblocks, as the dispatcher saw them",
                      note =
                          "the deepest line's raw indent: '" +
                              (deepest?.indent?.replace("\t", "\\t") ?: "") +
                              "' — block ids and tabs, not spaces",
                  )
                  .rows(
                      mine.map { e ->
                          listOf(
                              e.indent.split("\t").count { it.isNotEmpty() },
                              e.boundary?.name ?: "—",
                              e.blockId?.take(8) ?: "—",
                              e.message.substringBefore(" - '"),
                          )
                      },
                  )
                  .role("message", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: log_stats
      name: 6 - Stat lines and the heatmap
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 392.0, w: 475.6, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.StatsHeatmap
          import afield.app.diagnostics.logging.formatMillis

          /*
          A channel that reports a number every frame gets coloured by whether each value rose
          or fell since that channel last reported the same key. The contract is only a string
          format: key=value or key: value, optionally with a unit.

          formatMillis emits a unit that matches that grammar, which is why a slow compile
          reads compile=1.63s rather than compile=1629ms.
          */
          val durations = listOf(120_000L, 3_400_000L, 47_000_000L, 250_000_000L, 1_630_000_000L, 12_400_000_000L)
          val ladder =
              Table(
                      listOf("nanoseconds", "formatted"),
                      title = "formatMillis keeps digits where they matter",
                      note = "more digits below a millisecond, plain integers past 100ms, decimal seconds past a second",
                  )
                  .rows(durations.map { listOf(it, formatMillis(it)) })
                  .role("formatted", CellRole.ACCENT)

          val line = "fps=61.2 upload=3.4MB net:102% dropped=0"
          val torn =
              Table(
                      listOf("fragment", "treated as"),
                      title = "how a stats line is torn into colourable tokens",
                      note =
                          "history is kept per channel and per key, so two unrelated metrics sharing one " +
                              "channel do not colour each other",
                  )
                  .rows(
                      StatsHeatmap.fragments("logdemo", line).map {
                          listOf("'${it.text}'", if (it.style == null) "plain text" else "number")
                      },
                  )
                  .roleBy("treated as") { if (it == "number") CellRole.ACCENT else CellRole.DIM }

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ${ladder.h}

              ${torn.h}
          """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - launch: { box: log_channels, property: code }
  - launch: { box: log_mute, property: code }
  - launch: { box: log_filter, property: code }
  - launch: { box: log_mute_is_console_only, property: code }
  - launch: { box: log_blocks, property: code }
  - launch: { box: log_stats, property: code }
  - await: { wait: pending }

before:
name: path_tracing_medium_build
description: |
  Builds the loadable participating-medium document. Two boxes: a renderer, and a slatted
  strip light over a hazed room, which cycles `mediumDensity` through four values every 192
  samples so the same geometry is drawn clear, thin, and thick, over and over.

  This transcript is what built `dev_docs/agents/demos/path_tracing_medium/metadata.edn`;
  re-running it rebuilds that document. It only creates and connects the boxes -- it does not
  launch them, so no window opens while the document is being written.
operations:
  - create:
      box: pt_renderer
      name: path tracing renderer
      frame: { x: 40.0, y: 40.0, w: 320.0, h: 110.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Options

          prop<Window>(window)
          prop<Renderer>(renderer)
          Options.enableHDR = false
          once.renderer {
              window = Window("Field · participating medium")
              Renderer(window)
          }
          start(renderer::run)
  - create:
      box: pt_medium
      name: shafts of light through haze
      frame: { x: 320.0, y: 180.0, w: 400.0, h: 140.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.scene.fabricated.PathTraceEnvironment
          import afield.graphics.scene.fabricated.PathTraceMaterial
          import afield.graphics.scene.fabricated.PathTraceScene
          import afield.graphics.scene.fabricated.PathTracingRenderer
          import afield.graphics.vulkan.util.Camera

          prop<PathTracingRenderer>(tracer)

          /*
          A bright strip light with four slats under it, and nothing else lit. Everything is
          extruded along z and the camera looks down z, so the light's fan is seen in
          cross-section: shafts, and shadows between them.
          */
          val scene = PathTraceScene().apply {
              val floor = material(PathTraceMaterial.diffuse(0.32f, 0.30f, 0.27f))
              val wall = material(PathTraceMaterial.diffuse(0.16f, 0.17f, 0.21f))
              val slat = material(PathTraceMaterial.diffuse(0.10f, 0.09f, 0.08f))
              val lamp = material(PathTraceMaterial.emissive(340f, 300f, 230f))
              val ball = material(PathTraceMaterial.plastic(0.78f, 0.76f, 0.72f, 0.30f))
              quad(Vector3f(-6f, 0f, -4f), Vector3f(-6f, 0f, 4f), Vector3f(6f, 0f, 4f), Vector3f(6f, 0f, -4f), floor)
              quad(Vector3f(-6f, 0f, -4f), Vector3f(-6f, 5.4f, -4f), Vector3f(6f, 5.4f, -4f), Vector3f(6f, 0f, -4f), wall)
              quad(
                  Vector3f(-0.16f, 4.9f, -3.6f),
                  Vector3f(0.16f, 4.9f, -3.6f),
                  Vector3f(0.16f, 4.9f, 3.6f),
                  Vector3f(-0.16f, 4.9f, 3.6f),
                  lamp,
              )
              for (x in listOf(-1.75f, -0.62f, 0.62f, 1.75f)) {
                  quad(
                      Vector3f(x - 0.26f, 3.5f, -3.6f),
                      Vector3f(x + 0.26f, 3.5f, -3.6f),
                      Vector3f(x + 0.26f, 3.5f, 3.6f),
                      Vector3f(x - 0.26f, 3.5f, 3.6f),
                      slat,
                  )
              }
              sphere(Vector3f(1.5f, 0.85f, 0.6f), 0.85f, ball, 40, 20)
          }
          val camera = Camera(renderer).also {
              it.at.set(0.15f, 2.35f, 9.2f)
              it.target.set(0.15f, 2.25f, 0f)
              it.p.fov = 0.82
          }
          tracer = PathTracingRenderer(
              renderer,
              scene,
              PathTraceEnvironment.constant(0f),
              800,
              500,
              camera,
              name = "medium-demo",
          )
          tracer.maxBounces = 8
          tracer.samplesPerFrame = 2
          tracer.showEnvironment = false
          tracer.background = Vector4f(0f, 0f, 0f, 1f)
          tracer.exposure = 0.22f

          /*
          ---- the medium. Bounds matter: an unbounded medium has zero transmittance to
          ---- infinity, which would make an environment map unreachable. Here the box is
          ---- the room, so rays leaving it are simply out of the haze.
          */
          tracer.mediumBounds = Vector3f(-6f, 0f, -3.9f) to Vector3f(6f, 5.2f, 3.9f)
          tracer.mediumAlbedo = Vector3f(0.96f, 0.95f, 0.93f)
          tracer.mediumAnisotropy = 0.4f
          tracer.mediumDensity = 0.16f

          tracer.install()
          tracer.blitToScreen()
          println(
              "${tracer.emitterCount} emissive triangles of ${tracer.triangleCount}; " +
                  "the medium is ${tracer.mediumDensity} per world unit, albedo ${tracer.mediumAlbedo}, " +
                  "g ${tracer.mediumAnisotropy}",
          )

          /*
          ---- MOVE THIS ONE PARAMETER: mediumDensity. -----------------------------------
          The loop cycles it every 192 samples and prints the value. At 0.0 you get the room
          with hard-edged pools of light on the floor and nothing in the air. As it rises the
          shafts between the slats appear, the lamp gains a halo, and the far wall goes soft.
          Past about 0.35 the haze starts to swallow the geometry -- and because every collision
          spends one of maxBounces, the image also darkens there unless you raise it.

          Try mediumAnisotropy next: 0.8 pulls the glow into a tight forward halo around the
          lamp, -0.8 throws it back toward the camera and flattens the shafts.
          Comment out the frames block to hold one setting.
          */
          frames {
              while (true) {
                  for (density in listOf(0.0f, 0.08f, 0.16f, 0.40f)) {
                      tracer.mediumDensity = density
                      println("mediumDensity = $density")
                      // Changing it resets accumulation, but not until the next frame is recorded,
                      // so wait for the old budget to fall away before waiting for the new one.
                      while (tracer.samples >= 192) frame()
                      while (tracer.samples < 192) frame()
                  }
              }
          }
  - connect: { parent: pt_renderer, child: pt_medium }
  # Persist the assembled boxes as the loadable document. `save` takes the document
  # DIRECTORY, not the metadata.edn inside it.
  - save: { path: dev_docs/agents/demos/path_tracing_medium }

name: pattern_condense
description: >
  The shortest way to write a rhythm down. Three boxes: four rhythms drawn against their own
  condensations, a live check that the search invents no structure that is not there, and the
  loop closed from audio — samples in, a named figure out.

  `patCondense` searches Field's own mini-notation for the shortest string that plays the
  rhythm it is given, and it accepts a candidate only by playing it: every one goes back
  through `pat(...)` and its events are compared to the target's. That is why box 1 draws
  pairs rather than printing strings — the lower lane of a pair IS the string in its label,
  rendered, so a search that is wrong shows up as two lanes that do not coincide.

  Every box puts each output on its own channel. That is not decoration: boxes 1 and 3
  originally wrote the roll and then the table both to `main`, and the second silently
  overwrote the first, so the figure — the whole point — was never visible. Two writes to one
  channel is not an error, which is why nothing caught it and opening the document did.

  This transcript is what built `dev_docs/agents/demos/pattern_condense/metadata.edn`;
  re-running it rebuilds that document. See `dev_docs/PAT_CONDENSE.md` and the section on
  `public/docs/pattern_language.md`.
operations:
  - create:
      box: condense_basics
      name: 1 - Condense a rhythm
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 400.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          1 - Condense a rhythm.

          patCondense searches Field's own mini-notation for the shortest string that plays the
          rhythm you hand it, and it accepts a candidate only by playing it: every one goes back
          through pat(...) and its events are compared to the target's. So the lower lane of each
          pair below IS the string in its label, rendered. If a pair does not coincide, the search
          is wrong, and that is a thing to see rather than a thing to be told.

          POKE THIS: change a line in `rhythms`, or add one. A mask you invent comes back either as
          a named figure - x(p,s) for Euclidean, x(kN) / x(gN) for Kolakoski - or spelled out, and
          which one you get is decided by character count and nothing else.
          */
          val rhythms = listOf(
              "x ~ ~ x ~ x ~ ~",
              "x ~ ~ x x ~ x ~ ~ x ~ ~ x x ~ x",
              "bd [hh hh] sd [cp cp]",
              "a b c d e c a d",
          )

          val found = showPatCondense(*rhythms.toTypedArray(), channel = "roll")

          val rows =
              rhythms.zip(found).joinToString("\n") { (source, c) ->
                  "| `$source` | `${c.notation}` | ${c.notation.length}/${c.flat.length} | " +
                      "${"%.2f".format(c.compression)} | ${c.structure.joinToString(", ")} |"
              }

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ### ${found.count { it.exact }} of ${found.size} condensed exactly

              | given | shortest string that plays it | chars | ratio | structure |
              |---|---|---|---|---|
              $rows

              The last row is why the other three mean anything. `a b c d e c a d` has no repeat at any
              split the grammar can take, so nothing shortens it and it comes back as itself. A search
              scored on description length has to be shown *not* naming a figure as well as naming one.

              Bounds this run used: ${found.first().limits}

              The figure is on the **roll** channel beside this one. These rhythms are abstract — `x`,
              `bd`, `a` — so there is nothing to play here; box 3 is the one you can listen to.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - create:
      box: condense_invents_nothing
      name: 2 - Invent nothing
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 500.0, w: 400.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import kotlin.random.Random

          /*
          2 - Invent nothing.

          The failure mode of a description-length search is naming a figure that is one step away
          from the rhythm in front of it. This box runs that check live, on masks with no structure
          put into them.

          POKE THIS: change `seed`, or `density` (one step in N is on), or `trials`. The count of
          wrong namings has to stay 0 whatever you set, because every mask that came back as a
          whole-span figure is recomputed here from bjorklund / kolakoskiMask and compared.
          */
          val seed = 20260910
          val density = 3
          val trials = 300

          require(density > 0) { "density must be positive (one step in N is on)" }
          require(trials > 0) { "trials must be positive to compare compression" }

          val random = Random(seed)
          val euclidean = Regex("""^x\((\d+),(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")
          val kolakoskian = Regex("""^x\(([kg])(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")

          var named = 0
          var wrong = 0
          val ratios = mutableListOf<Double>()

          repeat(trials) {
              val mask = List(16) { random.nextInt(density) == 0 }
              val condensed = patCondense(mask)
              ratios += condensed.compression
              euclidean.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
                  named++
                  val pulses = m.groupValues[1].toInt()
                  val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
                  val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
                  val figure = List(steps) { i -> bjorklund(pulses, steps)[((i + offset) % steps + steps) % steps] }
                  if (figure != mask) wrong++
              }
              kolakoskian.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
                  named++
                  val reading = if (m.groupValues[1] == "k") KolakoskiReading.RUNS else KolakoskiReading.GAPS
                  val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
                  val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
                  if (kolakoskiMask(steps, reading, rotation = -offset) != mask) wrong++
              }
          }

          val median = ratios.sorted()[ratios.size / 2]
          val structured = patCondense(kolakoskiMask(16)).compression

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ### $trials random 16-step masks, seed $seed, one step in $density on

              | | |
              |---|---|
              | read as a single whole-span figure | **$named** |
              | of those, wrong | **$wrong** |
              | median compression | ${"%.3f".format(median)} |
              | the same number for `kolakoskiMask(16)` | ${"%.3f".format(structured)} |

              Noise compresses about ${"%.1f".format(median / structured)} times worse than the figure
              it is up against. That separation is the claim. If random masks compressed as well as
              structured ones, the search would be finding figures in nothing.

              None of this rests on the search's own opinion of itself: every string it returned was
              re-parsed and re-played before it was accepted, and the namings above are recomputed from
              the generators rather than read off the label.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - create:
      box: condense_from_audio
      name: 3 - Close the loop
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 940.0, w: 400.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          3 - Close the loop: samples in, structure out.

          patTranscribe recovers a step grid from audio and writes it out one slot per step, which
          is as far as listening alone can go. patCondense takes that string and returns the figure.
          So this box renders a bar to samples, throws the pattern away, listens to the samples, and
          gets the structure back.

          POKE THIS: change `bar`. Anything on an eight-step grid at MIDI 60 will be heard. Try
          "60 ~ ~ 60 60 ~ 60 ~", which comes back as 60(k8), or "60 60 ~ 60 ~ ~ 60 ~", which has no
          single figure and comes back as two halves.
          */
          val bar = "60 ~ ~ 60 ~ 60 ~ ~"

          val audio = patRenderStereo(
              pat(bar),
              cycles = 1,
              cps = 0.5,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.06, sustain = 0.6),
          )
          val heard = patTranscribe(audio.mono, PatSoundDocs.SR, minHz = 180.0, maxHz = 420.0)
          val condensed = patCondense(heard)

          showPatRollOf(
              "played" to pat(bar),
              "heard" to pat(heard.miniNotation),
              "condensed: ${condensed.notation}" to pat(condensed.notation),
              title = "audio in, structure out",
              subtitle = "${audio.mono.size} samples at ${PatSoundDocs.SR} Hz, and no knowledge of what made them",
              cycles = 1,
              channel = "roll",
          )

          /*
          The two players are the claim you can hear. The first is the EXACT buffer patTranscribe was
          given - not a re-render of `bar`, the same floats - so what you hear is what was listened to.
          The second is `condensed.notation` sent back through the same voice. If patCondense is right
          they are the same bar, and the point of a shortest notation is that shortening it cost nothing.
          */
          display(
              "played",
              afield.audio.engine.WavFloatArrayWriter.encodeStereo16(
                  audio.left,
                  audio.right,
                  PatSoundDocs.SR,
                  normalizePeak = 0.9f,
              ),
          )
          showPatAudio(
              pat(condensed.notation),
              cycles = 1,
              cps = 0.5,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.06, sustain = 0.6),
              channel = "condensed",
          )

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ### From samples to a figure

              | | |
              |---|---|
              | played | `$bar` |
              | rendered | ${audio.mono.size} samples, ${"%.2f".format(audio.mono.size.toDouble() / PatSoundDocs.SR)} s |
              | grid recovered | ${heard.grid?.describe() ?: "none"} |
              | heard | `${heard.miniNotation}` |
              | **condensed** | **`${condensed.notation}`** |

              The `heard` row is everything `patTranscribe` can say on its own. The last row is the same
              bar after `patCondense(heard)`, and it names the figure. Nothing between the render and the
              transcription looked at `bar`.

              Four outputs, each on its own channel: **roll** draws the three lanes, **played** is the
              buffer that was actually transcribed, **condensed** is `${condensed.notation}` rendered
              back through the same voice, and this table is **main**. The two players should be the
              same bar — that is the claim, and it is the one part of this box you can check by ear.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - launch: { box: condense_basics, property: code }
  - launch: { box: condense_invents_nothing, property: code }
  - launch: { box: condense_from_audio, property: code }
  - await: { wait: pending }

              rhythms.zip(found).joinToString("\n") { (source, c) ->
                  "| `$source` | `${c.notation}` | ${c.notation.length}/${c.flat.length} | " +
                      "${"%.2f".format(c.compression)} | ${c.structure.joinToString(", ")} |"
              }

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ### ${found.count { it.exact }} of ${found.size} condensed exactly

              | given | shortest string that plays it | chars | ratio | structure |
              |---|---|---|---|---|
              $rows

              The last row is why the other three mean anything. `a b c d e c a d` has no repeat at any
              split the grammar can take, so nothing shortens it and it comes back as itself. A search
              scored on description length has to be shown *not* naming a figure as well as naming one.

              Bounds this run used: ${found.first().limits}

              The figure is on the **roll** channel beside this one. These rhythms are abstract — `x`,
              `bd`, `a` — so there is nothing to play here; box 3 is the one you can listen to.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - create:
      box: condense_invents_nothing
      name: 2 - Invent nothing
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 500.0, w: 400.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import kotlin.random.Random

          /*
          2 - Invent nothing.

          The failure mode of a description-length search is naming a figure that is one step away
          from the rhythm in front of it. This box runs that check live, on masks with no structure
          put into them.

          POKE THIS: change `seed`, or `density` (one step in N is on), or `trials`. The count of
          wrong namings has to stay 0 whatever you set, because every mask that came back as a
          whole-span figure is recomputed here from bjorklund / kolakoskiMask and compared.
          */
          val seed = 20260910
          val density = 3
          val trials = 300

          require(density > 0) { "density must be positive (one step in N is on)" }
          require(trials > 0) { "trials must be positive to compare compression" }

          val random = Random(seed)
          val euclidean = Regex("""^x\((\d+),(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")
          val kolakoskian = Regex("""^x\(([kg])(\d+)(?:,(\d+))?\)$""")

          var named = 0
          var wrong = 0
          val ratios = mutableListOf<Double>()

          repeat(trials) {
              val mask = List(16) { random.nextInt(density) == 0 }
              val condensed = patCondense(mask)
              ratios += condensed.compression
              euclidean.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
                  named++
                  val pulses = m.groupValues[1].toInt()
                  val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
                  val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
                  val figure = List(steps) { i -> bjorklund(pulses, steps)[((i + offset) % steps + steps) % steps] }
                  if (figure != mask) wrong++
              }
              kolakoskian.matchEntire(condensed.notation)?.let { m ->
                  named++
                  val reading = if (m.groupValues[1] == "k") KolakoskiReading.RUNS else KolakoskiReading.GAPS
                  val steps = m.groupValues[2].toInt()
                  val offset = m.groupValues[3].ifEmpty { "0" }.toInt()
                  if (kolakoskiMask(steps, reading, rotation = -offset) != mask) wrong++
              }
          }

          val median = ratios.sorted()[ratios.size / 2]
          val structured = patCondense(kolakoskiMask(16)).compression
