              "main",
              """
              ### $trials random 16-step masks, seed $seed, one step in $density on

              | | |
              |---|---|
              | read as a single whole-span figure | **$named** |
              | of those, wrong | **$wrong** |
              | median compression | ${"%.3f".format(median)} |
              | the same number for `kolakoskiMask(16)` | ${"%.3f".format(structured)} |

              Noise compresses about ${"%.1f".format(median / structured)} times worse than the figure
              it is up against. That separation is the claim. If random masks compressed as well as
              structured ones, the search would be finding figures in nothing.

              None of this rests on the search's own opinion of itself: every string it returned was
              re-parsed and re-played before it was accepted, and the namings above are recomputed from
              the generators rather than read off the label.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - create:
      box: condense_from_audio
      name: 3 - Close the loop
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 940.0, w: 400.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          3 - Close the loop: samples in, structure out.

          patTranscribe recovers a step grid from audio and writes it out one slot per step, which
          is as far as listening alone can go. patCondense takes that string and returns the figure.
          So this box renders a bar to samples, throws the pattern away, listens to the samples, and
          gets the structure back.

          POKE THIS: change `bar`. Anything on an eight-step grid at MIDI 60 will be heard. Try
          "60 ~ ~ 60 60 ~ 60 ~", which comes back as 60(k8), or "60 60 ~ 60 ~ ~ 60 ~", which has no
          single figure and comes back as two halves.
          */
          val bar = "60 ~ ~ 60 ~ 60 ~ ~"

          val audio = patRenderStereo(
              pat(bar),
              cycles = 1,
              cps = 0.5,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.06, sustain = 0.6),
          )
          val heard = patTranscribe(audio.mono, PatSoundDocs.SR, minHz = 180.0, maxHz = 420.0)
          val condensed = patCondense(heard)

          showPatRollOf(
              "played" to pat(bar),
              "heard" to pat(heard.miniNotation),
              "condensed: ${condensed.notation}" to pat(condensed.notation),
              title = "audio in, structure out",
              subtitle = "${audio.mono.size} samples at ${PatSoundDocs.SR} Hz, and no knowledge of what made them",
              cycles = 1,
              channel = "roll",
          )

          /*
          The two players are the claim you can hear. The first is the EXACT buffer patTranscribe was
          given - not a re-render of `bar`, the same floats - so what you hear is what was listened to.
          The second is `condensed.notation` sent back through the same voice. If patCondense is right
          they are the same bar, and the point of a shortest notation is that shortening it cost nothing.
          */
          display(
              "played",
              afield.audio.engine.WavFloatArrayWriter.encodeStereo16(
                  audio.left,
                  audio.right,
                  PatSoundDocs.SR,
                  normalizePeak = 0.9f,
              ),
          )
          showPatAudio(
              pat(condensed.notation),
              cycles = 1,
              cps = 0.5,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.06, sustain = 0.6),
              channel = "condensed",
          )

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              ### From samples to a figure

              | | |
              |---|---|
              | played | `$bar` |
              | rendered | ${audio.mono.size} samples, ${"%.2f".format(audio.mono.size.toDouble() / PatSoundDocs.SR)} s |
              | grid recovered | ${heard.grid?.describe() ?: "none"} |
              | heard | `${heard.miniNotation}` |
              | **condensed** | **`${condensed.notation}`** |

              The `heard` row is everything `patTranscribe` can say on its own. The last row is the same
              bar after `patCondense(heard)`, and it names the figure. Nothing between the render and the
              transcription looked at `bar`.

              Four outputs, each on its own channel: **roll** draws the three lanes, **played** is the
              buffer that was actually transcribed, **condensed** is `${condensed.notation}` rendered
              back through the same voice, and this table is **main**. The two players should be the
              same bar — that is the claim, and it is the one part of this box you can check by ear.
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )
  - launch: { box: condense_basics, property: code }
  - launch: { box: condense_invents_nothing, property: code }
  - launch: { box: condense_from_audio, property: code }
  - await: { wait: pending }

import afield.graphics.scene.GltfSkinning.SkinningMethod
import afield.graphics.scene.GltfSkinning.SkinningOptions

/*
Box 5 is the candy wrapper on the CPU. This is the same twist on the GPU, both methods in ONE
draw call: the left cylinder is linear blend skinning and pinches to a point at 180 degrees, the
right one is dual quaternion skinning and keeps its radius. Same mesh, same palette, same shader;
the only difference between them is one word per instance saying which blend to run.

RUN BOX 0 FIRST, and stop box 6 if it is running -- both draw into box 0's window.

EDIT `methods` AND RE-RUN: make both LINEAR_BLEND and both pinch; make both DUAL_QUATERNION and
neither does.
*/
val methods = listOf(SkinningMethod.LINEAR_BLEND, SkinningMethod.DUAL_QUATERNION)

val model = GltfSupport.loadGltfBasic(
    RiggedFixture.locate(),
    GltfSupport.GltfLoadConfig(loadTextures = false),
)
val inst = model.meshes.first { it.skin != null }

val module =
    Module(
            Parameters(
                renderer = renderer,
                vertex = GpuSkinning.skinnedVertexShader,
                fragment = GpuSkinning.skinnedFragmentShader,
                name = "gpu twist, lbs vs dqs",
            ),
        )
        .pointer()

val m = Mesh(renderer, module)
module += "twist" to m
renderer += "gpu twist, lbs vs dqs" to module

val camera = Camera(renderer)
camera.p.orthoness = 0.3
camera.p.matchDepth = 2.0
camera.target = vec(0, 2, 0)
camera.at = vec(0, 2.4, -5.2)
camera.p()

val skinner = GpuSkinner(inst, instances = 2, renderer = renderer, name = "twist")
skinner.bindTo(m, camera, instanceCount = 2, tint = true)

// Seen from this camera +x is on the LEFT, so instance 0 goes to +1.3.
val places = listOf(Matrix4f().translate(vec(1.3, 0, 0)), Matrix4f().translate(vec(-1.3, 0, 0)))
val sk = skinner.skin.skeleton
val twist = sk.clip("twist")!!

// The waist as a number, from the CPU oracles on the same palette: the smallest distance from the
// bone axis of any vertex on the y = 2 ring. Printed so the picture is not the only evidence.
val restRadius = RiggedFixture.RADIUS
fun waist(method: SkinningMethod, palette: List<Matrix4f>): Float {
    val bind = FloatArray(skinner.vertexCount * 3) { skinner.bindPositions[it] }
    val out = GltfSkinning.skin(bind, null, inst.skin!!.influences, palette, SkinningOptions(method = method))
    return DualQuaternionSkinning.candyWrapperRadius(out.position, RiggedFixture.UPPER_JOINT_Y)
}

var n = 0
loop {
    // 0 -> 180 -> 0 degrees of twist, three seconds a cycle at 60 fps, on a loop.
    val seconds = (n / 90f) % twist.durationSeconds
    skinner.uploadPalettes(places.map { skinner.placedPalette(it, "twist", seconds) }, methods)
    skinner.updateCamera(m, camera)
    if (n % 45 == 0) {
        val rest = sk.palette(twist, seconds)
        println(
            "t = %.2f s   waist, %% of rest radius:   %s %.1f%%   |   %s %.1f%%"
                .format(
                    seconds,
                    methods[0],
                    100 * waist(methods[0], rest) / restRadius,
                    methods[1],
                    100 * waist(methods[1], rest) / restRadius,
                ),
        )
    }
    n++
    frame()
}

name: solidsl_inverse
description: >
  `afield.lang.solidsl`'s third reading — a Solid you can differentiate, and therefore solve. Three
  boxes: the gradient itself checked against central differences on the spot, an inverse fit that
  recovers three named parameters from a sampled target and renders all three shapes, and the
  refusals plus the one failure mode of inverse design (a parameter whose gradient is exactly zero,
  which presents as a *converged* optimisation).

  Nothing here needs Manifold, a GPU or a window: marching cubes and the mesh rasteriser are both
  pure Kotlin. This transcript is what built
  `dev_docs/agents/demos/solidsl_inverse/metadata.edn`; re-running it rebuilds that document.
operations:
  - create:
      box: gradient
      name: 1 - A solid, and its exact gradient
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 534.2, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.lang.solidsl.*

          /*
          ---- the shape, written once, as a value ------------------------------------------
          A ball blended onto a rod. Change a number and everything below follows, because a
          SolidExpr is a value rather than a closure — which is the whole of afield.lang.solidsl.
          */
          val part = smoothUnion(sphere(0.45), cylinder(1.90, 0.16).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), k = 0.18)

          // -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          /*
          Every Double in the tree that a parameter could be bound to, at its structural address.
          There are no names inside a SolidExpr — it is an anonymous tree of data classes — so the
          only stable way to point at the rod's radius is to say where it is.
          */
          println("---- what is bindable ----")
          part.numericSlots().forEach { println("  $it") }
          println()
          println("`segments` is absent, and that is a refusal rather than an oversight: it is an")
          println("integer facet count that toScalarField() ignores completely, so there is no")
          println("derivative to take. Try sphere(0.45, segments = 64).numericSlots().")
          println()

          /*
          Promote three of them into named parameters. `barRadius` drives BOTH radii, which is how
          a symmetry constraint is written: "the rod is a cylinder, not a frustum", in the
          parameterisation rather than in a comment.
          */
          val template =
              part
                  .parameterize {
                      param("sphereRadius", "SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius")
                      param("barHeight", "SmoothUnion/b/Translate/Cylinder.height")
                      param("barRadius") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field.startsWith("radius") }
                  }
                  .orThrow()

          println("---- the template ----")
          print(template.report())
          println()

          // The gradient at a point — position AND parameters, from one reverse-mode tape.
          val g = template.gradientAt(0.9, 0.0, 0.0, template.seed)
          println("---- the gradient at (0.9, 0, 0) ----")
          println("  $g")
          println("  the position gradient is the surface normal, unnormalised")
          println("  the parameter gradient says how the distance HERE moves when each number moves")
          println()

          /*
          And the second opinion, computed on the spot rather than remembered. `usableComponents`
          is the oracle declining to have an opinion where a central difference disagrees with
          itself between h and h/2 — at a sphere's own centre, on a polygon's outline, within h of
          any kink. A census that did not count those would pass while checking nothing.
          */
          println("---- analytic vs central differences, right now ----")
          val probes = listOf(
              Triple(0.9, 0.0, 0.0),
              Triple(0.0, 0.0, 1.2),
              Triple(0.31, -0.44, 0.62),
              Triple(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), // the ball's own centre
          )
          probes.forEach { (x, y, z) ->
              val c = template.checkGradient(x, y, z)
              println("  dParam (%5.2f, %5.2f, %5.2f)  %s".format(x, y, z, c))
          }
          println()

          /*
          The same four points, for the POSITION gradient — and the last one is the interesting
          one. At the ball's own centre sqrt(x2+y2+z2) has an infinite derivative, so the analytic
          answer is not a number and the check reports 0/3 usable rather than pretending. The
          PARAMETER gradient at that same point is exact: d/d(radius) = -1 everywhere, including
          there. That asymmetry is why fitting works at all on shapes full of radial primitives.
          */
          probes.forEach { (x, y, z) ->
              val c = template.checkPositionGradient(x, y, z)
              println("  dPos   (%5.2f, %5.2f, %5.2f)  %s".format(x, y, z, c))
          }
          println()

          // The third notes function in this package, beside fieldNotes() and allRefusals(). Every
          // place the derivative is a choice, and what was chosen.
          println("---- where the derivative is a choice ----")
          part.gradientNotes().forEach { println("  - $it") }
  - create:
      box: inverse
      name: 2 - Inverse design - let a gradient find the numbers
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 60.0, w: 600.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.lang.solidsl.*

          // ---- the problem ---------------------------------------------------------------------
          // Somebody hands you a bag of points with a signed distance at each. What shape is it?
          val truth = doubleArrayOf(0.45, 1.90, 0.16) // the answer, used ONLY to make the target
          val seed = doubleArrayOf(0.26, 1.05, 0.34) // where the search starts: wrong by 42%, 45%, 112%
          // -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          val template =
              smoothUnion(sphere(0.45), cylinder(1.90, 0.16).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), k = 0.18)
                  .parameterize {
                      param("sphereRadius", "SmoothUnion/a/Sphere.radius")
                      param("barHeight", "SmoothUnion/b/Translate/Cylinder.height")
                      param("barRadius") { it.node == "Cylinder" && it.field.startsWith("radius") }
                  }
                  .orThrow()

          val target = template.withValues(truth).sampleField(count = 2400, seed = 91)
          println("target: $target")
          println()

          /*
          One tape per evaluation carries all 2400 residuals and all 3 parameters, and one backward
          sweep reads every derivative off it. The alternative — central-differencing the loss —
          costs 2n extra full sweeps per step and needs an fdStep tuned per problem.
          */
          val fit = template.fitParameters(target, seed)
          println(fit.report())
          println()
          println("The counterfactual is in the same object, measured in the same run: `initialLoss`")
          println("is the seed's loss, not a number somebody wrote down last week.")
          println()
          println("truth was  ${truth.joinToString(", ")}")
          println("recovered  ${fit.values.joinToString(", ") { "%.9f".format(it) }}")
          println("error      ${truth.indices.joinToString(", ") { "%.2e".format(kotlin.math.abs(fit.values[it] - truth[it])) }}")
          println()

          // The fitted answer is an ordinary SolidExpr again — not a bag of numbers — so it goes
          // straight back to every other thing this package can do.
          println("fitted     ${fit.fitted}")
          println("GLSL       ${fit.fitted.toGlsl().statementCount} statements")
          println("bounds     ${fit.fitted.bounds()}")
          println()

          // Log scale, because the descent covers twenty orders of magnitude and a linear axis

  boxes: the gradient itself checked against central differences on the spot, an inverse fit that
  recovers three named parameters from a sampled target and renders all three shapes, and the
  refusals plus the one failure mode of inverse design (a parameter whose gradient is exactly zero,
  which presents as a *converged* optimisation).

  Nothing here needs Manifold, a GPU or a window: marching cubes and the mesh rasteriser are both
  pure Kotlin. This transcript is what built
  `dev_docs/agents/demos/solidsl_inverse/metadata.edn`; re-running it rebuilds that document.
operations:
  - create:

          only stable way to point at the rod's radius is to say where it is.

          println("integer facet count that toScalarField() ignores completely, so there is no")
          println("derivative to take. Try sphere(0.45, segments = 64).numericSlots().")

before:
name: alife_evolution
description: >
  Evolution over the ALife rule spaces of public/docs/alife_examples.md, as four pure-CPU boxes on
  ONE shared engine. alife.kt held 816 lines of morphology statistics and until 2026-09-05 not one
  of them had ever been used as a fitness -- `git grep -inE 'fitness|genome|evolve|mutation'` over
  alife*.kt returned nothing. These four boxes are the other half. Box 1 evolves a Lenia rule for a
  soliton (alive, in one piece, travelling), scoring straight off leniaRun's own DEATH/BOUNDED/
  SATURATION classification and wrapped centroid drift. Box 2 runs the same engine over a
  completely different genome -- 49 bits of birth and survival counts at radius 2, with real
  uniform crossover and lexicase selection over two soups. Box 3 illuminates the (density,
  activity) behaviour space with MAP-Elites instead of optimising it, and states the quality claim
  rather than the coverage one, because random sampling spreads over a descriptor space for free.
  Box 4 is the proof the engine is shared: FunctionEvolve.evolve no longer contains a search, its
  body is PopulationSearch.evolve(mu = 1), and the FIELD_TEST functions.evolve.worked-example
  reproduces bestScore = -0.15676727177844857 over 961 evaluations bit for bit across the refactor.
  Every box carries its own control arm -- PopulationSearch.random at the SAME budget under the
  SAME seed -- because a generator good enough to stumble onto a decent rule occasionally looks
  exactly like a successful search. None of the four opens a Window or a Renderer.
operations:
  - create:
      box: evolve_lenia
      name: "1 — Evolution against chance, on a Lenia rule"
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 60.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Field could always MEASURE artificial life. It could not search it.

          alife.kt is 816 lines of morphology statistics -- polarization, blobShapes,
          correlationLength, massRadiusDimension, stateEntropyBits, centroidDrift -- and until now not one
          of them was ever used as a fitness. This box uses one.

          The question: is there a Lenia rule whose seed stays alive, stays in ONE piece, and TRAVELS?
          That is what a soliton is, it is the one thing continuous Lenia is famous for, and every term of
          the score below is read straight off leniaRun, which already classifies a run into
          DEATH / BOUNDED / SATURATION and already reports a wrapped centroid drift.
          */

          val ops = LeniaGenome(radius = 6, dt = 0.1, shells = 3)
          val objective = leniaSolitonObjective(width = 48, height = 48, steps = 90, initialSeed = 5L, driftScale = 8.0)
          val budget = 220

          /*
          PopulationSearch.random is a CONTROL ARM, not a fourth driver. It draws from exactly the
          distribution `evolve` mutates within, at the same budget, under the same seed. Without it a
          result here would say nothing at all: a generator good enough to stumble onto a decent rule
          occasionally looks exactly like a successful search.
          */
          val control = PopulationSearch.random(ops, objective, budget, seed = 13L, label = "random")
          val evolved = PopulationSearch.evolve(
              ops,
              objective,
              budget,
              seed = 13L,
              mu = 6,
              lambda = 12,
              crossoverRate = 0.3,
              immigrantRate = 0.08,
              label = "evolve",
          )

          println(control.summary())
          println(evolved.summary())
          println()
          println(
              "margin %.4f  (%.1f%% above the control)"
                  .format(
                      evolved.bestFitness - control.bestFitness,
                      100.0 * (evolved.bestFitness / control.bestFitness - 1.0),
                  ),
          )
          println()

          val best = evolved.best!!.genome
          val run = leniaRun(leniaSeed(48, 48, best, seed = 5L), best, steps = 90, sampleEvery = 8)
          println("evolved rule: mu=%.4f sigma=%.4f".format(best.mu, best.sigma))
          println("  $run")
          println("  phase is MEASURED, not asserted: leniaRun classifies it from the mean field value.")
          println()
          println("`improvements` carries the genome of every generation whose leader improved. That is a")
          println("chain of RECORD HOLDERS, not a parent-child lineage -- with mu=6 and crossover on, the")
          println("odds that these six are literally descended from one another are near zero.")

          // The lineage, left to right. The control arm's best is the first panel: that is the thing
          // evolution has to beat, in the same picture, at the same budget.
          val panels = mutableListOf<Pair<String, Img>>()
          val cRule = control.best!!.genome
          panels +=
              "rnd %.2f".format(control.bestFitness) to
                  leniaRun(leniaSeed(48, 48, cRule, seed = 5L), cRule, steps = 90, sampleEvery = 8).field.upscaleNearest(3)
          val picks =
              evolved.improvements.indices.toList().let { idx ->
                  if (idx.size <= 5) idx else (1..5).map { (it * idx.size / 5) - 1 }
              }
          for (i in picks) {
              val imp = evolved.improvements[i]
              panels +=
                  "g%d %.2f".format(imp.generation, imp.fitness) to
                      leniaRun(leniaSeed(48, 48, imp.genome, seed = 5L), imp.genome, steps = 90, sampleEvery = 8)
                          .field
                          .upscaleNearest(3)
          }

          /*
          A FIXED 0..1 display range. A saturated Lenia field is constant at 1, and an auto-ranged colour
          map draws a constant field black -- i.e. identical to death. This is the one family where the
          range policy changes the answer rather than tidying it.
          */
          showImg(
              montage(panels, columns = 3, cellSide = 200, displayRange = 0f..1f),
              caption = "left to right: the random control's best, then each successive record holder",
          )
  - create:
      box: evolve_ca
      name: "2 — The same engine, a life-like rule table"
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 210.0
        w: 420.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          The same engine, a completely different genome.

          A life-like rule is a TABLE: which neighbour counts cause a birth, which cause survival. At a
          radius-2 neighbourhood that is 24 birth bits and 25 survival bits, a fixed-length bit string, and
          therefore a genome two parents can be recombined across. Field had exactly one other two-parent
          crossover before this (afield.lang.morpho.MorphoGenerator); LifeRuleGenome.crossover is uniform
          crossover over the rule table and it is real recombination, not a graft.

          Radius 2 rather than the classic Moore 8 is a deliberate choice and it is the most useful thing
          in this box. At radius 1 the space is 2^17 rules, and a few hundred INDEPENDENT draws land close
          to the optimum on their own -- the first version of this demo measured evolution winning by 3%
          for exactly that reason. A control arm that nearly wins is telling you the problem is easy, not
          that the search is good. At radius 2 the space is 2^49 and the margin is 27%.
          */

          val ops = LifeRuleGenome(radius = 2)
          val soups = listOf(
              randomSoup(48, 48, density = 0.35, seed = 101L),
              randomSoup(48, 48, density = 0.12, seed = 202L),
          )

          /*
          "Alive but not saturated, and still changing" -- activity times a Gaussian band on density.
          Each factor alone is trivially gamed. A rule that fills the grid and stays filled scores 1 on
          density and 0 on activity; a rule that flickers every cell scores ~1 on activity and ~0 on the
          band; an extinct rule scores the floor. Only the product is large for a rule that keeps a
          moderate population AND keeps rearranging it, which is what everybody means by an interesting
          rule and what nobody can state by looking.
          */
          val objective = caEdgeOfChaosObjective(soups, warmup = 20, scored = 30)
          val budget = 400

          val control = PopulationSearch.random(ops, objective, budget, seed = 7L, label = "random")

          /*

  soliton (alive, in one piece, travelling), scoring straight off leniaRun's own DEATH/BOUNDED/
  SATURATION classification and wrapped centroid drift. Box 2 runs the same engine over a
  completely different genome -- 49 bits of birth and survival counts at radius 2, with real
  uniform crossover and lexicase selection over two soups. Box 3 illuminates the (density,

  body is PopulationSearch.evolve(mu = 1), and the FIELD_TEST functions.evolve.worked-example
  reproduces bestScore = -0.15676727177844857 over 961 evaluations bit for bit across the refactor.

  SAME seed -- because a generator good enough to stumble onto a decent rule occasionally looks
  exactly like a successful search. None of the four opens a Window or a Renderer.

          Field could always MEASURE artificial life. It could not search it.

          That is what a soliton is, it is the one thing continuous Lenia is famous for, and every term of
          the score below is read straight off leniaRun, which already classifies a run into
          DEATH / BOUNDED / SATURATION and already reports a wrapped centroid drift.
          */

          val ops = LeniaGenome(radius = 6, dt = 0.1, shells = 3)
          val objective = leniaSolitonObjective(width = 48, height = 48, steps = 90, initialSeed = 5L, driftScale = 8.0)

          distribution `evolve` mutates within, at the same budget, under the same seed. Without it a
          result here would say nothing at all: a generator good enough to stumble onto a decent rule
          occasionally looks exactly like a successful search.

              seed = 13L,
              mu = 6,
              lambda = 12,

before:
name: alife_walls
description: |
  **A world with walls.** `afield.simulation.agents`' `alife_walls.kt` gives `alife_script`'s `ScriptWorld` an
  environment. Before it the world was a bare rectangle: the only spatial thing an agent could say was
  `avoidEdges(margin)`, and everything else it could steer around was another agent. Now there are
  obstacles, the collision that stops an agent crossing one is **swept** rather than discrete, and
  `route()` plans a way round rather than pressing into it.

  Three boxes, pure CPU:

    - **A wall, and three answers to hitting it.** Three agents, one barrier, one room, under
      `WallResponse.SLIDE`, `.BOUNCE` (with `restitution`) and `.STOP` — the contact counts and end
      positions print, so the three are compared rather than described.

                  .format(

                  ),
          )
          println(
              "climb  : mean field value %.3f"
                  .format(
                      climbers.map { lamps.at(it.position.x, it.position.y) }.average(),
                  ),
          )
          println(
              "         %d at the lamp at (150, 160), %d at the lamp at (45, 40), %d still travelling"
                  .format(
                      climbers.count { near(it, 150.0, 160.0) },
                      climbers.count { near(it, 45.0, 40.0) },
                      climbers.count { !near(it, 150.0, 160.0) && !near(it, 45.0, 40.0) },

          )

          println("it is standing and knows nothing about the other maximum. The split is the whole point.")

              channel = "arena",
              w = 440.0,
              h = 440.0,
              fitToSize = true,
          )

          // corners of the arena, and the shadow behind the block.
  - execute: { box: hit_a_wall, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: route_vs_seek, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: cling_and_climb, property: code }
  - await: {}

  Box 5 is the workbench's own worked example, rewritten from formula ops bit for bit, with its claims
  certified: every plateau exactly 1 (PROVEN), >= 0 (PROVEN), and <= 1 REFUTED by 4 ulps at 284.99994 s.
  The saved document at `dev_docs/agents/demos/certified_envelope/` is this same scene.
operations:
  - create:
      box: sampled
      name: "1 - An hour, and a glitch the plot never sees"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 40.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          One hour: a slow 40-second swing, plus a glitch 10 ms wide at 1234.57 s — exactly halfway
          between two of the viewer's 0.02 s samples. Built from Functions ops rather than a
          fn { } lambda, so every node has a formula. Box 2 needs that.
          */
          val signal = with(Functions) {
              sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45) + gaussian(1234.57, 0.002, 0.5, Functions.Domain.ALL)
          }

          // The sampled envelope, drawn the way the function workbench draws it: min and max per bin.
          val viewer = SignalViewer(listOf(SignalChannel("x", signal::eval)), 0.0, 3600.0)
          displaySignal(
              viewer,
              "main",
              SignalViewerOptions(label = "sampled envelope only", viewKey = "certified_envelope:sampled"),
          )

          // The same query the plot makes, read back as numbers. Bin 342 holds the glitch.
          val bins = viewer.window(0.0, 3600.0, 1000).lanes[0].current
          val bin = (1234.57 / 3.6).toInt()
          display(
              "numbers",
              Table(listOf("what", "value"), title = "what the sampled plot can see")
                  .row("f(1234.57), the glitch's peak", signal(1234.57))
                  .row("sampled max, bin $bin", bins.high[bin])
                  .row("sampled max, whole hour", bins.high.max())
                  .row("missed by", signal(1234.57) - bins.high[bin])
                  .role("value", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: certified
      name: "2 - The certified band catches it"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 760.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          The same signal as box 1. certifiedSignalChannel draws its sampled envelope in white and,
          behind it in amber, a certified bound per bin: every value the function takes in the bin
          lies inside, whether or not a sample landed on it. Nothing here is sampled more finely.
          */
          val signal = with(Functions) {
              sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45) + gaussian(1234.57, 0.002, 0.5, Functions.Domain.ALL)
          }
          val viewer = SignalViewer(listOf(certifiedSignalChannel("x", signal)), 0.0, 3600.0)
          displaySignal(
              viewer,
              "main",
              SignalViewerOptions(label = "sampled envelope, with its certified band", viewKey = "certified_envelope:certified"),
          )

          // The band, read back: bin 342 is bounded above by the glitch's true height.
          val band = signal.certifiedEnvelope(0.0, 3600.0, 1000)
          val bin = (1234.57 / 3.6).toInt()
          display(
              "numbers",
              Table(listOf("what", "value"), title = "the certified band, as numbers")
                  .row("f(1234.57), the glitch's peak", signal(1234.57))
                  .row("certified max, bin $bin", band.high[bin])
                  .row("certified min, bin $bin", band.low[bin])
                  .row("enclosures for 1000 bins", band.enclosures)
                  .role("value", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: range
      name: "3 - certifiedRange, with witnesses"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1480.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Branch-and-bound over the hour: the true maximum is at least the value reached at the
          // witness, and at most the proven bound. The same for the minimum.
          val signal = with(Functions) {
              sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45) + gaussian(1234.57, 0.002, 0.5, Functions.Domain.ALL)
          }
          val range = signal.certifiedRange(0.0, 3600.0, tolerance = 1e-9)
          val max = range.max!!
          val min = range.min!!
          display(
              "range",
              Table(
                      listOf("side", "reached", "at x", "proven bound", "enclosures"),
                      title = "certifiedRange(0, 3600): certified = ${range.certified}",
                  )
                  .row("max", max.value, max.witness, max.bound, max.enclosures)
                  .row("min", min.value, min.witness, min.bound, min.enclosures)
                  .role("at x", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )

          // Yes/no questions with the same guarantee. A refutation carries the x that breaks the claim.
          val claims = listOf(
              signal.certifiedNeverExceeds(0.7, 0.0, 3600.0),
              signal.certifiedNeverExceeds(0.8, 0.0, 3600.0),
              signal.certifiedReaches(0.75, 0.0, 3600.0),
          )
          display(
              "claims",
              Table(listOf("claim", "verdict", "witness x"))
                  .rows(claims.map { listOf(it.claim, it.kind.name, it.witness) })
                  .roleBy("verdict") { if (it == "PROVEN") CellRole.OK else CellRole.WARN },
          )
  - create:
      box: limits
      name: "4 - What refuses, and an exact hold"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1800.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          What refuses. The function workbench's channels are fn(0.0..3600.0, name) { seconds -> ... }
          lambdas: one opaque node each, so there is nothing for an interval walk to read. It refuses by
          name rather than guess.
          */
          val lambdaChannel = with(Functions) { fn(0.0..3600.0, "x") { t -> 0.45 + 0.2 * kotlin.math.sin(t) } }
          val refused = lambdaChannel.enclose(0.0, 3600.0)

          // The workbench's claim that an event holds exactly 1 for 30 seconds, rebuilt from formula ops:
          // rise 185..285, hold to 315, fall to 415, over the moving background.
          val held = with(Functions) {
              val one = c(1.0, Functions.Domain.ALL)
              val background = sin(1.0 / 40.0, amplitude = 0.2, offset = 0.45)
              val envelope =
                  smoothStep(185.0, 285.0, Functions.Domain.ALL) * (one - smoothStep(315.0, 415.0, Functions.Domain.ALL))
              one - (one - background) * (one - envelope)
          }
          val checks = listOf(
              held.certifiedEquals(1.0, 285.0, 315.0),
              held.certifiedEquals(1.0, 284.0, 315.0),
              held.certifiedNeverExceeds(1.0, 0.0, 3600.0, slack = 1e-12),
          )
          display(
              "limits",
              Table(listOf("question", "answer"), title = "refusals and exact holds")
                  .row("enclose the lambda channel", "certified = ${refused.certified}: ${refused.refusal}")
                  .rows(checks.map { listOf(it.claim, it.kind.name + (it.witness?.let { w -> " at x = $w" } ?: "")) })
                  .role("answer", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - create:
      box: workbench
      name: "5 - The worked example, certified"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 2120.0, w: 340.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          The function workbench's worked example (public/docs/assets/function_conversation/final.kt),
          twice. `lambda` is its channel code, verbatim: one fn { } per channel, which the interval walk
          refuses. `formula` is the same function from formula-bearing ops. The only construct that needed
          a lambda was the piecewise event selection; here it is exact 0/1 `step` indicators, with every
          product and sum in the lambda's order, so the two agree bit for bit.
          */
          val events = listOf(
              StudyEvent("e1", 185.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e2", 785.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e3", 1425.0, 200.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e5", 2585.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
              StudyEvent("e6", 3185.0, 100.0, 30.0, 100.0),
          )
          val names = listOf("x", "y", "z")

          fun smooth01(value: Double): Double {
              val u = value.coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
              return u * u * u * (10.0 + u * (-15.0 + 6.0 * u))
          }
          fun backgroundOf(seconds: Double, channel: Int): Double {
              val drift = 2.0 * PI / 3.0 * kotlin.math.sin(2.0 * PI * seconds / 100.0)
              val phase = 2.0 * PI * seconds / 40.0 + (channel - 1) * drift
              return 0.45 + 0.20 * kotlin.math.sin(phase) + 0.04 * kotlin.math.sin(2.0 * PI * seconds / 230.0)
          }
          fun shoulderOf(base: Double, age: Double, span: Double): Double {
              val u = (age / span).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)
              val cycles = 0.06 * age + 0.5 * (0.80 - 0.06) * age * age / span
              val pulse = 0.5 - 0.5 * kotlin.math.cos(2.0 * PI * cycles)
              val strength = smooth01(u)
              val pulsed = (1.0 - strength) * base + strength * (0.25 + (1.0 - 0.25) * pulse)
              val merge = smooth01((u - (1.0 - 0.20)) / 0.20)
              return (1.0 - merge) * pulsed + merge
          }
          fun lambda(index: Int, name: String) = with(Functions) {
              fn(0.0..3600.0, name) { seconds ->
                  val base = backgroundOf(seconds, index)
                  val event = events.firstOrNull { seconds >= it.start && seconds <= it.end }
                  when {
                      event == null -> base
                      seconds < event.plateauStart -> {
                          val age = seconds - event.start
                          val lag = if (event.id == "e3" && name == "y" && age < 180.0) {
                              val u = age / 180.0
                              val v = 1.0 - u
                              6.0 * 64.0 * u * u * u * v * v * v
                          } else 0.0
                          shoulderOf(base, age - lag, event.rise)
                      }
                      seconds <= event.plateauEnd -> 1.0
                      else -> shoulderOf(base, event.end - seconds, event.fall)
                  }
              }
          }

          fun formula(index: Int, name: String) = with(Functions) {
              val all = Functions.Domain.ALL
              fun k(v: Double) = c(v, all)
              val t = identity(all)
              val one = k(1.0)
              fun sinOf(p: Functions.Fn) = sin(frequency = k(0.0), phase = p) // sin(0*x + p) is sin(p), exactly
              fun cosOf(p: Functions.Fn) = cos(frequency = k(0.0), phase = p)
              fun smooth(v: Functions.Fn): Functions.Fn {
                  val u = v.clamp(0.0, 1.0)
                  return u * u * u * (k(10.0) + u * (k(-15.0) + k(6.0) * u))
              }
              val drift = k(2.0 * PI / 3.0) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(100.0))
              val base =
                  k(0.45) +
                      k(0.20) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(40.0) + k((index - 1).toDouble()) * drift) +
                      k(0.04) * sinOf(k(2.0 * PI) * t / k(230.0))
              fun shoulder(age: Functions.Fn, span: Double): Functions.Fn {
                  val u = (age / k(span)).clamp(0.0, 1.0)
                  val cycles = k(0.06) * age + k(0.5 * (0.80 - 0.06)) * age * age / k(span)
                  val pulse = k(0.5) - k(0.5) * cosOf(k(2.0 * PI) * cycles)
                  val strength = smooth(u)
                  val pulsed = (one - strength) * base + strength * (k(0.25) + k(1.0 - 0.25) * pulse)
                  val merge = smooth((u - k(1.0 - 0.20)) / k(0.20))
                  return (one - merge) * pulsed + merge
              }
              fun from(a: Double) = step(a, all) // exactly [x >= a]; [x <= b] is 1 - from(nextUp(b))
              var sum: Functions.Fn = k(0.0) * t
              var inside: Functions.Fn = k(0.0)
              for (e in events) {
                  val age = t - k(e.start)
                  val local = if (e.id == "e3" && name == "y") {
                      val u = age / k(180.0)
                      val v = one - u
                      age - (k(180.0) - age).sign().clamp(0.0, 1.0) * (k(6.0 * 64.0) * u * u * u * v * v * v)
                  } else age
                  sum =
                      sum +
                          ((from(e.start) - from(e.plateauStart)) * shoulder(local, e.rise) +
                              (from(e.plateauStart) - from(Math.nextUp(e.plateauEnd))) * one +
                              (from(Math.nextUp(e.plateauEnd)) - from(Math.nextUp(e.end))) * shoulder(k(e.end) - t, e.fall))
                  inside = inside + (from(e.start) - from(Math.nextUp(e.end)))
              }
              sum + (one - inside) * base
          }

          val rows = mutableListOf<List<Any?>>()
          for ((i, name) in names.withIndex()) {
              val l = lambda(i, name)
              val f = formula(i, name)
              val grid = (0..72_000).map { it * 0.05 }
              val mismatches = grid.count { l(it).toRawBits() != f(it).toRawBits() }
              val holds = events.count { f.certifiedEquals(1.0, it.plateauStart, it.plateauEnd).proven }
              val above = f.certifiedNeverExceeds(1.0, 0.0, 3600.0)
              val witness = above.witness!!
              rows +=
                  listOf(
                      name,
                      "${FnIntervals.unsupportedOps(l)} / ${FnIntervals.unsupportedOps(f)}",
                      "$mismatches of ${grid.size}",
                      "$holds of ${events.size} PROVEN",
                      f.certifiedNeverBelow(0.0, 0.0, 3600.0).kind.name,
                      "${above.kind} at $witness: lambda ${l(witness)}",
                  )
          }
          display(
              "claims",
              Table(
                      listOf("ch", "refused ops (lambda / formula)", "bit mismatches", "== 1 on plateau", ">= 0", "<= 1"),
                      title = "the worked example's claims, on its formula rewrite",
                  )
                  .rows(rows)
                  .role("<= 1", CellRole.WARN),
          )

          // How far above 1: certifiedRange's proven bound is the certificate for <= 1 + 1e-9 (x only; ~11 s).
          val xMax = formula(0, "x").certifiedRange(0.0, 3600.0, tolerance = 9e-10).max!!
          display(
              "max",
              Table(listOf("what", "value"), title = "channel x, the whole hour")
                  .row("max reached", xMax.value.toString())
                  .row("at x", xMax.witness.toString())
                  .row("proven bound", xMax.bound.toString())
                  .row("enclosures", xMax.enclosures)
                  .role("value", CellRole.ACCENT),
          )
  - execute: { box: sampled, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: certified, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: range, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: limits, property: code }
  - await: {}
  - execute: { box: workbench, property: code }
  - await: {}

name: close_node_demo
description: >
  Loadable demo of the interior-`FLine.Close` fixes (2026-08-01). Two pure-compute boxes, no Window
  and no Renderer — both draw with showPlaneGrid, which is drawToSVG -> display and needs no AWT and
  no GPU.

  THE DEFECT. `FLine.Close` is `Node(0)` and stores no point of its own, while `Node.to` is
  `storage[0]` — so reading `.to` on a Close throws IndexOutOfBoundsException. 0954ebfb fixed every
  *trailing* Close, the `nodes.last().to` pattern. This is the *interior* one: `nodes[i - 1].to`
  inside a loop, which fires whenever a Close has more geometry after it. Of the 290 operation/curve
  pairs in the regression corpus, 80 threw at 7abe8736, across 18 distinct public functions.

  And two functions were producing the wrong answer rather than throwing: `byReversing` could not
  reverse a closed contour at all (its `close()` came out where the reversed subpath's *first*
  instruction belongs, so the shape came apart), and `bySubdividing` dropped Close nodes on the
  floor, so a subdivided glyph's contours came out open.

  WHERE IT COMES FROM, which is the part worth seeing. Not from glyphs: AWT's `javaShapeToFLine`
  turns SEG_CLOSE into a `lineTo` back to the last moveTo, so a glyph outline has no Close at all.
  It comes from `afield.graphics.render.arrow(startHead = true, endHead = true)` — a shipped drawing
  primitive whose two arrowheads each end in `close()`, so a double-headed arrow has an interior
  Close in it and no user cleverness was required to build one.

  Box 1 (close_node_reversal) computes BOTH reversals live, side by side: the old single backwards
  walk is written out in the box rather than remembered, so the comparison is happening in front of
  you. Box 2 (close_node_arrow) takes the stdlib's own double-headed arrow and runs the whole family
  over it, reporting what each one does and what it used to do.

  Replay into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript). Each `execute` op omits
  inline code, so it runs the box's stored `code` property.
operations:
  - create:
      box: close_node_reversal
      name: reversing a closed contour
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          A square that relies on close() for its fourth side, and a two-contour outline whose
          counter also relies on close(). Write those closing sides as an explicit lineTo back to
          the start and the reversal below comes out right — the defect only shows on a shape
          where the Close is carrying a segment nothing else draws.
          */
          val square = fline {
              moveTo(0, 0)
              lineTo(200, 0)
              lineTo(200, 200)
              lineTo(0, 200)
              close()
          }

          val glyph = fline {
              moveTo(0, 0)
              cubicTo(vec(-40, 150, 0), vec(60, 260, 0), vec(160, 250, 0))
              cubicTo(vec(260, 240, 0), vec(300, 120, 0), vec(250, 20, 0))
              close()
              moveTo(80, 70)
              cubicTo(vec(60, 140, 0), vec(110, 190, 0), vec(170, 180, 0))
              cubicTo(vec(220, 172, 0), vec(230, 110, 0), vec(200, 62, 0))
              close()
          }

          /*
          The old implementation, written out here rather than remembered: one backwards walk
          over the whole node list, emitting each instruction's reverse as it goes. The `.to`
          reads are `endPointOf` so this runs at all — the crash is not what this box is about —
          but the *structure* is the old one, and the structure is the defect: a Close met on the
          way back is emitted right there, which in the reversed order is immediately after the
          moveTo, where the subpath's first instruction belongs.
          */
          val oldByReversing = { line: FLine ->
              val out = FLine()
              if (line.nodes.isNotEmpty()) {
                  out.moveTo(line.currentPoint!!)
                  for (i in line.nodes.size - 1 downTo 1) {
                      val node = line.nodes[i]
                      val lands = line.endPointOf(i - 1)
                      when (node) {
                          is FLine.LineTo -> out.lineTo(lands)
                          is FLine.CubicTo -> out.cubicTo(node.c2, node.c1, lands)
                          is FLine.MoveTo -> out.moveTo(lands)
                          is FLine.Close -> out.close()
                      }
                  }
              }
              out
          }

          val ghost = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 9.0
                  color = vec(0.45, 0.5, 0.58, 0.55)
              }
          }
          val cyan = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 3.0
                  color = vec(0.35, 0.85, 1.0, 0.95)
              }
          }

          // How much of the shape the reversal actually retraces. A reversal that drops a segment
          // is shorter than what it reversed, and that is the whole story in one number.
          val coverage = { original: FLine, reversed: FLine ->
              val a = original.cursor().lengthD()
              val b = reversed.cursor().lengthD()
              "%.0f of %.0f units retraced (%.0f%%)".format(b, a, 100.0 * b / a)
          }

          val squareOld = oldByReversing(square)
          val squareNew = square.byReversing()
          val glyphOld = oldByReversing(glyph)
          val glyphNew = glyph.byReversing()

          showPlaneGrid(
              "closed square, old reversal\n${coverage(square, squareOld)}" to listOf(ghost(square), cyan(squareOld)),
              "closed square, byReversing today\n${coverage(square, squareNew)}" to listOf(ghost(square), cyan(squareNew)),
              "two contours, old reversal\n${coverage(glyph, glyphOld)}" to listOf(ghost(glyph), cyan(glyphOld)),
              "two contours, byReversing today\n${coverage(glyph, glyphNew)}" to listOf(ghost(glyph), cyan(glyphNew)),
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 420,
              cellHeight = 230,
          )

          // Reversing twice is the identity now, which the old walk could not manage on anything
          // closed: it is not even length-preserving once, so it cannot be an involution.
          val roundTrip = { l: FLine ->
              val back = l.byReversing().byReversing()
              val same = l.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName } == back.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName }
              if (same) "identical" else "DIFFERENT: ${back.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName }}"
          }

          listOf(
                  "grey = the original, cyan = its reversal",
                  "square   reverse-twice: ${roundTrip(square)}",
                  "glyph    reverse-twice: ${roundTrip(glyph)}",
              )
              .joinToString("\n")
  - create:
      box: close_node_arrow
      name: the shipped primitive that has an interior Close in it
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 700.0, w: 470.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Not a hand-built fixture: this is what afield.graphics.render.arrow returns when you ask for a
          head at both ends. Its appendHead ends each arrowhead with close(), so the node list is
            MoveTo LineTo | MoveTo LineTo LineTo Close | MoveTo LineTo LineTo Close
          and the first Close has a whole arrowhead after it.
          */
          val a = arrow(vec(0.0, 0.0), vec(300.0, 120.0), startHead = true, endHead = true)

          val closes = a.nodes.withIndex().filter { it.value is FLine.Close }.map { it.index }
          val interior = closes.filter { it < a.nodes.size - 1 }

          val ghost = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 9.0
                  color = vec(0.45, 0.5, 0.58, 0.55)
              }
          }
          val cyan = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 3.0
                  color = vec(0.35, 0.85, 1.0, 0.95)
              }
          }

          // Everything here threw IndexOutOfBoundsException on this exact line before 2026-08-01.
          val reversed = a.byReversing()
          val subdivided = a.bySubdividing(1)
          val dashes = a.byDashing(14f, 8f).map { cyan(it).copy { thickness = 3.0 } }
          val hull = a.byConvexHull2D()

          showPlaneGrid(
              "arrow(startHead, endHead)\n${a.nodes.size} nodes, Closes at $closes" to listOf(cyan(a)),
              "byReversing\n${reversed.nodes.size} nodes, ${reversed.nodes.count { it is FLine.Close }} Closes kept" to
                  listOf(ghost(a), cyan(reversed)),
              "bySubdividing(1)\n${subdivided.nodes.count { it is FLine.Close }} Closes kept" to
                  listOf(ghost(a), cyan(subdivided)),
              "byDashing(14, 8)\n${dashes.size} dashes" to (listOf(ghost(a)) + dashes),
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 420,
              cellHeight = 230,
          )

          // The sweep, run live: every one of these used to throw on this arrow.
          val ops = listOf<Pair<String, (FLine) -> Any?>>(
              "byReversing" to { l -> l.byReversing() },
              "bySubdividing" to { l -> l.bySubdividing(1) },
              "bySimplifying" to { l -> l.bySimplifying(2f) },
              "byConvexHull2D" to { l -> l.byConvexHull2D() },
              "byFiltering" to { l -> l.byFiltering { _, _ -> true } },
              "windingNumber" to { l -> l.windingNumber2D(vec(150f, 60f)) },
              "contains" to { l -> l.contains2D(vec(150f, 60f)) },
              "centroid2D" to { l -> l.centroid2D() },
              "fast2DBounds" to { l -> l.fast2DBounds() },
              "byDashing" to { l -> l.byDashing(14f, 8f).size },
          )
          val results = ops.map { (name, op) ->
              val r = runCatching { op(a.copy()) }
              if (r.isSuccess) "  ok    $name" else "  THREW $name: ${r.exceptionOrNull()}"
          }
          val bad = results.count { it.contains("THREW") }

          (listOf(
                  "arrow(startHead = true, endHead = true): ${a.nodes.size} nodes, " +
                      "Closes at $closes, of which ${interior.size} interior",
                  "convex hull: ${hull.nodes.size} nodes",
                  "",
                  "$bad of ${ops.size} operations throw on it:",
              ) + results)
              .joinToString("\n")
  - execute:
      box: close_node_reversal
  - execute:
      box: close_node_arrow
after:
name: close_node_demo
description: >
  Loadable demo of the interior-`FLine.Close` fixes (2026-08-01). Two pure-compute boxes, no Window
  and no Renderer — both draw with showPlaneGrid, which is drawToSVG -> display and needs no AWT and
  no GPU.

  THE DEFECT. `FLine.Close` is `Node(0)` and stores no point of its own, while `Node.to` is
  `storage[0]` — so reading `.to` on a Close throws IndexOutOfBoundsException. 0954ebfb fixed every
  *trailing* Close, the `nodes.last().to` pattern. This is the *interior* one: `nodes[i - 1].to`
  inside a loop, which fires whenever a Close has more geometry after it. Of the 290 operation/curve
  pairs in the regression corpus, 80 threw at 7abe8736, across 18 distinct public functions.

  And two functions were producing the wrong answer rather than throwing: `byReversing` could not
  reverse a closed contour at all (its `close()` came out where the reversed subpath's *first*
  instruction belongs, so the shape came apart), and `bySubdividing` dropped Close nodes on the
  floor, so a subdivided glyph's contours came out open.

  WHERE IT COMES FROM, which is the part worth seeing. Not from glyphs: AWT's `javaShapeToFLine`
  turns SEG_CLOSE into a `lineTo` back to the last moveTo, so a glyph outline has no Close at all.
  It comes from `afield.graphics.render.arrow(startHead = true, endHead = true)` — a shipped drawing
  primitive whose two arrowheads each end in `close()`, so a double-headed arrow has an interior
  Close in it and no user cleverness was required to build one.

  Box 1 (close_node_reversal) computes BOTH reversals live, side by side: the old single backwards
  walk is written out in the box rather than remembered, so the comparison is happening in front of
  you. Box 2 (close_node_arrow) takes the stdlib's own double-headed arrow and runs the whole family
  over it, reporting what each one does and what it used to do.

  Replay into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript). Each `execute` op omits
  inline code, so it runs the box's stored `code` property.
operations:
  - create:
      box: close_node_reversal
      name: reversing a closed contour
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          A square that relies on close() for its fourth side, and a two-contour outline whose
          counter also relies on close(). Write those closing sides as an explicit lineTo back to
          the start and the reversal below comes out right — the defect only shows on a shape
          where the Close is carrying a segment nothing else draws.
          */
          val square = fline {
              moveTo(0, 0)
              lineTo(200, 0)
              lineTo(200, 200)
              lineTo(0, 200)
              close()
          }

          val glyph = fline {
              moveTo(0, 0)
              cubicTo(vec(-40, 150, 0), vec(60, 260, 0), vec(160, 250, 0))
              cubicTo(vec(260, 240, 0), vec(300, 120, 0), vec(250, 20, 0))
              close()
              moveTo(80, 70)
              cubicTo(vec(60, 140, 0), vec(110, 190, 0), vec(170, 180, 0))
              cubicTo(vec(220, 172, 0), vec(230, 110, 0), vec(200, 62, 0))
              close()
          }

          /*
          The old implementation, written out here rather than remembered: one backwards walk
          over the whole node list, emitting each instruction's reverse as it goes. The `.to`
          reads are `endPointOf` so this runs at all — the crash is not what this box is about —
          but the *structure* is the old one, and the structure is the defect: a Close met on the
          way back is emitted right there, which in the reversed order is immediately after the
          moveTo, where the subpath's first instruction belongs.
          */
          val oldByReversing = { line: FLine ->
              val out = FLine()
              if (line.nodes.isNotEmpty()) {
                  out.moveTo(line.currentPoint!!)
                  for (i in line.nodes.size - 1 downTo 1) {
                      val node = line.nodes[i]
                      val lands = line.endPointOf(i - 1)
                      when (node) {
                          is FLine.LineTo -> out.lineTo(lands)
                          is FLine.CubicTo -> out.cubicTo(node.c2, node.c1, lands)
                          is FLine.MoveTo -> out.moveTo(lands)
                          is FLine.Close -> out.close()
                      }
                  }
              }
              out
          }

          val ghost = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 9.0
                  color = vec(0.45, 0.5, 0.58, 0.55)
              }
          }
          val cyan = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 3.0
                  color = vec(0.35, 0.85, 1.0, 0.95)
              }
          }

          // How much of the shape the reversal actually retraces. A reversal that drops a segment
          // is shorter than what it reversed, and that is the whole story in one number.
          val coverage = { original: FLine, reversed: FLine ->
              val a = original.cursor().lengthD()
              val b = reversed.cursor().lengthD()
              "%.0f of %.0f units retraced (%.0f%%)".format(b, a, 100.0 * b / a)
          }

          val squareOld = oldByReversing(square)
          val squareNew = square.byReversing()
          val glyphOld = oldByReversing(glyph)
          val glyphNew = glyph.byReversing()

          showPlaneGrid(
              "closed square, old reversal\n${coverage(square, squareOld)}" to [ghost(square), cyan(squareOld)],
              "closed square, byReversing today\n${coverage(square, squareNew)}" to [ghost(square), cyan(squareNew)],
              "two contours, old reversal\n${coverage(glyph, glyphOld)}" to [ghost(glyph), cyan(glyphOld)],
              "two contours, byReversing today\n${coverage(glyph, glyphNew)}" to [ghost(glyph), cyan(glyphNew)],
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 420,
              cellHeight = 230,
          )

          // Reversing twice is the identity now, which the old walk could not manage on anything
          // closed: it is not even length-preserving once, so it cannot be an involution.
          val roundTrip = { l: FLine ->
              val back = l.byReversing().byReversing()
              val same = l.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName } == back.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName }
              if (same) "identical" else "DIFFERENT: ${back.nodes.map { it::class.simpleName }}"
          }

          [
                  "grey = the original, cyan = its reversal",
                  "square   reverse-twice: ${roundTrip(square)}",
                  "glyph    reverse-twice: ${roundTrip(glyph)}",
              ]
              .joinToString("\n")
  - create:
      box: close_node_arrow
      name: the shipped primitive that has an interior Close in it
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 700.0, w: 470.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Not a hand-built fixture: this is what afield.graphics.render.arrow returns when you ask for a
          head at both ends. Its appendHead ends each arrowhead with close(), so the node list is
            MoveTo LineTo | MoveTo LineTo LineTo Close | MoveTo LineTo LineTo Close
          and the first Close has a whole arrowhead after it.
          */
          val a = arrow(vec(0.0, 0.0), vec(300.0, 120.0), startHead = true, endHead = true)

          val closes = a.nodes.withIndex().filter { it.value is FLine.Close }.map { it.index }
          val interior = closes.filter { it < a.nodes.size - 1 }

          val ghost = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 9.0
                  color = vec(0.45, 0.5, 0.58, 0.55)
              }
          }
          val cyan = { l: FLine ->
              l.copy {
                  thickness = 3.0
                  color = vec(0.35, 0.85, 1.0, 0.95)
              }
          }

          // Everything here threw IndexOutOfBoundsException on this exact line before 2026-08-01.
          val reversed = a.byReversing()
          val subdivided = a.bySubdividing(1)
          val dashes = a.byDashing(14f, 8f).map { cyan(it).copy { thickness = 3.0 } }
          val hull = a.byConvexHull2D()

          showPlaneGrid(
              "arrow(startHead, endHead)\n${a.nodes.size} nodes, Closes at $closes" to [cyan(a)],
              "byReversing\n${reversed.nodes.size} nodes, ${reversed.nodes.count { it is FLine.Close }} Closes kept" to
                  [ghost(a), cyan(reversed)],
              "bySubdividing(1)\n${subdivided.nodes.count { it is FLine.Close }} Closes kept" to [ghost(a), cyan(subdivided)],
              "byDashing(14, 8)\n${dashes.size} dashes" to ([ghost(a)] + dashes),
              columns = 2,
              cellWidth = 420,
              cellHeight = 230,
          )

          // The sweep, run live: every one of these used to throw on this arrow.
          val ops = listOf<Pair<String, (FLine) -> Any?>>(
              "byReversing" to { l -> l.byReversing() },
              "bySubdividing" to { l -> l.bySubdividing(1) },
              "bySimplifying" to { l -> l.bySimplifying(2f) },
              "byConvexHull2D" to { l -> l.byConvexHull2D() },
              "byFiltering" to { l -> l.byFiltering { _, _ -> true } },
              "windingNumber" to { l -> l.windingNumber2D(vec(150f, 60f)) },
              "contains" to { l -> l.contains2D(vec(150f, 60f)) },
              "centroid2D" to { l -> l.centroid2D() },
              "fast2DBounds" to { l -> l.fast2DBounds() },
              "byDashing" to { l -> l.byDashing(14f, 8f).size },
          )
          val results = ops.map { (name, op) ->
              val r = runCatching { op(a.copy()) }
              if (r.isSuccess) "  ok    $name" else "  THREW $name: ${r.exceptionOrNull()}"
          }
          val bad = results.count { it.contains("THREW") }

          ([
                  "arrow(startHead = true, endHead = true): ${a.nodes.size} nodes, " +
                      "Closes at $closes, of which ${interior.size} interior",
                  "convex hull: ${hull.nodes.size} nodes",
                  "",
                  "$bad of ${ops.size} operations throw on it:",
              ] + results)
              .joinToString("\n")
  - execute:
      box: close_node_reversal
  - execute:
      box: close_node_arrow

before:
name: keybindings_inspect
description: >
  One box that asks Field what its shortcuts currently are, reading the same resolved bindings the
  keypresses themselves use (afield.app.settings.UserKeybindingsManager.resolved). Backs the "Asking Field
  directly" capture on public/docs/keybindings.md, and is worth running on its own when a shortcut
  is not doing what a keybindings.yaml says it should. The box code here is exactly what that page
  shows.

  Capture-only, so it lives under transcripts/docs_capture/: AgentTranscriptMaterializer scans the
  transcripts/ directory itself and would expect a committed starting-point bundle for it.
operations:
  - create:
      box: agent_keybindings_inspect
      name: What is bound right now
      frame:
        x: 80.0
        y: 80.0
        w: 640.0
        h: 170.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // Point the watcher at ~/.afield/keybindings.yaml — a no-op unless something moved it,
          // which the rebinding figure further up this page does.
          afield.app.settings.UserKeybindingsManager.watchFile(null)

          val live = afield.app.settings.UserKeybindingsManager.resolved
          val ids = listOf("new-box", "open-command-palette", "show-cheatsheet", "execute-fragment", "connect")
          // A command with no binding yet is the interesting row, so it says so in a role rather than
          // looking like any other cell.
          val bound =
              Table(listOf("command", "bound to"))
                  .rows(
                      ids.map { id ->
                          listOf(id, (live.effective[id] ?: live.bindings[id])?.joinToString(" or ") ?: "not registered yet")
                      },
                  )
                  .roleBy("bound to") { if (it == "not registered yet") CellRole.WARN else null }

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
              {muted:${live.path.md}}

              {muted:${live.problems.size} problem(s) in it}

              ${bound.h}
          """,
              width = 560,
          )
  - execute:
      box: agent_keybindings_inspect
      property: code
      type: all
  - wait:
      millis: 400

      name: custom types
      frame: { x: 40.0, y: 30.0, w: 300.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          interpolant("overshoot") { lerp(1 + 2.7 * (u - 1).pow(3) + 1.7 * (u - 1).pow(2)) }

                  Keyframe(1.5, 0.8, "wobble"),
                  Keyframe(3.0, 0.3, "chaos"),
                  Keyframe(4.5, 0.6, "linear"),

          )
  - execute: { box: kf_custom_video, property: code }
  # Before the recording starts: time for a cold compile and the editor to receive its keys.
  - wait:
      millis: 12000

before:
name: spatial_navigation_overlay
description: >
  Four boxes in a plus, laid out so the spatial-navigation overlay has something unambiguous to
  draw. Backs the overlay figure on `public/docs/spatial_navigation.md`.

  The middle box is the anchor the figure is taken from; the other three sit due north, due east
  and due south of it. The offsets are deliberately axis-aligned and far apart, because
  `findDirectionalSpatialTargets` picks a direction from the dominant axis of the centre-to-centre
  offset (`abs(dx) > abs(dy)` -> east/west, else north/south) and then keeps the nearest box in
  each direction, counting sideways distance as a fifth of distance along the direction of travel.
  A cluster that was nearly diagonal would let one box flip between two directions depending on
  where the canvas happened to be panned. West is left empty on purpose: the page says a direction
  with no box in it is absent from the overlay, and the figure should show that.

  Boxes are created but not launched. The overlay is drawn from box geometry and names, so nothing
  here needs to run, and a box that does not run cannot fail a capture.

  Capture-only, so it lives under transcripts/docs_capture/: AgentTranscriptMaterializer scans the
  transcripts/ directory itself and would expect a committed starting-point bundle for anything
  directly inside it.
operations:
  - create:
      box: spatial_nav_north
      name: palette
      frame:
        x: 430.0
        y: 170.0
        w: 360.0
        h: 150.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // The colours the curve below is drawn with.
          val ramp = listOf(Vec4(0.96, 0.62, 0.26, 1.0), Vec4(0.30, 0.62, 0.90, 1.0))
  - create:
      box: spatial_nav_center
      name: curve
      frame:
        x: 430.0
        y: 390.0
        w: 360.0
        h: 150.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // The box the figure is anchored on: the one you are standing on.
          val path = FLine().moveTo(0.0, 0.0).cubicTo(60.0, -80.0, 180.0, 80.0, 240.0, 0.0)
  - create:
      box: spatial_nav_east
      name: render
      frame:
        x: 840.0
        y: 390.0
        w: 360.0
        h: 150.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // Due east of `curve`, so the overlay offers it under the right arrow.
          lines("main", path.stroked(2.0))
  - create:
      box: spatial_nav_south
      name: export
      frame:
        x: 430.0
        y: 610.0
        w: 360.0
        h: 150.0
      properties:
        code: |
          // Due south of `curve`, so the overlay offers it under the down arrow.
          print(path.arcLength())
  - wait:
      millis: 400

before:
name: threejs_editable_fill_pixels
description: >
  Pixel verification for the three.js viewer's *client-side* fill — the `editable = true` path, where
  `tessellateCoplanarGroups` in `threejs_viewer.html` triangulates in the browser rather than reading
  the server's triangles. `ThreeJsViewerTessellationParityTest` executes that JavaScript on GraalJS and
  compares it to `afield.geometry.path.PlanarTessellation`, which is a strong statement about the numbers and
  no statement at all about the pixels; this transcript is the pixels.

  Three boxes, each `editable = true` so the client does the work:

    1. `fill_editable_planes` — one filled FLine holding six subpaths: three congruent unit squares in
       three perpendicular planes, each with a square hole. Every face must be solid, every hole must be
       a hole, and nothing may be inside out.
    2. `fill_editable_overlap` — two congruent overlapping squares, each listing a vertex that falls
       inside the other. Until 2026-08-04 this froze the tab: the nesting pass could pick each ring as
       the other's parent, and the depth walk never terminated. Both squares should now fill.

before:
name: drawing_notation
description: >
  A starting point for the drawing layer and the `notation` API: six boxes that draw on the
  document's drawing, read it, listen to it, and read it the way two graphic scores of the 1950s
  are read. Press Alt+D to draw; press it again to go back to the boxes.

  Run `draw` first: it circles itself and draws an arrow to `listen` (drag either box and the
  arrow follows). `read` prints every mark and what it is over. `listen` prints each stroke you
  draw by hand. `projection 1`, after Morton Feldman, is a three-row grid: draw rectangles in it
  and the box reads them as onsets, durations and registers. `fontana mix`, after John Cage,
  draws six curves, a grid and a point: draw a straight line across the sheet (L) and the box
  measures where it crosses each curve. `crescendo` draws a hand-made hairpin and reads its width
  at each beat as a dynamic marking.

  Companion to public/docs/drawing_and_notation.md. Pure CPU; no Window, no Renderer.
operations:
  - create:
      box: dn_draw
      name: draw
      frame: { x: 200.0, y: 200.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Drawing from code. Everything this block makes belongs to this box: run it again and
          // the marks are replaced, not duplicated. Marks drawn by hand are never touched.
          val listener = inside.boxes.values.first { it.name == "listen" }
          notation {
              stroke = "#1971c2"
              text("drawn by ${name}", frame.x, frame.y - 34)
              ellipse(frame.x - 20, frame.y - 20, frame.w + 40, frame.h + 40)
              arrow(from = thisBox, to = listener, label = "tells") // drag either box: the arrow follows
          }
  - create:
      box: dn_listen
      name: listen
      frame: { x: 620.0, y: 320.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Listening to the drawing: run this, then draw a stroke anywhere (Alt+D, then P).
          // The handler runs when the stroke is finished; stop the box to remove it.
          notation.onStroke { s ->
              println("a stroke of ${s.points.size} points, ${s.length.toInt()} long, from ${s.start} to ${s.end}")
          }
  - create:
      box: dn_read
      name: read
      frame: { x: 200.0, y: 460.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Reading the drawing: every mark, hand-drawn or not, with what it is over and what it joins.
          for (m in notation.marks) {
              val where = m.box?.let { " over '${it.name}'" } ?: ""
              val joins = if (m.kind == MarkType.ARROW) " from '${m.fromBox?.name}' to '${m.toBox?.name}'" else ""
              println("${m.kind.name.lowercase()} ${m.label ?: ""}$where$joins")
          }
  - create:
      box: dn_projection
      name: projection 1
      frame: { x: 1120.0, y: 700.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          After Morton Feldman's Projection 1 (1950): time runs left to right; the grid's three rows
          are high, middle and low. Draw boxes (Alt+D, then R) in the grid, and this box reads them
          as events: when each starts, how long it lasts, which register it sits in.
          */
          notation("grid") {
              stroke = "#868e96"
              frame("projection", 100, 700, 960, 270)
              for (row in 1..2) line(listOf(vec(100, 700 + row * 90), vec(1060, 700 + row * 90)))
              rect(160, 715, 120, 60, fill = "#1971c2") // one to start with
          }
          val score = notation.space("projection", x = 0.0..16.0, y = 3.0..0.0) // 16 beats; 3 rows
          fun register(v: Double) = when {
              v >= 2 -> "high"
              v >= 1 -> "middle"
              else -> "low"
          }
          fun read() =
              score.events
                  .filter { it.mark.kind == MarkType.RECTANGLE }
                  .forEach {
                      println("beat %.1f for %.1f, %s".format(it.start, it.duration, register(it.value)))
                  }
          read()
          notation.onChange("projection") { read() }
  - create:
      box: dn_fontana
      name: fontana mix
      frame: { x: 2160.0, y: 120.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          After John Cage's Fontana Mix (1958): six curves, a grid, a point, and a straight line.
          Cage's performer laid a line from a point inside the grid to one outside it and measured
          where it crossed the curves. Here the line is yours: draw one across the sheet (Alt+D, then L)
          and this box reads it. Run the box first; it draws the sheet.
          */
          val colors = listOf("#e03131", "#1971c2", "#2f9e44", "#f08c00", "#9c36b5", "#0c8599")
          notation("sheet") {
              frame("fontana mix", 1200, 100, 900, 520)
              for (i in 0 until 6) {
                  val curve = (0..48).map { k -> vec(1230 + k * 17.5, 170 + i * 75 + 55 * sin(k / 5.0 + i * 1.9)) }
                  stroke(curve, name = "curve ${i + 1}", stroke = colors[i])
              }
              rect(1530, 250, 240, 200, name = "grid", stroke = "#868e96")
              ellipse(1605, 320, 12, 12, name = "point", fill = "#868e96")
          }

          fun read(line: Mark) {
              val crossings = notation.intersect(line.start!!, line.end!!).filter { it.mark.name?.startsWith("curve") == true }
              println("${crossings.size} crossings along the line:")
              crossings.forEach { println("  ${it.mark.name}  %.2f of the way along".format(it.value)) }
          }

          notation.lines.lastOrNull { it.handDrawn }?.let(::read)
          notation.onChange("fontana") { edit ->
              (edit.added + edit.updated).lastOrNull { it.kind == MarkType.LINE }?.let(::read)
          }
  - create:

name: drawing_notation

  document's drawing, read it, listen to it, and read it the way two graphic scores of the 1950s
  are read. Press Alt+D to draw; press it again to go back to the boxes.

  arrow follows). `read` prints every mark and what it is over. `listen` prints each stroke you
  draw by hand. `projection 1`, after Morton Feldman, is a three-row grid: draw rectangles in it

  draws six curves, a grid and a point: draw a straight line across the sheet (L) and the box
  measures where it crosses each curve. `crescendo` draws a hand-made hairpin and reads its width

operations:

      frame: { x: 200.0, y: 200.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }

          notation {

              text("drawn by ${name}", frame.x, frame.y - 34)
              ellipse(frame.x - 20, frame.y - 20, frame.w + 40, frame.h + 40)
              arrow(from = thisBox, to = listener, label = "tells") // drag either box: the arrow follows
          }
  - create:
      box: dn_listen
      name: listen
      frame: { x: 620.0, y: 320.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Listening to the drawing: run this, then draw a stroke anywhere (Alt+D, then P).
          // The handler runs when the stroke is finished; stop the box to remove it.
          notation.onStroke { s ->
              println("a stroke of ${s.points.size} points, ${s.length.toInt()} long, from ${s.start} to ${s.end}")
          }

      box: dn_read
      name: read
      frame: { x: 200.0, y: 460.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Reading the drawing: every mark, hand-drawn or not, with what it is over and what it joins.
          for (m in notation.marks) {
              val where = m.box?.let { " over '${it.name}'" } ?: ""
              val joins = if (m.kind == MarkType.ARROW) " from '${m.fromBox?.name}' to '${m.toBox?.name}'" else ""
