  imaging_field.kt). Six pure-compute boxes, no Window and no Renderer — each one builds real
  Img pipelines and paints the result into its own output with showImg / showImgGrid (which go
  through Img.toPngBytes -> PngEncoder -> display, no AWT):
    1. img basics    — build an Img from a function, resize/crop/flip, luma, HSV channels, and the
                       Otsu threshold, all in one showImgGrid.
    2. filters       — salt-and-pepper noise vs gaussianBlur / median / bilateral / unsharpMask,
                       with the mean-abs residual against the clean source printed for each.
    3. gradients+canny — Sobel dx/dy/magnitude/orientation, then canny(), then the same edges
                       converted to FLines with toContourFLines (count printed).
    4. features      — Harris and FAST corners on a synthetic square (their coordinates printed
                       against the known truth), plus houghLines recovering planted lines.
    5. morphology    — Otsu -> open/close -> connectedComponents (areas + centroids printed) ->
                       distanceTransform, colour-mapped through afield.lang.rectsl.Colormaps.
    6. motion        — pyramidal Lucas-Kanade flow between two frames related by a known affine
                       warp, then findHomographyRansac fitted to the tracks and compared, in
                       pixels, to the transform that was planted.
  Replay this file into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) to see all
  six on screen, then change a sigma, a threshold or the planted motion and re-run a box to watch
  it update live. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs the box's stored `code`
  property. Executed end-to-end by examples.demo-transcript.exec.
operations:
  - create:
      box: imaging_basics
      name: Img basics — build, resample, luma, HSV, threshold
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 440.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          An Img is width x height x channels floats, interleaved, origin top-left. This one is
          2400x1800 — 4.3 megapixels, 52 MB of float RGB — because that is the size at which the
          question "is this fast enough to actually use?" has a meaningful answer.
          */
          val card =
              Img.generateRGB(2400, 1800) { x, y ->
                  val u = x / 2399f
                  val v = y / 1799f
                  val disc = if (hypot(x - 600.0, y - 600.0) <= 340.0) 1f else 0f
                  val bar = if (y in 1300..1420 && x in 200..2199) 1f else 0f
                  Triple(
                      (0.15f + 0.7f * u * (1f - disc) + disc * 0.9f + bar).coerceIn(0f, 1f),
                      (0.15f + 0.6f * v + disc * 0.25f + bar).coerceIn(0f, 1f),
                      (0.55f - 0.4f * u + disc * 0.1f + bar).coerceIn(0f, 1f),
                  )
              }

          val gray = card.luma() // BT.709 perceptual grayscale
          val hsv = card.rgbToHsv() // h, s, v each in 0..1
          val small = card.resize(600, 450) // area-averaged (anti-aliased) downsample
          val backUp = small.resize(2400, 1800) // bilinear upsample: the detail is really gone
          val t = gray.otsuThreshold() // computed, not guessed
          val mask = gray.threshold(t)

          showImgGrid(
              "source RGB (${card.width}x${card.height})" to card,
              "luma()" to gray,
              "hue channel" to hsv.channel(0),
              "saturation channel" to hsv.channel(1),
              "resize(600,450) then back up" to backUp,
              "thresholdOtsu() @ ${"%.3f".format(t)}" to mask,
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 260,
          )
          println(
              "Img ${card.width}x${card.height} x${card.channels} ch, mean ${"%.3f".format(card.mean())}, " +
                  "otsu ${"%.3f".format(t)}, foreground ${mask.data.count { it > 0.5f }} px",
          )

          // The threshold is a mask; a mask has outlines; outlines are geometry. Everything the
          // family produces that is geometry rather than raster ends up in a lines() call.
          lines(mask.toContourFLines(minPerimeter = 120, simplifyTolerance = 12.0))
  - create:
      box: imaging_filters
      name: filters — gaussian / median / bilateral / unsharp
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 500.0, w: 430.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // A clean synthetic source, and the same source with 4% salt-and-pepper corruption.
          val clean =
              Img.generate(2400, 1800) { x, y ->
                  var v = 0.12f + 0.10f * (y / 1800f)
                  if (hypot(x - 600.0, y - 700.0) <= 340.0) v = 0.85f
                  if (x in 1200..1850 && y in 300..950) v = 0.65f
                  if (y in 1350..1420 && x in 200..2199) v = 0.95f
                  v
              }
          val rng = kotlin.random.Random(11)
          val noisy = clean.copy()
          repeat((noisy.pixelCount * 0.04).toInt()) {
              noisy.data[rng.nextInt(noisy.pixelCount)] = if (rng.nextBoolean()) 0f else 1f
          }

          /*
          These radii are in PIXELS, and they deliberately did not scale with the image. The
          separable filters are O(k) per pixel, so gaussianBlur is ~linear in area; median and
          bilateral are O(r^2) per pixel, so scaling their radius with the image would multiply
          their cost by 10,000x rather than 100x. Salt-and-pepper is single-pixel noise at any
          image size, so a pixel-scale radius is also the correct choice here, not a concession.
          */
          val gauss = noisy.gaussianBlur(2.0)
          val med = noisy.median(2)
          val bil = noisy.bilateral(sigmaSpace = 3.0, sigmaRange = 0.12)
          val sharp = clean.gaussianBlur(2.0).unsharpMask(sigma = 2.0, amount = 1.4)

          showImgGrid(
              "clean source" to clean,
              "+ 4% salt-and-pepper" to noisy,
              "gaussianBlur(2.0)" to gauss,
              "median(2)" to med,
              "bilateral(3.0, 0.12)" to bil,
              "blur then unsharpMask(2.0, 1.4)" to sharp,
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 260,
          )
          // The median is the right tool for impulse noise; the numbers say so, not the picture.
          println(
              "residual vs clean — gaussian ${"%.4f".format(gauss.meanAbsDiff(clean))}, " +
                  "median ${"%.4f".format(med.meanAbsDiff(clean))}, " +
                  "bilateral ${"%.4f".format(bil.meanAbsDiff(clean))}",
          )
  - create:
      box: imaging_edges
      name: gradients + Canny + the FLines the edges become
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 920.0, w: 420.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          val src =
              Img.generate(2400, 1800) { x, y ->
                  var v = 0.12f + 0.08f * (y / 1800f)
                  if (hypot(x - 620.0, y - 700.0) <= 340.0) v = 0.85f
                  if (x in 1200..1850 && y in 300..950) v = 0.68f
                  val tx = x - 2100.0
                  val ty = y - 400.0
                  if (ty in 0.0..600.0 && kotlin.math.abs(tx) <= ty * 0.5) v = 0.95f
                  v
              }

          // Sobel here is scaled to true units-per-pixel: a unit step edge integrates to 1.
          val grad = src.sobel()
          val edges = src.canny(low = 0.05, high = 0.11, sigma = 1.2)
          val auto = src.cannyAuto() // thresholds derived from this image's own gradients

          // Edges are geometry, and geometry in Field is an FLine. minPerimeter and the simplify
          // tolerance are pixel distances, so they scale with the image.
          val flines = edges.toContourFLines(minPerimeter = 120, simplifyTolerance = 12.0)

          showImgGrid(
              "source" to src,
              "sobel().dx (signed, coolwarm)" to grad.dx.colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "sobel().dy (signed, coolwarm)" to grad.dy.colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "magnitude (inferno)" to grad.magnitude().normalized().colormap("inferno"),
              "orientation as hue x magnitude" to grad.toColorImg(),
              "canny(0.05, 0.11)" to edges,
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 260,
          )
          println(
              "|grad| max ${"%.3f".format(grad.magnitude().max())}; " +
                  "canny ${edges.data.count { it > 0.5f }} px, cannyAuto ${auto.data.count { it > 0.5f }} px; " +
                  "${flines.size} FLines, ${flines.sumOf { it.nodes.size }} nodes total",
          )

          // The raster above is what Canny computed; this is what it *means* — three closed
          // outlines you can now transform, intersect or animate like any other Field geometry.
          lines(flines)
  - create:
      box: imaging_features
      name: features — Harris / FAST corners and Hough lines
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1340.0, w: 430.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // A square whose corners are at exactly known coordinates.
          val square = Img.generate(2000, 2000) { x, y -> if (x in 500..1499 && y in 500..1499) 0.92f else 0.08f }
          val harris = square.harrisCorners(threshold = 0.05, minDistance = 120, maxCount = 20)
          val fast = square.fastCorners(threshold = 0.2, minDistance = 120, maxCount = 20)

          val truth = listOf(500.0 to 500.0, 1499.0 to 500.0, 500.0 to 1499.0, 1499.0 to 1499.0)
          val worst = truth.maxOf { (ex, ey) -> harris.minOf { hypot(it.x - ex, it.y - ey) } }

          // Three lines at exactly known (rho, theta), plus a decoy ring Hough must not fit.
          val lineMask = Img.zeros(2000, 2000, 1)
          for (x in 100 until 1900) lineMask.set(x, 400, 0, 1f) // rho = 400,  theta = pi/2
          for (y in 100 until 1900) lineMask.set(1500, y, 0, 1f) // rho = 1500, theta = 0
          for (t in 0 until 2400) {
              val x = 200 + t * 0.6
              val y = 600 + t * 0.6
              if (x < 1999 && y < 1999) lineMask.set(x.toInt(), y.toInt(), 0, 1f)
          }
          for (i in 0 until 3600) {
              val a = 2.0 * PI * i / 3600
              val x = (600 + 220 * kotlin.math.cos(a)).toInt()
              val y = (1500 + 220 * kotlin.math.sin(a)).toInt()
              if (x in 0..1999 && y in 0..1999) lineMask.set(x, y, 0, 1f)
          }
          // threshold is a vote count, so it scales with the number of edge pixels on a line.
          // Named `houghs`, not `lines`, so it cannot shadow the lines() drawing call below.
          val houghs = houghLines(lineMask, thetaSteps = 360, threshold = 1000, maxLines = 5)

          showImgGrid(
              "harrisResponse (signed, coolwarm)" to square.harrisResponse().colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "shiTomasiResponse (viridis)" to square.shiTomasiResponse().normalized().colormap("viridis"),
              "edge mask: 3 lines + a decoy ring" to lineMask,
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 260,
          )
          println("harris ${harris.size} corners, worst ${"%.2f".format(worst)} px from the true square corners")
          println(
              "fast ${fast.size} corners at " +
                  fast.sortedBy { it.y * 1000 + it.x }.joinToString(", ") { "(${it.x.toInt()},${it.y.toInt()})" },
          )
          println(
              "hough " +
                  houghs.joinToString(", ") {
                      "(rho=${"%.0f".format(it.rho)}, theta=${"%.2f".format(it.theta)}, votes=${it.votes})"
                  },
          )

          /*
          A HoughLine is an INFINITE line — (rho, theta) names a whole line, not a segment — so
          it has no drawable form until you say which rectangle you are drawing it into. That is
          what toFLine(w, h) is for, and why it is nullable: a peak can name a line that misses.
          */
          lines(
              cornersToFLines(harris, size = 40.0) + houghs.mapNotNull { it.toFLine(lineMask.width, lineMask.height) },
          )
  - create:
      box: imaging_morphology
      name: morphology, connected components, distance transform
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1760.0, w: 450.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Three disjoint discs of known radius, then noise on top of them.
          val discs = listOf(Triple(550.0, 600.0, 280.0), Triple(1500.0, 550.0, 200.0), Triple(1100.0, 1350.0, 140.0))
          val clean =
              Img.generate(2200, 1800) { x, y ->
                  if (discs.any { (cx, cy, r) -> hypot(x - cx, y - cy) <= r }) 0.85f else 0.15f
              }
          val rng = kotlin.random.Random(3)
          val noisy = clean.copy()
          repeat((noisy.pixelCount * 0.03).toInt()) {
              noisy.data[rng.nextInt(noisy.pixelCount)] = if (rng.nextBoolean()) 0f else 1f
          }

          val mask = noisy.thresholdOtsu()
          val cleaned = mask.open(2, StructuringElement.DISC).close(2, StructuringElement.DISC)
          val cc = cleaned.connectedComponents(8)
          val dt = cleaned.distanceTransform()

          showImgGrid(
              "noisy source" to noisy,
              "thresholdOtsu()" to mask,
              "open(2,DISC).close(2,DISC)" to cleaned,
              "erode(4)" to cleaned.erode(4, StructuringElement.DISC),
              "dilate(4)" to cleaned.dilate(4, StructuringElement.DISC),
              "distanceTransform (magma)" to dt.normalized().colormap("magma"),
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 250,
          )
          println("${cc.count} components after cleaning (planted ${discs.size} discs):")
          cc.components
              .sortedByDescending { it.area }
              .forEach {
                  println(
                      "  area=${it.area} centroid=(${"%.1f".format(it.centroidX)}, ${"%.1f".format(it.centroidY)}) " +
                          "bbox=${it.boundingWidth}x${it.boundingHeight} fill=${"%.2f".format(it.fillRatio)}",
                  )
              }
          println("distance-transform peak ${"%.1f".format(dt.max())} (largest planted radius ${discs.maxOf { it.third }})")

          // Connected components are blobs; blobs have outlines. Same story as Canny — the raster
          // is the evidence, the FLines are the result you can actually build on.
          lines(cleaned.toContourFLines(minPerimeter = 120, simplifyTolerance = 8.0))
  - create:
      box: imaging_motion
      name: motion — Lucas–Kanade flow and the homography RANSAC fits to it
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 2180.0, w: 520.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Two frames related by a transform we choose, so the answer is known in advance.
          Multi-octave on purpose. Lucas-Kanade is coarse-to-fine: it halves the image several
          times and tracks the big picture first. A texture with only fine detail (period ~30 px)
          aliases away after four halvings and the tracker has nothing to lock onto — that
          version tracked 0 of 125 seeds at this size. Coarse octaves survive to the top of the
          pyramid; the fine ones sharpen the final refinement.
          */
          val a =
              Img.generate(2000, 2000) { x, y ->
                  (0.5 +
                          0.20 * kotlin.math.sin(x * 0.021) * kotlin.math.cos(y * 0.017) +
                          0.14 * kotlin.math.sin((x + y) * 0.011) +
                          0.10 * kotlin.math.sin(x * 0.21) * kotlin.math.cos(y * 0.17) +
                          0.06 * kotlin.math.cos((x - 2.0 * y) * 0.07))
                      .toFloat()
                      .coerceIn(0f, 1f)
              }
          val planted = Affine2D.rotationAbout(0.05, 1000.0, 1000.0).compose(Affine2D.translation(50.0, -30.0))
          val b = a.warpAffine(planted, border = Border.CLAMP)

          // Seed only where the 2x2 tracking system is well conditioned. The displacement is now
          // 10x larger in pixels, so the pyramid needs another level to keep it inside the window.
          val seeds =
              a.goodFeaturesToTrack(maxCount = 200, minDistance = 90)
                  .filter { it.x in 240.0..1760.0 && it.y in 240.0..1760.0 }
                  .map { it.toVec2() }
          val flow = opticalFlowLK(a, b, seeds, windowRadius = 8, levels = 5)
          val fit = findHomographyRansac(
              flow.sourcePoints(),
              flow.targetPoints(),
              threshold = 1.5,
              iterations = 1200,
              seed = 3L,
          )

          // How far is the recovered model from the one we planted, in pixels, on a probe grid?
          var worst = 0.0
          for (gx in 400..1600 step 400) for (gy in 400..1600 step 400) {
              val (fx, fy) = fit.homography.apply(gx.toDouble(), gy.toDouble())
              val (tx, ty) = planted.apply(gx.toDouble(), gy.toDouble())
              worst = maxOf(worst, hypot(fx - tx, fy - ty))
          }

          showImgGrid(
              "frame A" to a,
              "frame B (rot 0.05 rad + shift 50,-30)" to b,
              "|A - B| (inferno)" to frameDifference(a, b).normalized().colormap("inferno"),
              "B warped back by the fitted model" to b.warpPerspective(fit.homography.inverse(), border = Border.CLAMP),
              columns = 2,
              cellSide = 280,
          )
          val (mdx, mdy) = flow.medianDisplacement()
          println(
              "${flow.tracked().size}/${seeds.size} tracked; median displacement " +
                  "(${"%.2f".format(mdx)}, ${"%.2f".format(mdy)}) px",
          )
          println("RANSAC ${fit.inlierCount} inliers of ${flow.tracked().size} after ${fit.iterations} iterations")
          println("recovered model agrees with the planted transform to ${"%.3f".format(worst)} px over the probe grid")
          println(fit.homography.toString())

          // One arrow FLine per track. This is the whole family's shape in one line: raster in,
          // geometry out, and the geometry goes to lines() like anything else you draw in Field.
          lines(flow.toFLines(scale = 6.0, minMagnitude = 0.5))
  - execute: { box: imaging_basics, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_filters, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_edges, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_features, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_morphology, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_motion, property: code }
  - await:
      wait: pending
  - wait:
      millis: 500

          // tolerance are pixel distances, so they scale with the image.
          val flines = edges.toContourFLines(minPerimeter = 120, simplifyTolerance = 12.0)

              "source" to src,
              "sobel().dx (signed, coolwarm)" to grad.dx.colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "sobel().dy (signed, coolwarm)" to grad.dy.colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "magnitude (inferno)" to grad.magnitude().normalized().colormap("inferno"),

              cellSide = 260,

  - create:
      box: imaging_features
      name: features — Harris / FAST corners and Hough lines
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1340.0, w: 430.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // A square whose corners are at exactly known coordinates.
          val square = Img.generate(2000, 2000) { x, y -> if (x in 500..1499 && y in 500..1499) 0.92f else 0.08f }
          val harris = square.harrisCorners(threshold = 0.05, minDistance = 120, maxCount = 20)
          val fast = square.fastCorners(threshold = 0.2, minDistance = 120, maxCount = 20)

          val truth = [500.0 to 500.0, 1499.0 to 500.0, 500.0 to 1499.0, 1499.0 to 1499.0]
          val worst = truth.maxOf { (ex, ey) -> harris.minOf { hypot(it.x - ex, it.y - ey) } }

          // Three lines at exactly known (rho, theta), plus a decoy ring Hough must not fit.
          val lineMask = Img.zeros(2000, 2000, 1)
          for (x in 100 until 1900) lineMask.set(x, 400, 0, 1f) // rho = 400,  theta = pi/2
          for (y in 100 until 1900) lineMask.set(1500, y, 0, 1f) // rho = 1500, theta = 0
          for (t in 0 until 2400) {
              val x = 200 + t * 0.6
              val y = 600 + t * 0.6
              if (x < 1999 && y < 1999) lineMask.set(x.toInt(), y.toInt(), 0, 1f)
          }
          for (i in 0 until 3600) {
              val a = 2.0 * PI * i / 3600
              val x = (600 + 220 * kotlin.math.cos(a)).toInt()
              val y = (1500 + 220 * kotlin.math.sin(a)).toInt()
              if (x in 0..1999 && y in 0..1999) lineMask.set(x, y, 0, 1f)
          }
          // threshold is a vote count, so it scales with the number of edge pixels on a line.
          // Named `houghs`, not `lines`, so it cannot shadow the lines() drawing call below.
          val houghs = houghLines(lineMask, thetaSteps = 360, threshold = 1000, maxLines = 5)

          showImgGrid(
              "harrisResponse (signed, coolwarm)" to square.harrisResponse().colormapDiverging("coolwarm"),
              "shiTomasiResponse (viridis)" to square.shiTomasiResponse().normalized().colormap("viridis"),
              "edge mask: 3 lines + a decoy ring" to lineMask,
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 260,
          )
          println("harris ${harris.size} corners, worst ${"%.2f".format(worst)} px from the true square corners")
          println(
              "fast ${fast.size} corners at " +
                  fast.sortedBy { it.y * 1000 + it.x }.joinToString(", ") { "(${it.x.toInt()},${it.y.toInt()})" },
          )
          println(
              "hough " +
                  houghs.joinToString(", ") {
                      "(rho=${"%.0f".format(it.rho)}, theta=${"%.2f".format(it.theta)}, votes=${it.votes})"
                  },

          it has no drawable form until you say which rectangle you are drawing it into. That is
          what toFLine(w, h) is for, and why it is nullable: a peak can name a line that misses.
          */
          lines(
              cornersToFLines(harris, size = 40.0) + houghs.mapNotNull { it.toFLine(lineMask.width, lineMask.height) },
          )
  - create:
      box: imaging_morphology
      name: morphology, connected components, distance transform
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1760.0, w: 450.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Three disjoint discs of known radius, then noise on top of them.
          val discs = [Triple(550.0, 600.0, 280.0), Triple(1500.0, 550.0, 200.0), Triple(1100.0, 1350.0, 140.0)]
          val clean =
              Img.generate(2200, 1800) { x, y ->
                  if (discs.any { (cx, cy, r) -> hypot(x - cx, y - cy) <= r }) 0.85f else 0.15f
              }
          val rng = kotlin.random.Random(3)
          val noisy = clean.copy()
          repeat((noisy.pixelCount * 0.03).toInt()) {
              noisy.data[rng.nextInt(noisy.pixelCount)] = if (rng.nextBoolean()) 0f else 1f
          }

          val mask = noisy.thresholdOtsu()
          val cleaned = mask.open(2, StructuringElement.DISC).close(2, StructuringElement.DISC)
          val cc = cleaned.connectedComponents(8)
          val dt = cleaned.distanceTransform()

          showImgGrid(
              "noisy source" to noisy,
              "thresholdOtsu()" to mask,
              "open(2,DISC).close(2,DISC)" to cleaned,
              "erode(4)" to cleaned.erode(4, StructuringElement.DISC),
              "dilate(4)" to cleaned.dilate(4, StructuringElement.DISC),
              "distanceTransform (magma)" to dt.normalized().colormap("magma"),
              columns = 3,
              cellSide = 250,
          )
          println("${cc.count} components after cleaning (planted ${discs.size} discs):")
          cc.components
              .sortedByDescending { it.area }
              .forEach {
                  println(
                      "  area=${it.area} centroid=(${"%.1f".format(it.centroidX)}, ${"%.1f".format(it.centroidY)}) " +
                          "bbox=${it.boundingWidth}x${it.boundingHeight} fill=${"%.2f".format(it.fillRatio)}",
                  )
              }
          println("distance-transform peak ${"%.1f".format(dt.max())} (largest planted radius ${discs.maxOf { it.third }})")

          // Connected components are blobs; blobs have outlines. Same story as Canny — the raster
          // is the evidence, the FLines are the result you can actually build on.
          lines(cleaned.toContourFLines(minPerimeter = 120, simplifyTolerance = 8.0))
  - create:
      box: imaging_motion
      name: motion — Lucas–Kanade flow and the homography RANSAC fits to it
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 2180.0, w: 520.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Two frames related by a transform we choose, so the answer is known in advance.
          Multi-octave on purpose. Lucas-Kanade is coarse-to-fine: it halves the image several
          times and tracks the big picture first. A texture with only fine detail (period ~30 px)
          aliases away after four halvings and the tracker has nothing to lock onto — that
          version tracked 0 of 125 seeds at this size. Coarse octaves survive to the top of the
          pyramid; the fine ones sharpen the final refinement.
          */
          val a =
              Img.generate(2000, 2000) { x, y ->
                  (0.5 +
                          0.20 * kotlin.math.sin(x * 0.021) * kotlin.math.cos(y * 0.017) +
                          0.14 * kotlin.math.sin((x + y) * 0.011) +
                          0.10 * kotlin.math.sin(x * 0.21) * kotlin.math.cos(y * 0.17) +
                          0.06 * kotlin.math.cos((x - 2.0 * y) * 0.07))
                      .toFloat()
                      .coerceIn(0f, 1f)
              }
          val planted = Affine2D.rotationAbout(0.05, 1000.0, 1000.0).compose(Affine2D.translation(50.0, -30.0))
          val b = a.warpAffine(planted, border = Border.CLAMP)

          // Seed only where the 2x2 tracking system is well conditioned. The displacement is now
          // 10x larger in pixels, so the pyramid needs another level to keep it inside the window.
          val seeds =
              a.goodFeaturesToTrack(maxCount = 200, minDistance = 90)
                  .filter { it.x in 240.0..1760.0 && it.y in 240.0..1760.0 }
                  .map { it.toVec2() }
          val flow = opticalFlowLK(a, b, seeds, windowRadius = 8, levels = 5)
          val fit = findHomographyRansac(
              flow.sourcePoints(),
              flow.targetPoints(),
              threshold = 1.5,
              iterations = 1200,
              seed = 3L,
          )

          // How far is the recovered model from the one we planted, in pixels, on a probe grid?
          var worst = 0.0
          for (gx in 400..1600 step 400) for (gy in 400..1600 step 400) {
              val (fx, fy) = fit.homography.apply(gx.toDouble(), gy.toDouble())
              val (tx, ty) = planted.apply(gx.toDouble(), gy.toDouble())
              worst = maxOf(worst, hypot(fx - tx, fy - ty))
          }

          showImgGrid(
              "frame A" to a,
              "frame B (rot 0.05 rad + shift 50,-30)" to b,
              "|A - B| (inferno)" to frameDifference(a, b).normalized().colormap("inferno"),
              "B warped back by the fitted model" to b.warpPerspective(fit.homography.inverse(), border = Border.CLAMP),
              columns = 2,
              cellSide = 280,
          )
          val (mdx, mdy) = flow.medianDisplacement()
          println(
              "${flow.tracked().size}/${seeds.size} tracked; median displacement " +
                  "(${"%.2f".format(mdx)}, ${"%.2f".format(mdy)}) px",
          )
          println("RANSAC ${fit.inlierCount} inliers of ${flow.tracked().size} after ${fit.iterations} iterations")
          println("recovered model agrees with the planted transform to ${"%.3f".format(worst)} px over the probe grid")
          println(fit.homography.toString())

          // One arrow FLine per track. This is the whole family's shape in one line: raster in,
          // geometry out, and the geometry goes to lines() like anything else you draw in Field.
          lines(flow.toFLines(scale = 6.0, minMagnitude = 0.5))

  - execute: { box: imaging_edges, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_features, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_morphology, property: code }
  - execute: { box: imaging_motion, property: code }
  - await:
      wait: pending
  - wait:
      millis: 500

name: keyframe_code_blend description: > Loadable demo of afield.stdlib/keyframeCodeBlend.kt — blending two *code* keyframes by aligning them and interpolating the numbers they differ in. Five pure-compute boxes, no Window and no Renderer: the StackSL programs are compiled by the same StackSLCompiler the live `stack.auto` setter uses and then run through afield.lang.stacksl.cpu, which interprets the emitted GLSL on the CPU — including its push constants, which is what lets the convention be demonstrated rather than described. 1. kfb_breakdown — the alignment, and what it refuses. Two looks for one patch, same words and different numbers: three moving sites (a warp scale, an offset, a tint vector) and no divergence, so a blend exists. Prints the plan, then the single program a runtime blend runs — each moving literal replaced by `a b ?pc.keyframeBlend .x mix`, which pushes one value exactly as the literal did. Then the same pair with one word changed (`fbm` for `noise`): one divergence, and the blend drops to stepping, because a program built from the left structure with the right numbers would be neither keyframe at either end. 2. kfb_runtime — the same blend, rendered. One program, expanded once, drawn five times with only the push constant changing, as a contact strip from t=0 to t=1. The two endpoint programs are rendered separately and compared pixel for pixel: the largest channel difference at either end is 0.0000, which is the claim the rewrite actually makes. The shader declares `vec4 keyframeBlend` in a `layout(push_constant)` block called `pc`, which is the whole of the convention. 3. kfb_static — where a runtime blend cannot reach, and what happens then. `0.35s3` is an amount modulated by a sine, and `0.2_0.5` is a random range; both grammars want literals in those positions, so no mix expression can be written there. The plan reports runtimeCapable=false and a RUNTIME request comes back as STATIC — a new program per t, printed at three values of t so the numbers can be read moving. Note that the modifier's *frequency* is unchanged and comes back as `3` rather than `3.0`: a site is atomic, and an untouched number keeps its spelling. 4. kfb_kotlin — the other language. Two `sourceBlock { }` expressions differing in two of their three literals; the blend rewrites each moving literal as `afield.animation.keyframes.kfMix(left, right, afield.animation.keyframes.keyframeBlendAmount(id, 0))`, fully qualified so it resolves in a box that imported nothing. Prints the plan and the one expression a runtime blend evaluates, and stops there — see box 5 for why the invocation is not here. 5. kfb_kotlin_run — the generated Kotlin, actually evaluated. Builds a SourceBackedBlock whose box is kfb_kotlin and whose source is the blended expression, then drives the blend parameter and invokes it at five values of t, printing each result beside an expectation computed independently in Kotlin; they agree to four decimals. The first invocation is a real K2 compile of generated source, and the later ones reuse the lambda, which is what "compiles once" means here. It is a separate box on purpose. A SourceBackedBlock hydrates by compiling and evaluating its source on its own box's engine, and asking that engine to evaluate while it is already mid-evaluation re-runs the body that is running — which hydrates again. Measured at 327 nested runs of one body and 355 seconds before it unwound. Hydrating into an *idle* box is fine, which is what this split relies on: kfb_kotlin's body runs exactly once while this box invokes a block that compiles there. ") strip.append("") strip.append("blend ") strip.append(t) strip.append("
") } strip.append("
") display("blend-strip", strip.toString()) // The endpoints, drawn from the endpoint programs themselves. val ends = listOf(0.0 to warm, 1.0 to cool).map { (t, program) -> val v = keyframeBlendVector(t) val raster = StackSLCpu.renderFragment( StackSLCpu.expandStackAuto(template, program), dim, dim, uniforms = mapOf("pc.keyframeBlend" to GlslValue.vec4(v.x, v.y, v.z, v.w)), ) t to raster.rgba } ends.forEach { (t, want) -> val got = rasters.getValue(t) var worst = 0.0f for (i in want.indices) worst = maxOf(worst, kotlin.math.abs(want[i] - got[i])) println("at blend %.1f the one program differs from the keyframe it should be by %.4f".format(t, worst)) } println() println("one program, five draws, only the push constant changing:") println(blended) - create: box: kfb_static name: Where a runtime blend cannot reach frame: { x: 80.0, y: 720.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* Two StackSL token forms carry their numbers inside a grammar that wants literals: a modifier chain (`0.35s3` — an amount modulated by a sine at frequency 3) and a random range (`0.2_0.5`). Hydrating into an *idle* box is fine, which is what this split relies on: kfb_kotlin's body runs exactly once while this box invokes a block that compiles there. Replay this file into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) to see all five on screen, then change a number in one of the two looks, change a *word* in one of them, or add a fourth literal to the Kotlin pair and re-run the box to watch the breakdown change. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs the box's stored `code` property. Companion page: public/docs/keyframer_examples.md. Companion tests: afield.animation.keyframes.KeyframeCodeBlendTest, afield.app.server.KeyframeBrowserProtocolTest. operations: - create: box: kfb_breakdown name: What the alignment finds, and what it refuses frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* A code keyframe is a program. Two of them have no midpoint in general — half a program is not a program — so a keyframe blend steps them. Unless they differ only in numbers, which is the case worth finding, because that is the case a person authoring two looks for one patch keeps producing. */ val warm = "uv 3.0 * fbm 0.15 + [1.0,0.55,0.2] *" val cool = "uv 8.0 * fbm 0.45 + [0.2,0.5,1.0] *" val plan = planStackSLCodeBlend(warm, cool, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)) println(plan.describe()) println("blendable=" + plan.blendable + " runtimeCapable=" + plan.runtimeCapable) println() /* One program, for every t. Each moving literal became a push of both endpoints, a read of the blend push constant, and `mix` — which leaves one value on the stack, exactly as the literal it replaced did, so the surrounding stack arithmetic is untouched. */ println("the one program a runtime blend runs:") println(plan.runtimeSource) println() /* And the refusal. `elsewhere` swaps one token, `noise` for `fbm`: that is a different op, not a moving literal, and a push constant can only mix values, so the blend steps from one program to the other instead of interpolating. */ val elsewhere = "uv 3.0 * noise 0.15 + [1.0,0.55,0.2] *" val stepped = planStackSLCodeBlend(warm, elsewhere, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)) println(stepped.describe()) display(plan) - create: box: kfb_runtime name: The push-constant convention, rendered frame: { x: 80.0, y: 400.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* The claim a runtime blend makes is not that it produces a plausible picture in the middle. It is that at 0 it *is* the left keyframe and at 1 it *is* the right one. That is checkable, and this box checks it: one program, five draws, and the two ends compared pixel for pixel against the programs they are supposed to be. */ import afield.lang.stacksl.cpu.GlslValue import afield.lang.stacksl.cpu.StackSLCpu /* The convention, in a shader: a vec4 called keyframeBlend in the push-constant block. Nothing declares it for you — a `stack.auto` slot cannot declare a uniform of its own, which is why the parameter arrives by agreement rather than by machinery. */ val template = """ #version 450 layout(location = 0) in vec2 fragUV; layout(location = 0) out vec4 outColor; layout(push_constant) uniform Controls { vec4 keyframeBlend; } pc; {{ stack.auto.program }} void main() { vec4 stackInput = vec4(fragUV, 0.0, 0.0); outColor = vec4(clamp(program(stackInput).rgb, 0.0, 1.0), 1.0); } """ .trimIndent() val warm = "uv 3.0 * fbm 0.15 + [1.0,0.55,0.2] *" val cool = "uv 8.0 * fbm 0.45 + [0.2,0.5,1.0] *" val blended = planStackSLCodeBlend(warm, cool, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)).runtimeSource val dim = 56 // Expanded once. A runtime program does not depend on t, so this is the only compile. val expanded = StackSLCpu.expandStackAuto(template, blended) val strip = StringBuilder("
") val rasters = mutableMapOf() for (t in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]) { val v = keyframeBlendVector(t) val raster = StackSLCpu.renderFragment( expanded, dim, dim, uniforms = mapOf("pc.keyframeBlend" to GlslValue.vec4(v.x, v.y, v.z, v.w)), ) rasters[t] = raster.rgba val b64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(raster.toPngBytes()) strip.append("
") strip.append("") strip.append("blend ") strip.append(t) strip.append("
") } strip.append("
") display("blend-strip", strip.toString()) // The endpoints, drawn from the endpoint programs themselves. val ends = [0.0 to warm, 1.0 to cool].map { (t, program) -> val v = keyframeBlendVector(t) val raster = StackSLCpu.renderFragment( StackSLCpu.expandStackAuto(template, program), dim, dim, uniforms = mapOf("pc.keyframeBlend" to GlslValue.vec4(v.x, v.y, v.z, v.w)), ) t to raster.rgba } ends.forEach { (t, want) -> val got = rasters.getValue(t) var worst = 0.0f for (i in want.indices) worst = maxOf(worst, kotlin.math.abs(want[i] - got[i])) println("at blend %.1f the one program differs from the keyframe it should be by %.4f".format(t, worst)) } println() println("one program, five draws, only the push constant changing:") println(blended) - create: box: kfb_static name: Where a runtime blend cannot reach frame: { x: 80.0, y: 720.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* Two StackSL token forms carry their numbers inside a grammar that wants literals: a modifier chain (`0.35s3` — an amount modulated by a sine at frequency 3) and a random range (`0.2_0.5`). No mix expression can be written at either position, so a runtime blend cannot reach them and says so rather than pretending. */ val quiet = "uv 0.35s3 * fbm 0.2_0.5 +" val loud = "uv 0.80s3 * fbm 0.6_0.9 +" val plan = planStackSLCodeBlend(quiet, loud, CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME)) println(plan.describe()) println("asked for RUNTIME, will run " + plan.effectiveMode) println("because " + plan.downgradeReason) println() /* A different program per t, and therefore a compile per t: fine for a scrub, not for a frame loop. Note the modifier's frequency: unchanged between the two, so it comes back as `3` rather than `3.0`. A site is atomic — one moving component rewrites the whole token — and keeping an untouched number's spelling is what stops that showing. */ [0.0, 0.5, 1.0].forEach { t -> println("t=" + t + " " + plan.bake(t)) } display(plan) - create: box: kfb_kotlin name: The same blend, in Kotlin frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1040.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* A Kotlin keyframe is a `sourceBlock { }`: a callable that remembers its own source. Two of them blend the same way, and for the same reason — the interesting pair is the one that differs only in numbers. The transport differs: a shader reads a push constant, and a generated Kotlin expression reads a registry slot addressed by an integer written into its text, because generated text cannot close over a value. */ val quiet = sourceBlock { 2.0f * 3.0f + 1.0f } val loud = sourceBlock { 8.0f * 3.0f + 5.0f } println("left source: " + quiet.source) println("right source: " + loud.source) println() var amount: Any? = quiet val scope = KeyframeScope() scope.target("amount", get = { amount }, set = { v -> amount = v }) scope.codeBlend = CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME) val a = scope.Key(mutableMapOf("amount" to quiet)) val b = scope.Key(mutableMapOf("amount" to loud)) val plan = scope.codeBlendPlans(a, b).getValue("amount") println(plan.describe()) println("the one expression a runtime blend evaluates:") println(plan.runtimeSource) println() println("the middle literal is unchanged between the two, so it is left alone.") /* The invocation is in kfb_kotlin_run, not here. A SourceBackedBlock hydrates by compiling and evaluating its source in its own box, and asking for that from inside this box's own running code re-enters: the nested evaluation replays this snippet, which hydrates again. Invoke one from a frame loop, a control callback, or another box. */ display(plan) - create: box: kfb_kotlin_run name: The generated Kotlin, evaluated frame: { x: 80.0, y: 1360.0, w: 420.0, h: 102.0 } properties: code: | /* The same plan, rebuilt here — building one is pure, so it costs an alignment and nothing else. Then the blended expression is handed to a SourceBackedBlock whose box is kfb_kotlin, so it compiles and runs *there* while this box is the one evaluating. */ val plan = planKotlinCodeBlend( "2.0f * 3.0f + 1.0f", "8.0f * 3.0f + 5.0f", CodeBlendOptions(mode = CodeBlendMode.RUNTIME), ) val block = SourceBackedBlock("kfb_kotlin", plan.runtimeSource) println(plan.runtimeSource) println() // One block, five values of t. The first invocation compiles the generated text through // K2; the rest reuse the lambda, and only the registry slot changes. [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0].forEach { t -> plan.drive(t) val got = block() as Float val want = (2.0f + 6.0f * t.toFloat()) * 3.0f + (1.0f + 4.0f * t.toFloat()) println("t=%.2f block() = %8.4f independently %8.4f".format(t, got, want)) } display(plan) - execute: box: kfb_breakdown - execute: box: kfb_runtime - execute: box: kfb_static - execute: box: kfb_kotlin - execute: box: kfb_kotlin_run

before:
name: keyframe_key_discovery
description: >
  The keyframe browser, and whether it can show you your own keys.

  Three boxes, no GPU, no window: a KeyframeScope needs neither, and each box writes its key directory
  into a fresh temp dir so nothing lands in this document.

    1. kf_before_after  — six keys named `a b c d d2 d3`, the shapes a real session actually produced,
                   browsed twice in one box. The top panel uses `pattern = "??"`, which was the last
                   pattern that session tried; it shows two of the six and now says so, with a button
                   that widens it in one click. The bottom panel uses the default. The printed numbers
                   are the whole story: the old default `**/*.json` found **zero** of these six,
                   because `saveKey` writes the path it is handed and appends no extension, so
                   `capture().save("d3".path)` produces a file called `d3`. `?` is exactly one
                   character and `??` exactly two, so no single-length glob spans `a b c d` and
                   `d2 d3` — and `{?,??}` always did, with nothing anywhere saying so.
    2. kf_junk_vs_damage — four good keys, two files that were never keys, and one key Field wrote and
                   that is now truncated. One red row, two grey ones. What tells the truncated key
                   apart from the junk is not its bytes — it is unparseable either way — but the
                   `.versions` directory still beside it, which is both the proof Field wrote it and
                   the thing you now want.
    3. kf_orphaned_slots — the disagreement that was silent in one direction only. Three keys saved
                   back when the pass had a `blur`; the scope today watches `radius` and a `feather`
                   nothing has ever saved. `glow@feather` gets the amber "never saved" row the browser
                   already had; `glow@blur` is saved in all three keys, renders with its real range,
                   and applies to nowhere — so it is now struck through and named in the header. Also
                   shows why `scopeAttached` is a flag of its own: a read-only browse and a scope
                   watching nothing both leave `scopeSlots` empty and must not read the same.

  The saved document at `dev_docs/agents/demos/keyframe_key_discovery/` is this same scene.
  Companion tests: afield.animation.keyframes.KeyframeBrowserTest and
  afield.app.server.KeyframeBrowserProtocolTest.
operations:
  - create:
      box: kf_before_after
      name: 1 - Six keys, and the pattern that showed two
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 600.0, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Six saved keys, and whether the browser can show them to you.

          The names are not invented. They are copied from a live session: `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, `d2`, `d3`,
          saved with `kfs.capture().save("d3".path)` — which writes a file called `d3`, with no extension,
          because `saveKey` writes the path it is handed and appends nothing.

          Run this box. Two browsers appear. The top one is what you used to get.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          // A temp directory, so this demo writes nothing into your document.
          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-key-discovery")

          // A live scope, so both browsers get Apply and the "you have never saved this" row.
          val glow = Structure()
          glow.bind("radius") { 4.0f }
          glow.bind("intensity") { 0.35f }
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()
          kfs.target("glow@radius", glow)
          kfs.target("glow@intensity", glow)

          // Six keys, saved the ordinary way — through the real writer, so each gets a real `.versions`
          // history beside it.
          listOf(1f, 3f, 6f, 10f, 15f, 21f).forEachIndexed { i, r ->
              val name = listOf("a", "b", "c", "d", "d2", "d3")[i]
              glow.bind("radius") { r }
              glow.bind("intensity") { 0.1f + i * 0.15f }
              kfs.capture().save(dir.resolve(name), "look $name")
          }

          // And the file macOS leaves in any folder a Finder window has opened. Nobody asked for it.
          Files.writeString(dir.resolve(".DS_Store"), "Bud1 (this is not a key)")

          /*
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          The numbers, before the pictures.
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          */

          val old = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "**/*.json")
          val narrow = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "??")
          val now = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob)

          println(
              "keys on disk: " + dir.toFile().list()!!.filter { !it.endsWith(".versions") && !it.startsWith(".") }.sorted(),
          )
          println("plus, uninvited: " + dir.toFile().list()!!.filter { it.startsWith(".") }.sorted())
          println()
          println("the old default, '**/*.json':  ${old.files.size} keys  <- 'No key files matched'")
          println("the last pattern tried, '??':  ${narrow.files.size} keys  (${narrow.skipSummary()})")
          println(
              "brace alternation, '{?,??}':   ${KeyframeCollection.load(dir, "{?,??}").files.size} keys" +
                  "  <- this always worked, and nothing said so",
          )
          println("the default now, '$everyKeyGlob':          ${now.files.size} keys  (${now.skipSummary()})")
          println()
          println("what '??' hid: " + narrow.skipped.filter { it.kind.name == "Hidden" }.map { it.relative })
          println("problems, either way: ${now.problems.size}  <- .DS_Store is ignored, not an error")

          /*
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          The two browsers. Compare the headers.
          ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
          */

          // BEFORE: the pattern the session ended on. Two keys of six, and — this is the fix — a line under
          // the header saying so, with a button that widens it in one click.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, pattern = "??", channel = "before: pattern = \"??\"", scope = kfs, height = 320)

          // AFTER: the default. Every key at any depth, with the OS turd counted as ignored rather than
          // reported as a problem.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, channel = "after: the default", scope = kfs, height = 380)
  - create:
      box: kf_junk_vs_damage
      name: 2 - Junk is not damage
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 60.0, w: 381.8, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Two files fail to decode. Only one of them is your problem.

          This directory holds four good keys, two files that were never keys, and one key that Field wrote
          and that is now truncated. A `.DS_Store` — a file the operating system wrote without asking — is
          not a corrupt key, and a list that files both under one red heading is a permanent false alarm.
          A permanent false alarm teaches you to stop reading the alarm.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-junk-vs-damage")
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()

          // Four keys, saved properly.
          listOf("a" to 1f, "b" to 2f, "c" to 3f, "d" to 4f).forEach { (n, r) ->
              kfs.saveKey(dir.resolve(n), kfs.Key(mutableMapOf("glow@radius" to r)), "look $n")
          }

          // One key, saved properly and then truncated — a write that stopped halfway.
          kfs.saveKey(dir.resolve("e"), kfs.Key(mutableMapOf("glow@radius" to 5f)), "look e")
          val e = dir.resolve("e")
          Files.writeString(e, Files.readString(e).take(14))

          // Two files that were never keys.
          Files.writeString(dir.resolve(".DS_Store"), "Bud1 (not a key)")
          Files.writeString(dir.resolve("notes.txt"), "remember to try the wider glow")

          val c = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob)

          println("rows:     " + c.files.map { it.relative })
          println("problems: " + c.problems)
          println("ignored:  " + c.skipped.filter { it.kind.name == "NotAKey" }.map { it.relative })
          println("notice:   " + c.skipSummary())
          println()
          /*
          The ownership test, spelled out. `e` is not valid JSON any more, so a content-only ladder would
          have filed it as "not JSON, not a key": a damaged key reported as junk, which is the
          misclassification that loses work. What proves Field wrote it
          is the `.versions` directory still sitting beside it, which is also exactly what you now want.
          */
          println(
              "e is unparseable, and e.versions still holds " +
                  (dir.resolve("e.versions").toFile().list()?.count { it.endsWith(".json") } ?: 0) +
                  " file(s) — so the damage is recoverable, and the row says to open the version rail",
          )

          // One red row, two grey ones. Hover the notice to read the per-file reasons.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, channel = "junk is not damage", scope = kfs, height = 380)
  - create:
      box: kf_orphaned_slots
      name: 3 - A saved slot that applies to nowhere
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 226.0, w: 592.8, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          A saved slot that applies to nowhere.

          The browser has always drawn one half of this: a slot the scope watches that no key holds — the
          "you have never saved this" row. The other half was silent. A slot a *key* holds that the scope no
          longer watches renders as an ordinary row, with its real saved range across every key, and
          `KeyframeScope.loadKey` is explicit about what happens next: "a file whose values have since left
          the scope loads fine — the extra names simply have nowhere to go on apply."

          So a rename half-done looks exactly like a working slot, and Apply quietly drops it.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-orphaned-slots")

          // Three keys saved back when the pass had a `blur` as well as a `radius`.
          run {
              val old = Structure()
              val past = KeyframeScope()
              past.target("glow@radius", old)
              past.target("glow@blur", old)
              listOf(1f to 4f, 6f to 5f, 11f to 6f).forEachIndexed { i, (r, b) ->
                  old.bind("radius") { r }
                  old.bind("blur") { b }
                  past.capture().save(dir.resolve(listOf("a", "b", "c")[i]), "look ${listOf("a", "b", "c")[i]}")
              }
          }

          // The pass as it is today: `blur` is gone, and a `feather` has arrived that nothing has ever saved.
          val glow = Structure()
          glow.bind("radius") { 7f }
          glow.bind("feather") { 0.5f }
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()
          kfs.target("glow@radius", glow)
          kfs.target("glow@feather", glow)

          val c = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, kfs)

          println("slots in view:      " + c.slotNames)
          println("watched by the scope: " + c.scopeSlots.sorted())
          println("saved, and wired to nothing: " + c.orphanedSlots + "   <- Apply drops these")
          println()
          c.slots().forEach { s ->
              val tag = when {
                  s.orphaned -> "ORPHANED  (saved in ${s.presentIn}/${s.total} keys, applies to nowhere)"
                  s.inScope && s.presentIn == 0 -> "never saved (the scope watches it, no key holds it)"
                  else -> "live"
              }
              println("  ${s.name.padEnd(14)} ${tag}")
          }
          println()
          /*
          The flag is not just "scopeSlots is empty". A read-only browse cannot know which slots are live,
          and must not accuse every row; an attached scope watching nothing must accuse every row. Both
          leave scopeSlots empty, so `scopeAttached` is what tells them apart.
          */
          val readOnly = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, scope = null)
          println("read-only browse: scopeAttached=${readOnly.scopeAttached}, orphaned=${readOnly.orphanedSlots}")
          println("  (no scope, so no accusation — this is why scopeAttached exists as its own flag)")

          // `glow@blur` is struck through and named in the header; `glow@radius` is plain; `glow@feather` is
          // the amber "never saved" row this browser already had.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, channel = "saved, but wired to nothing", scope = kfs, height = 400)
  - execute:
      box: kf_before_after
  - execute:
      box: kf_junk_vs_damage
  - execute:
      box: kf_orphaned_slots

  - create:
      box: kf_junk_vs_damage
      name: 2 - Junk is not damage
      frame: { x: 700.0, y: 60.0, w: 381.8, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Two files fail to decode. Only one of them is your problem.

          This directory holds four good keys, two files that were never keys, and one key that Field wrote
          and that is now truncated. A `.DS_Store` — a file the operating system wrote without asking — is
          not a corrupt key, and a list that files both under one red heading is a permanent false alarm.
          A permanent false alarm teaches you to stop reading the alarm.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-junk-vs-damage")
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()

          // Four keys, saved properly.
          ["a" to 1f, "b" to 2f, "c" to 3f, "d" to 4f].forEach { (n, r) ->
              kfs.saveKey(dir.resolve(n), kfs.Key(mutableMapOf("glow@radius" to r)), "look $n")
          }

          // One key, saved properly and then truncated — a write that stopped halfway.
          kfs.saveKey(dir.resolve("e"), kfs.Key(mutableMapOf("glow@radius" to 5f)), "look e")
          val e = dir.resolve("e")
          Files.writeString(e, Files.readString(e).take(14))

          // Two files that were never keys.

          Files.writeString(dir.resolve("notes.txt"), "remember to try the wider glow")

          val c = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob)

          println("problems: " + c.problems)

  - create:
      box: kf_orphaned_slots
      name: 3 - A saved slot that applies to nowhere
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 226.0, w: 592.8, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          A saved slot that applies to nowhere.

          The browser has always drawn one half of this: a slot the scope watches that no key holds — the
          "you have never saved this" row. The other half was silent. A slot a *key* holds that the scope no
          longer watches renders as an ordinary row, with its real saved range across every key, and
          `KeyframeScope.loadKey` is explicit about what happens next: "a file whose values have since left
          the scope loads fine — the extra names simply have nowhere to go on apply."

          So a rename half-done looks exactly like a working slot, and Apply quietly drops it.
          */

          import java.nio.file.Files

          val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("keyframe-orphaned-slots")

          // Three keys saved back when the pass had a `blur` as well as a `radius`.
          run {
              val old = Structure()
              val past = KeyframeScope()
              past.target("glow@radius", old)
              past.target("glow@blur", old)
              [1f to 4f, 6f to 5f, 11f to 6f].forEachIndexed { i, (r, b) ->
                  old.bind("radius") { r }
                  old.bind("blur") { b }
                  past.capture().save(dir.resolve(["a", "b", "c"][i]), "look ${listOf("a", "b", "c")[i]}")
              }
          }

          // The pass as it is today: `blur` is gone, and a `feather` has arrived that nothing has ever saved.
          val glow = Structure()
          glow.bind("radius") { 7f }
          glow.bind("feather") { 0.5f }
          val kfs = KeyframeScope()
          kfs.target("glow@radius", glow)
          kfs.target("glow@feather", glow)

          val c = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, kfs)

          println("slots in view:      " + c.slotNames)
          println("watched by the scope: " + c.scopeSlots.sorted())
          println("saved, and wired to nothing: " + c.orphanedSlots + "   <- Apply drops these")
          println()
          c.slots().forEach { s ->
              val tag = when {
                  s.orphaned -> "ORPHANED  (saved in ${s.presentIn}/${s.total} keys, applies to nowhere)"
                  s.inScope && s.presentIn == 0 -> "never saved (the scope watches it, no key holds it)"
                  else -> "live"
              }
              println("  ${s.name.padEnd(14)} ${tag}")
          }
          println()
          /*
          The flag is not just "scopeSlots is empty". A read-only browse cannot know which slots are live,
          and must not accuse every row; an attached scope watching nothing must accuse every row. Both
          leave scopeSlots empty, so `scopeAttached` is what tells them apart.
          */
          val readOnly = KeyframeCollection.load(dir, everyKeyGlob, scope = null)
          println("read-only browse: scopeAttached=${readOnly.scopeAttached}, orphaned=${readOnly.orphanedSlots}")
          println("  (no scope, so no accusation — this is why scopeAttached exists as its own flag)")

          // `glow@blur` is struck through and named in the header; `glow@radius` is plain; `glow@feather` is
          // the amber "never saved" row this browser already had.
          keyframeBrowser(dir, channel = "saved, but wired to nothing", scope = kfs, height = 400)
  - execute:
      box: kf_before_after
  - execute:
      box: kf_junk_vs_damage
  - execute:
      box: kf_orphaned_slots

before:
name: kolakoski_euclid
description: >
  Kolakoski counts, Euclid places. A Euclidean rhythm spreads a density you chose in advance as
  evenly as it can; the Kolakoski word is the only sequence over {1,2} that is its own run-length
  encoding. This scene crosses them: the word says HOW MANY hits a group gets, and bjorklund says
  WHERE inside the group they sit — locally maximally even, globally self-describing.

  Box 1 is the flat version, five lines of it: eight groups of three slots, twelve onsets, rolled
  against `euclid(12,24)` and `kolakoski(24)` at the same density so the difference is a figure
  rather than a claim, and played at both distributions so it is also a sound. Box 2 is the tree —
  every pulse asks the word how many children it has, bjorklund places them on the parent's own
  slot grid, and each child runs until the next one, so a level always tiles the bar and a count of
  1 is a pulse that holds. The level sizes are the word's own partial sums: 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7. Box 3
  puts a player on the canvas rather than in an output, through the `customization` property, which
  is saved with the document.

  Three things this scene is careful about, each of which was wrong first. Tempo: the bar is 24
  slots, so at the usual docs `cps = 2` the figure plays 24 hits a second and fuses into a growl —
  it runs at 0.35. Voice: `showDirtAudio` mixes the real Dirt-Samples offline, where `showPatAudio`
  would render `sd` and `hh` as filtered white noise; with no sample library present it falls back
  to that synth voice and still runs. And visibility: every output gets its own channel and every
  channel is opened, because an unopened channel is collapsed to zero height and a second write to
  one channel replaces the first.
operations:
  - create:
      box: kolakoski_x_euclid
      name: 1 - counts and placement
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 405.3, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          1 - Kolakoski counts, Euclid places.

          The Kolakoski word is the only sequence over {1,2} that is its own run-length encoding.
          Here its terms are read as DENSITIES rather than durations: each one says how many hits
          go into the next group of three slots, and `bd(c,3)` spreads those hits as evenly as the
          group allows. Locally maximally even; globally self-describing.

          POKE THIS: the 3 in "[bd($it,3)]" is the group size, and kolakoskiWord(8) is how many
          groups. Try `kolakoskiWord(8, a = 2, b = 3)` with a group of 4 - no group is ever empty
          and none is ever full, so the bar keeps moving without ever locking to the grid.
          */
          val counts = kolakoskiWord(8) // 1 2 2 1 1 2 1 2 - sums to 12
          val hybrid = pat(counts.joinToString(" ") { "[bd($it,3)]" }) // [bd(1,3)] [bd(2,3)] ...

          showPatRollOf(
              "kolakoski x euclid" to hybrid,
              "euclid(12,24)" to struct(euclid(12, 24), pat("bd")),
              "kolakoski(24)" to struct(kolakoski(24), pat("bd")),
              title = "12 onsets in 24 slots, three ways",
              cycles = 2,
              channel = "roll",
          )
          /*
          TEMPO. This bar is 24 slots, not 4, so cps means something very different here than it does
          in `pat("bd sd hh sd")`: a slot lasts 1/(24*cps) seconds and the figure plays 12*cps hits per
          second. At the usual docs tempo of cps = 2 that is 24 kicks a second - a 24Hz pulse train,
          which the ear hears as a low growl rather than as a rhythm. 0.35 puts it at 4.2 hits/s.
          */
          val cps = 0.35

          /*
          showDirtAudio, not showPatAudio: the same call shape, but it mixes the real Dirt-Samples
          offline instead of patVoice's 62Hz sine. A player in the output AND a real file on disk -
          `"name.wav".file` resolves into this document's own files/ folder.
          */
          val dirt = showDirtAudio(hybrid, cycles = 3, cps = cps, channel = "audio")

          // The same density, maximally even, at the same tempo - the thing the hybrid is NOT.
          showDirtAudio(struct(euclid(12, 24), pat("bd")), cycles = 3, cps = cps, channel = "audio-even")

          val audio = dirt.audio
          val wav = "kolakoski-flat.wav".file
          afield.audio.engine.WavFloatArrayWriter.writeStereo16(wav, audio.left, audio.right, PatSoundDocs.SR, 0.9f)
          println(
              "wrote $wav — ${"%.1f".format(12 * cps)} hits/s, samples: ${dirt.usedSamples}, matched ${dirt.matched}, synth fallback ${dirt.unmatched}",
          )

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
          ### The same density, distributed three ways

          - **kolakoski x euclid** - the hybrid. Counts from the word, placement from bjorklund.
          - **euclid(12,24)** - maximally even, and therefore a flat alternation.
          - **kolakoski(24)** - the word read as run lengths instead, the figure Field already had.

          `patCondense(hybrid).notation` is `${patCondense(hybrid).notation}` - the language recognising
          the Kolakoski in it on its own.
          """,
          )

          /*
          Two things an output has to get right to be visible at all. A channel that is never opened
          is collapsed - the player is in the DOM at zero size - and a channel holds ONE thing, so a
          markdown() into "main" would have replaced the player had it not been given its own channel.
          */
          displayOpen("roll")
          displayOpen("audio")
          displayOpen("audio-even")
          displayOpen("main")
  - create:
      box: kolakoski_tree
      name: 2 - the branching tree
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 226.0, w: 381.8, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          2 - Kolakoski branches, Euclid places, and the levels are pulse levels.

          Every pulse asks the word how many children it has. bjorklund puts those children on the
          parent's own `slots` grid as evenly as it can, and each child runs until the next one - so
          a level always tiles the bar, and a count of 1 is a pulse that simply holds. The level
          sizes are the word's own partial sums: 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 11, ...

          POKE THIS: `slots` is where the Euclid lives - on 3 slots two children split the parent
          2:1, not down the middle. `a`/`b` is the alphabet: {2,3} on 4 slots never leaves a lone
          hit. `depth` is how far down the tree the music goes.
          */
          val depth = 5
          val slots = 3
          val a = 1
          val b = 2

          fun tile(depth: Int, slots: Int, a: Int, b: Int): List<List<PatArc>> {
              val word = kolakoskiWord(4 shl depth, a, b) // more terms than the tree can eat
              var level = listOf(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
              var cursor = 0
              val levels = mutableListOf(level)
              repeat(depth) {
                  val next = mutableListOf<PatArc>()
                  for (parent in level) {
                      val children = word[cursor++].coerceAtMost(slots)
                      val step = parent.dur / PatQ.of(slots)
                      val on = bjorklund(children, slots).withIndex().filter { it.value }.map { it.index }
                      on.forEachIndexed { k, slot ->
                          val start = parent.start + step * PatQ.of(slot)
                          val end = if (k + 1 < on.size) parent.start + step * PatQ.of(on[k + 1]) else parent.end
                          next += PatArc(start, end)
                      }
                  }
                  level = next
                  levels += level
              }
              return levels
          }

          fun asPat(arcs: List<PatArc>, name: String = "bd") = fromCycle { sub ->
              arcs.mapNotNull { arc -> arc.intersect(sub)?.let { PatEvent(it, name, whole = arc) } }
          }

          val t = tile(depth, slots, a, b)

          // The word starts on a 1, so R1 is R0 held - the first branch that splits anything is R2.
          showPatRollOf(
              *t.mapIndexed { n, level -> "R$n (${level.size})" to asPat(level) }.toTypedArray(),
              title = "each pulse subdivides into ${a} or ${b} on a ${slots}-slot grid",
              cycles = 1,
              channel = "tree",
          )

          /*
          The rings as hierarchical pulse levels: one voice per level, so every hit of a fine level
          sits inside exactly one hit of the level above it.
          Coarse loud, fine quiet. Every coarse onset is also a fine onset - that is what a tree means -
          so at equal gain all four voices land together on the strong hits and the hierarchy turns into
          a pile. The gain ramp makes it foreground and background instead. Short samples for the same
          reason: sd:2 and click decay before the next level arrives.
          */
          val voices = listOf("bd" to 1.0, "sd:2" to 0.7, "hh:2" to 0.45, "click" to 0.35)
          val played = t.takeLast(voices.size)
          val music = stack(
              *played
                  .mapIndexed { i, level ->
                      asPat(level, voices[i].first) with gain(voices[i].second)
                  }
                  .toTypedArray(),
          )

          showPatRollOf(
              *played
                  .mapIndexed { i, level ->
                      "${voices[i].first} (${level.size})" to asPat(level, voices[i].first)
                  }
                  .toTypedArray(),
              title = "the last four levels, one voice each",
              cycles = 2,
              channel = "levels",
          )
          val dirt = showDirtAudio(music, cycles = 8, cps = 1.0, channel = "audio") // real samples, not patVoice
          val audio = dirt.audio
          val wav = "kolakoski-tree-${slots}-${a}${b}-d$depth.wav".file
          afield.audio.engine.WavFloatArrayWriter.writeStereo16(wav, audio.left, audio.right, PatSoundDocs.SR, 0.9f)
          println("wrote $wav — samples: ${dirt.usedSamples}, matched ${dirt.matched}, synth fallback ${dirt.unmatched}")

          markdown(
              "main",
              """
          ### Level sizes: ${t.joinToString(", ") { it.size.toString() }}

          Those are the partial sums of the Kolakoski word - each level eats as many terms as the level
          above it has pulses, and the sum of those terms is the next level's size.
          """,
          )

          displayOpen("tree")
          displayOpen("audio")
          displayOpen("levels")
          displayOpen("main")
  - create:
      box: wav_on_canvas
      name: 3 - a wav on the canvas
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 392.0, w: 393.5, h: 136.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          3 - A player that lives on the canvas, not in an output.

          showPatAudio puts an <audio> in the box's OUTPUT, which is recomputed every run and is not
          saved with the document. `customization` is a box property - JS run against the box's own
          element on the canvas, and it IS saved - so an audio element appended there is part of the
          document: reopen it tomorrow, press play, no run needed.

          POKE THIS: change the pattern. Keep the clip short - it travels as base64 inside the document,
          so ~4s of stereo is ~700KB of property. cps is low because the bar is 24 slots wide: see the
          tempo note in kolakoski_x_euclid.
          */
          val counts = kolakoskiWord(8)
          val hybrid = pat(counts.joinToString(" ") { "[bd($it,3)]" })

          val dirt = patRenderStereoDirt(hybrid, cycles = 2, cps = 0.35) // 5.7s; 24-slot bar, so 4.2 hits/s
          val rendered = dirt.audio
          val bytes = afield.audio.engine.WavFloatArrayWriter.encodeStereo16(
              rendered.left,
              rendered.right,
              PatSoundDocs.SR,
              0.9f,
          )

          // The file on disk, for dragging into an editor...
          val wav = "kolakoski-canvas.wav".file
          wav.writeBytes(bytes)

          // ...and the same bytes pinned into this box on the canvas.
          val b64 = java.util.Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(bytes)
          customization =
              """
              this.style.background = "var(--field-bg)"
              if (!this.querySelector("audio.field-wav")) {
                  this.insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend",
                      "<audio class='field-wav' controls style='width:100%'></audio>")
              }
              this.querySelector("audio.field-wav").src = "data:audio/wav;base64,$b64"
          """

          println("${bytes.size / 1024}KB of wav, on the canvas and at $wav — samples: ${dirt.usedSamples} ${dirt.matched}")
  - launch: { box: kolakoski_x_euclid, property: code }
  - launch: { box: kolakoski_tree, property: code }
  - launch: { box: wav_on_canvas, property: code }
  - await: { wait: pending }
