              pat("45*16") with cutoff(curve) with gain(0.7),
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.SAW, baseHz = 110.0, decay = 0.012, sustain = 0.3),
              channel = "sound",
          )
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 4 ── the flagship listen: two cycles flat, two cycles following an LFO.
  - create:
      box: pat_demo_gain
      name: 4 — hear the difference
      frame: { x: 820.0, y: 520.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Sixteen hats a cycle. `whenCycle` is the existing operator for "from cycle 2 on, play
          this instead", so the first half of the file is what the old surface could express and
          the second half is the identical pattern with the gain following a sine.
          */
          val hats = pat("hh*16")
          val demo = hats.whenCycle({ it >= 2 }) { hats with gain(sine().range(0.08, 1.0)) }

          showPatRollOf(
              "flat (cycles 0-1)" to hats,
              "gain(sine()) (cycles 2-3)" to (hats with gain(sine().range(0.08, 1.0))),
              title = "the same sixteen hats, before and after",
              subtitle = "rectangle height is the gain each note latched",
              cycles = 2,
              paramKey = "gain",
          )
          displayOpen("main")

          val audio = showPatAudio(
              demo,
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.NOISE, decay = 0.006, sustain = 0.05),
              channel = "sound",
          )
          displayOpen("sound")

          // The same measurement the smoke test makes, live: per-note level, flat then modulated.
          val onsets = PatSoundDocs.onsetPeaks(audio.mono)
          val flat = onsets.take(onsets.size / 2).map { it.rms }
          val modulated = onsets.drop(onsets.size / 2).map { it.rms }
          println("${onsets.size} hats detected")
          println("flat half level CV      = %.4f".format(PatSoundDocs.variation(flat)))
          println("modulated half level CV = %.4f".format(PatSoundDocs.variation(modulated)))
  # 5 ── the pitch surface, and the part Tidal has no answer for.
  - create:
      box: pat_demo_voice_leading
      name: 5 — voice leading
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1020.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Spelled from each chord's own root, a progression makes the hand leap. voiceLead()
          // picks each chord's inversion and octave to minimise how far the voices have to move.
          val progression = chords("c'maj7 a'min7 d'min7 g'dom7")
          val asWritten = progression.events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }.map { it.value }
          val voiceLed =
              progression
                  .voiceLead(center = 60)
                  .events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
                  .sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }
                  .map { it.value }

          showPatRoll("voice-leading")
          displayOpen("main")

          println("as written : $asWritten")
          println("voice-led  : $voiceLed")
          println(
              "movement   : %.0f semitones as written, %.0f voice-led"
                  .format(
                      patTotalVoiceMovement(asWritten),
                      patTotalVoiceMovement(voiceLed),
                  ),
          )
          println(
              "harmony unchanged: " +
                  asWritten.zip(voiceLed).all { (a, b) ->
                      a.map { Math.floorMod(it, 12) }.toSortedSet() == b.map { Math.floorMod(it, 12) }.toSortedSet()
                  },
          )

          // Hear both: two cycles as written, two voice-led.
          val arped = progression.arpeggiate().texts()
          val led = progression.voiceLead(center = 60).arpeggiate().texts()
          showPatAudio(
              arped.whenCycle({ it >= 2 }) { led },
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 1.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.SINE, decay = 0.02, sustain = 0.45),
              channel = "sound",
          )
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 6 ── the box to edit: a whole groove from the arrangement surface.
  - create:
      box: pat_demo_playground
      name: 6 — playground (edit me)
      frame: { x: 820.0, y: 1020.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // A little piece. Change any string or any number and re-run this box: the roll and the
          // audio player both come from the same pattern, so they can never disagree.
          val kick = struct(euclid(3, 8), pat("bd"))
          val snare = pat("~ sd ~ sd") with gain(0.8)
          val hats = pat("hh*16?0.3") with gain(sine().range(0.1, 0.55))
          val drums = stack(kick, snare, hats).off(1, 16) { it with gain(0.18) }

          // A bass line spelled in a scale, with a filter that opens across two cycles.
          val bass = run(8).scale("minPent", root = 36).texts().with(sustain(0.5), cutoff(saw().rangex(200, 2400)))

          // A chord pad, voice-led so it does not leap, arpeggiated up.
          val pad = chords("<c'min7 a'maj7> f'maj7").voiceLead(center = 67).arpeggiate().texts()

          showPatRollOf(
              "drums" to drums,
              "bass" to bass,
              "pad" to pad,
              title = "a groove, from the arrangement surface",
              subtitle = "euclid / off / ?degrade / scale / voiceLead / arpeggiate",
              cycles = 2,
          )
          displayOpen("main")

          showPatAudio(
              drums,
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.01, sustain = 0.08),
              channel = "drums",
          )
          showPatAudio(
              bass,
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.SAW, decay = 0.03, sustain = 0.5),
              channel = "bass",
          )
          showPatAudio(
              pad,
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.TRIANGLE, decay = 0.05, sustain = 0.6),
              channel = "pad",
          )
          displayOpen("drums")
          displayOpen("bass")
          displayOpen("pad")

          println("drums: ${drums.events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).size} events/cycle")
          println("bass : ${bass.events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).map { it.value }}")
          println("pad  : ${pad.events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).map { it.value }}")
  # 7 ── groove: swing you can hear, and the substitution primitive.
  - create:
      box: pat_demo_groove
      name: 7 — groove and substitution
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 1560.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // swing() is exact rational time, not a nudge in milliseconds: every off-beat lands a
          // third of a subdivision late and the pattern stays exactly quantised.
          val hats = pat("hh*8")
          showPatRoll("groove")
          displayOpen("main")

          println("straight : " + hats.events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).map { "${it.arc.start}" })
          println(
              "swing(4) : " +
                  hats
                      .swing(4)
                      .events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
                      .sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }
                      .map { "${it.arc.start}" },
          )

          // squeeze replaces each event with a whole pattern, compressed into that event's arc —
          // mini-notation nesting, over Kotlin values. Compare `join`, which does not rescale.
          val nested = pat("a b").squeeze { if (it == "a") pat("1 2 3") else pat("4 5") }
          println(
              "squeeze  : " +
                  nested
                      .events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
                      .sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }
                      .map { "${it.value}@${it.arc.start}" },
          )

          // Two cycles straight, then two swung. This is the one to listen to.
          showPatAudio(
              hats.whenCycle({ it >= 2 }) { hats.swing(4) },
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(wave = PatWave.NOISE, decay = 0.008, sustain = 0.06),
              channel = "swing",
          )
          displayOpen("swing")

          // And a full bar from one Euclidean figure: bd on the onsets, hh on everything else.
          showPatAudio(
              euclidFull(3, 8, pat("bd"), pat("hh") with gain(0.35)),
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 2.0,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.012, sustain = 0.1),
              channel = "euclid",
          )
          displayOpen("euclid")
  # 8 ── mini-notation: the step markers, seen and heard against their bracketed equivalents.
  - create:
      box: pat_demo_mini_notation
      name: 8 — mini-notation markers
      frame: { x: 820.0, y: 1560.0, w: 300.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          Three standalone step markers. Each is shorthand for a bracketed form, so each pair
          below must come out arc-for-arc identical — and the roll draws them one above the other
          so you can check by eye as well as by assertion.
          */
          showPatRoll("mini-notation")
          displayOpen("main")

          val pairs = [
              "bd sd . hh hh hh" to "[bd sd] [hh hh hh]", // `.` groups
              "bd _ _ sd" to "bd@3 sd", // `_` extends
              "bd ! ! sd" to "bd!3 sd", // bare `!` repeats
          ]
          for ((shorthand, bracketed) in pairs) {
              val a = pat(shorthand).events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }
              val b = pat(bracketed).events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).sortedBy { it.arc.start.toDouble() }
              val same = a.map { it.arc } == b.map { it.arc } && a.map { it.value } == b.map { it.value }
              println(
                  "%-20s == %-22s : %s   %s"
                      .format(
                          shorthand,
                          bracketed,
                          same,
                          a.joinToString(" ") { "${it.value}@${it.arc.start}" },
                      ),
              )
          }

          // A `.` inside a token is still part of the token — decimals and sample payloads are safe.
          println(
              "0.5 1.25 -> " + pat("0.5 1.25").nums().events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).map { it.value },
          )
          println("my_atom  -> " + pat("my_atom b").events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).map { it.value })

          // A sample-index suffix becomes an `n` parameter without changing the atom.
          pat("bd:3 sd 808:12").events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE)).forEach {
              println("atom ${it.value} -> n=${it.annotations["n"]}, span=\"${it.sourceSpan?.text}\"")
          }

          // Hear the dot: two cycles of five even notes, then the same five notes grouped.
          showPatAudio(
              pat("bd sd hh hh hh").whenCycle({ it >= 2 }) { pat("bd sd . hh hh hh") },
              cycles = 4,
              cps = 1.0,
              voice = patVoice(decay = 0.012, sustain = 0.12),
              channel = "dot",
          )
          displayOpen("dot")
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_signals }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_structure }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_parameter }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_gain }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_voice_leading }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_playground }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_groove }
  - execute: { box: pat_demo_mini_notation }

before:
name: petri_sound
description: >
  Loadable demo of Petri nets as a sequencer (afield.simulation.petri) — the model and firing engine in
  PetriNets.kt, the `PatPattern` bridge in PetriMusic.kt, the notation in PetriNotation.kt, the
  structural analysis in PetriAnalysis.kt and the drawing in PetriVisual.kt. Seven pure-compute
  boxes; no Window, no Renderer, no GPU, no audio device.
  Every box draws its net with `showPetriNet` and renders what the net plays with `showDirtAudio`
  (DirtRender.kt) — mixed *offline* from the real Tidal Dirt-Samples library if it is installed on
  this machine, and from the synthetic `patVoice` if it is not, saying which in its output either
  way. So you SEE the token move and HEAR actual drums in the same output, with no audio device
  anywhere. A net emits a `PatPattern<String>`, which is why one call is enough — a Petri net is a
  pattern like any other:
    1. smallest loop   — one token, two transitions, alternating bd/sd. The net-as-clock in eight
                         lines, drawn and played.
    2. polyrhythm      — five against three. Nothing in the source says fifteen; `settle()` finds it
                         and four cycles of audio let you hear the two rings drift apart and come
                         back.
    3. structure       — a section token walking verse -> verse -> chorus while a separate ring plays
                         the bar. Petri nets as medium-term song form, not just rhythm.
    4. tokens          — tokens carrying `euclid` patterns as their colour, so what a transition
                         plays depends on which token reached it.
    5. philosophers    — the non-musical one, for contrast: the same engine finding a deadlock, then
                         a starvation, then neither. Silent on purpose.
    6. playground      — a whole groove in the `#petri` notation, drawn, analysed and played. This is
                         the box to edit.
    7. live            — the other playback path: the real polyphonic Dirt player through the
                         transport, tempo-synced and interruptible, behind a `live` flag that is
                         false by default because `audio { }` opens a real output device.
  Replay into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) or open the materialized
  document; then change any net and re-run that box. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs
  the box's stored `code` property. See public/docs/petri_nets.md and public/docs/petri_cheatsheet.md.
operations:
  # 1 ── the smallest thing that plays: a token going round.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_loop
      name: 1 — the smallest loop
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A place holds tokens; a transition fires when all its inputs have one. Give a
          transition a sound after the `:` and firing it plays that sound. That is the whole
          idea — everything else is more of it.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !timing step
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict order

              kick : 1
              kick -[ hit  @1/8 : bd ]-> hats
              hats -[ back @1/8 : sd ]-> kick
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 640.0, h = 300.0)

          // `emits()` is a PatPattern<String>, exactly like `pat("bd sd")` is. So every pattern
          // combinator applies, and so does the pattern-language's own audio renderer.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 4, cps = 1.0, channel = "sound").describe())

          println(
              "plays: " +
                  net.emits()
                      .events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
                      .filter { it.hasOnset }
                      .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                      .joinToString(" ") { it.value },
          )
          println("period: ${net.period()} cycles")

          displayOpen("sound")
  # 2 ── the reason to use a net at all: a bar length nobody wrote down.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_polyrhythm
      name: 2 — five against three
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 210.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          // Two independent rings, one five long and one three long, sharing a clock. Nothing in
          // this source says "fifteen" — that is a property of the net, and the net can tell you.
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/15

              a0 : 1
              a0 -[ a0.go : bd ]-> a1
              a1 -[ a1.go      ]-> a2
              a2 -[ a2.go : bd ]-> a3
              a3 -[ a3.go      ]-> a4
              a4 -[ a4.go      ]-> a0

              b0 : 1
              b0 -[ b0.go : hh ]-> b1
              b1 -[ b1.go      ]-> b2
              b2 -[ b2.go : hh ]-> b0
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 700.0, h = 340.0)

          val lasso = net.settle()!!
          println("settles after ${lasso.loopSteps} steps = ${lasso.duration} cycles")
          println("${net.tInvariants().size} T-invariants — one per independent ring")

          // Four cycles, so you can hear the two rings pull apart and line back up.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 4, cps = 0.75, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 3 ── the medium timescale: a token that is the arrangement.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_structure
      name: 3 — song structure
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 360.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Two nets in one. The fast ring plays the bar; the slow ring is the arrangement, one
          token walking verse -> verse -> chorus and back. Same mechanism at both timescales,
          which is the argument for using a net rather than a sequencer and a separate song mode.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/4

              verse.a : 1
              verse.a -[ v1 @1     ]-> verse.b
              verse.b -[ v2 @1     ]-> chorus
              chorus  -[ back @1   ]-> verse.a

              beat : 1
              &verse.a + beat -[ vbeat @1/4 : bd ]-> beat2
              &verse.b + beat -[ vbeat2 @1/4 : bd ]-> beat2
              &chorus + beat  -[ cbeat @1/4 : sd ]-> beat2
              beat2 -[ off @1/4 : hh ]-> beat
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 760.0, h = 420.0)

          // Eight cycles: two verses, a chorus, and round again — audibly.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 8, cps = 2.0, channel = "sound").describe())
          println("bar length: ${net.period()} cycles")
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 4 ── what a token can be: not a dot, a rhythm.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_tokens
      name: 4 — tokens that are rhythms
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 510.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A token's colour can be anything, including a whole PatPattern. So a place is a
          *section*, one circulating token is "which section is sounding", and the net enforces
          that exactly one of them is — no scheduler required.
          */
          val song = petriSong(
              "verse" to (pat("bd ~ sd ~") to 4),
              "chorus" to (pat("bd*4 hh*8") to 4),
          )

          showPetriNet(song, w = 660.0, h = 340.0)

          // `unfold` plays whatever pattern each firing consumed, across that firing's whole arc:
          // the slow net schedules the fast one, and both are the same mechanism.
          val notes = song.pattern().unfold<String>()

          fun bar(c: Long) =
              notes
                  .events(PatArc(PatQ.of(c), PatQ.of(c + 1)))
                  .filter { it.hasOnset }
                  .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                  .joinToString(" ") { it.value }
          for (c in 0L..7L) println("cycle %d   %s".format(c, bar(c)))

          // Eight cycles: four bars of verse, four of chorus, and audibly round again.
          println(showDirtAudio(notes, cycles = 8, cps = 2.0, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 5 ── the same engine, no music at all.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_philosophers
      name: 5 — dining philosophers (silent)
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 660.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Nothing in the model knows what a note is. Here is the same engine as a concurrency
          checker: five philosophers, five forks, and the shape of the net computed in a loop —
          which is the one thing the `#petri` notation cannot do.
          */
          fun table(reverseLast: Boolean, fairly: Boolean) = petri {
              conflict = if (fairly) PetriConflict.ROUND_ROBIN else PetriConflict.ORDER
              grid = cyc(1, 4)
              for (i in 0 until 5) place("fork.$i", tokens = 1)
              for (i in 0 until 5) {
                  val left = i
                  val right = (i + 1) % 5
                  val reversed = reverseLast && i == 4
                  t("grab.$i") {
                      from("fork.${if (reversed) right else left}")
                      to("holding.$i")
                  }
                  t("eat.$i") {
                      from("holding.$i")
                      from("fork.${if (reversed) left else right}")
                      to("eating.$i")
                  }
                  t("done.$i") {
                      from("eating.$i")
                      to("fork.$left")
                      to("fork.$right")
                  }
              }
          }

          val naive = table(reverseLast = false, fairly = false)
          showPetriNet(naive, w = 760.0, h = 460.0)

          for ((label, net) in
              listOf(
                  "all left-handed" to naive,
                  "one reaches right first" to table(reverseLast = true, fairly = false),
                  "…and round-robin conflict" to table(reverseLast = true, fairly = true),
              )) {
              val stuck = net.deadTransitions()
              println(
                  "%-26s deadlocks=%-5s never fires: %s"
                      .format(
                          label,
                          net.willDeadlock(),
                          stuck.ifEmpty { listOf("—") }.joinToString(", "),
                      ),
              )
          }

          // The middle line is where breaking the symmetry removes the deadlock and leaves a
          // starvation behind it. Two faults, two different fixes.
  # 6 ── the box to edit.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_playground
      name: 6 — playground
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 810.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A groove with a bit of everything: a read arc, a weighted arc, a capacity and
          priorities. `bd hh` goes round fast; meanwhile `build` watches `mid` without
          consuming it, and every third time it has counted, the weighted arc drains all
          three at once and you get a snare — `crash` has no output side, so it is a drain and
          the net stays bounded and periodic. Change a number and run the box again.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict priority

              pulse : 1
              fill  : 0 ^3

              pulse  -[ a @1/8 pri=9 : bd ]-> mid
              mid    -[ b @1/8 pri=9 : hh ]-> pulse

              &mid   -[ build @1/8 pri=3      ]-> fill
              3*fill -[ crash @1/8 pri=1 : sd ]->
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 760.0, h = 400.0)

          println("period: ${net.period()}   deadlocks: ${net.willDeadlock()}")
          for (c in 0L..3L) println(
              "cycle %d   %s"
                  .format(
                      c,
                      net.emits()
                          .events(PatArc(PatQ.of(c), PatQ.of(c + 1)))
                          .filter { it.hasOnset }
                          .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                          .joinToString(" ") { it.value },
                  ),
          )
          println(net.report())

          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 8, cps = 1.5, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 7 ── the live path: the same net, through the speakers, in time.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_live
      name: 7 — play it live
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 960.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Boxes 1-6 render *offline* — they mix a wav and hand you a player, which needs no
          audio device and so works in a docs build and in CI. This is the other path: the real
          polyphonic Dirt player, driven by the transport, tempo-synced and interruptible.
          */
          val root = DirtRender.dirtSampleRoot()
          println(
              root?.let { "samples: $it" }
                  ?: "no Dirt-Samples found — set ${DirtRender.ENV_VAR}, or install the SuperCollider quark",
          )

          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict priority

              pulse : 1
              fill  : 0 ^3

              pulse  -[ a @1/8 pri=9 : bd ]-> mid
              mid    -[ b @1/8 pri=9 : hh ]-> pulse
              &mid   -[ build @1/8 pri=3      ]-> fill
              3*fill -[ crash @1/8 pri=1 : sd ]->
          """,
              )
          showPetriNet(net, w = 700.0, h = 360.0)

          /*
          Flip to true to hear it. It is false by default because `audio { }` opens a real
          output device, and this transcript is replayed end to end in CI on machines that have
          none — everything below still compiles either way, which is the point of the flag
          rather than a comment.
          */
          val live = false

          if (live && root != null) {
              val kit = dirtPlayer(library = dirt(root.toString()))
              audio { kit }
              net.emits().playDirt(kit, cps = 1.5)
              println("playing — stop the box to stop the sound")
          } else {
              println("set `live = true` and run again to hear this through the speakers")

after:
name: petri_sound
description: >
  Loadable demo of Petri nets as a sequencer (afield.simulation.petri) — the model and firing engine in
  PetriNets.kt, the `PatPattern` bridge in PetriMusic.kt, the notation in PetriNotation.kt, the
  structural analysis in PetriAnalysis.kt and the drawing in PetriVisual.kt. Seven pure-compute
  boxes; no Window, no Renderer, no GPU, no audio device.
  Every box draws its net with `showPetriNet` and renders what the net plays with `showDirtAudio`
  (DirtRender.kt) — mixed *offline* from the real Tidal Dirt-Samples library if it is installed on
  this machine, and from the synthetic `patVoice` if it is not, saying which in its output either
  way. So you SEE the token move and HEAR actual drums in the same output, with no audio device
  anywhere. A net emits a `PatPattern<String>`, which is why one call is enough — a Petri net is a
  pattern like any other:
    1. smallest loop   — one token, two transitions, alternating bd/sd. The net-as-clock in eight
                         lines, drawn and played.
    2. polyrhythm      — five against three. Nothing in the source says fifteen; `settle()` finds it
                         and four cycles of audio let you hear the two rings drift apart and come
                         back.
    3. structure       — a section token walking verse -> verse -> chorus while a separate ring plays
                         the bar. Petri nets as medium-term song form, not just rhythm.
    4. tokens          — tokens carrying `euclid` patterns as their colour, so what a transition
                         plays depends on which token reached it.
    5. philosophers    — the non-musical one, for contrast: the same engine finding a deadlock, then
                         a starvation, then neither. Silent on purpose.
    6. playground      — a whole groove in the `#petri` notation, drawn, analysed and played. This is
                         the box to edit.
    7. live            — the other playback path: the real polyphonic Dirt player through the
                         transport, tempo-synced and interruptible, behind a `live` flag that is
                         false by default because `audio { }` opens a real output device.
  Replay into a fresh Field with the agent backdoor (field_run_transcript) or open the materialized
  document; then change any net and re-run that box. Each `execute` op omits inline code, so it runs
  the box's stored `code` property. See public/docs/petri_nets.md and public/docs/petri_cheatsheet.md.
operations:
  # 1 ── the smallest thing that plays: a token going round.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_loop
      name: 1 — the smallest loop
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A place holds tokens; a transition fires when all its inputs have one. Give a
          transition a sound after the `:` and firing it plays that sound. That is the whole
          idea — everything else is more of it.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !timing step
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict order

              kick : 1
              kick -[ hit  @1/8 : bd ]-> hats
              hats -[ back @1/8 : sd ]-> kick
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 640.0, h = 300.0)

          // `emits()` is a PatPattern<String>, exactly like `pat("bd sd")` is. So every pattern
          // combinator applies, and so does the pattern-language's own audio renderer.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 4, cps = 1.0, channel = "sound").describe())

          println(
              "plays: " +
                  net.emits()
                      .events(PatArc(PatQ.ZERO, PatQ.ONE))
                      .filter { it.hasOnset }
                      .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                      .joinToString(" ") { it.value },
          )
          println("period: ${net.period()} cycles")

          displayOpen("sound")
  # 2 ── the reason to use a net at all: a bar length nobody wrote down.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_polyrhythm
      name: 2 — five against three
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 210.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          // Two independent rings, one five long and one three long, sharing a clock. Nothing in
          // this source says "fifteen" — that is a property of the net, and the net can tell you.
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/15

              a0 : 1
              a0 -[ a0.go : bd ]-> a1
              a1 -[ a1.go      ]-> a2
              a2 -[ a2.go : bd ]-> a3
              a3 -[ a3.go      ]-> a4
              a4 -[ a4.go      ]-> a0

              b0 : 1
              b0 -[ b0.go : hh ]-> b1
              b1 -[ b1.go      ]-> b2
              b2 -[ b2.go : hh ]-> b0
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 700.0, h = 340.0)

          val lasso = net.settle()!!
          println("settles after ${lasso.loopSteps} steps = ${lasso.duration} cycles")
          println("${net.tInvariants().size} T-invariants — one per independent ring")

          // Four cycles, so you can hear the two rings pull apart and line back up.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 4, cps = 0.75, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 3 ── the medium timescale: a token that is the arrangement.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_structure
      name: 3 — song structure
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 360.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Two nets in one. The fast ring plays the bar; the slow ring is the arrangement, one
          token walking verse -> verse -> chorus and back. Same mechanism at both timescales,
          which is the argument for using a net rather than a sequencer and a separate song mode.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/4

              verse.a : 1
              verse.a -[ v1 @1     ]-> verse.b
              verse.b -[ v2 @1     ]-> chorus
              chorus  -[ back @1   ]-> verse.a

              beat : 1
              &verse.a + beat -[ vbeat @1/4 : bd ]-> beat2
              &verse.b + beat -[ vbeat2 @1/4 : bd ]-> beat2
              &chorus + beat  -[ cbeat @1/4 : sd ]-> beat2
              beat2 -[ off @1/4 : hh ]-> beat
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 760.0, h = 420.0)

          // Eight cycles: two verses, a chorus, and round again — audibly.
          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 8, cps = 2.0, channel = "sound").describe())
          println("bar length: ${net.period()} cycles")
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 4 ── what a token can be: not a dot, a rhythm.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_tokens
      name: 4 — tokens that are rhythms
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 510.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A token's colour can be anything, including a whole PatPattern. So a place is a
          *section*, one circulating token is "which section is sounding", and the net enforces
          that exactly one of them is — no scheduler required.
          */
          val song = petriSong(
              "verse" to (pat("bd ~ sd ~") to 4),
              "chorus" to (pat("bd*4 hh*8") to 4),
          )

          showPetriNet(song, w = 660.0, h = 340.0)

          // `unfold` plays whatever pattern each firing consumed, across that firing's whole arc:
          // the slow net schedules the fast one, and both are the same mechanism.
          val notes = song.pattern().unfold<String>()

          fun bar(c: Long) =
              notes
                  .events(PatArc(PatQ.of(c), PatQ.of(c + 1)))
                  .filter { it.hasOnset }
                  .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                  .joinToString(" ") { it.value }
          for (c in 0L..7L) println("cycle %d   %s".format(c, bar(c)))

          // Eight cycles: four bars of verse, four of chorus, and audibly round again.
          println(showDirtAudio(notes, cycles = 8, cps = 2.0, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 5 ── the same engine, no music at all.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_philosophers
      name: 5 — dining philosophers (silent)
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 660.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Nothing in the model knows what a note is. Here is the same engine as a concurrency
          checker: five philosophers, five forks, and the shape of the net computed in a loop —
          which is the one thing the `#petri` notation cannot do.
          */
          fun table(reverseLast: Boolean, fairly: Boolean) = petri {
              conflict = if (fairly) PetriConflict.ROUND_ROBIN else PetriConflict.ORDER
              grid = cyc(1, 4)
              for (i in 0 until 5) place("fork.$i", tokens = 1)
              for (i in 0 until 5) {
                  val left = i
                  val right = (i + 1) % 5
                  val reversed = reverseLast && i == 4
                  t("grab.$i") {
                      from("fork.${if (reversed) right else left}")
                      to("holding.$i")
                  }
                  t("eat.$i") {
                      from("holding.$i")
                      from("fork.${if (reversed) left else right}")
                      to("eating.$i")
                  }
                  t("done.$i") {
                      from("eating.$i")
                      to("fork.$left")
                      to("fork.$right")
                  }
              }
          }

          val naive = table(reverseLast = false, fairly = false)
          showPetriNet(naive, w = 760.0, h = 460.0)

          for ((label, net) in
              [
                  "all left-handed" to naive,
                  "one reaches right first" to table(reverseLast = true, fairly = false),
                  "…and round-robin conflict" to table(reverseLast = true, fairly = true),
              ]) {
              val stuck = net.deadTransitions()
              println(
                  "%-26s deadlocks=%-5s never fires: %s"
                      .format(
                          label,
                          net.willDeadlock(),
                          stuck.ifEmpty { ["—"] }.joinToString(", "),
                      ),
              )
          }

          // The middle line is where breaking the symmetry removes the deadlock and leaves a
          // starvation behind it. Two faults, two different fixes.
  # 6 ── the box to edit.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_playground
      name: 6 — playground
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 810.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          A groove with a bit of everything: a read arc, a weighted arc, a capacity and
          priorities. `bd hh` goes round fast; meanwhile `build` watches `mid` without
          consuming it, and every third time it has counted, the weighted arc drains all
          three at once and you get a snare — `crash` has no output side, so it is a drain and
          the net stays bounded and periodic. Change a number and run the box again.
          */
          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict priority

              pulse : 1
              fill  : 0 ^3

              pulse  -[ a @1/8 pri=9 : bd ]-> mid
              mid    -[ b @1/8 pri=9 : hh ]-> pulse

              &mid   -[ build @1/8 pri=3      ]-> fill
              3*fill -[ crash @1/8 pri=1 : sd ]->
          """,
              )

          showPetriNet(net, w = 760.0, h = 400.0)

          println("period: ${net.period()}   deadlocks: ${net.willDeadlock()}")
          for (c in 0L..3L) println(
              "cycle %d   %s"
                  .format(
                      c,
                      net.emits()
                          .events(PatArc(PatQ.of(c), PatQ.of(c + 1)))
                          .filter { it.hasOnset }
                          .sortedBy { it.arc.start }
                          .joinToString(" ") { it.value },
                  ),
          )
          println(net.report())

          println(showDirtAudio(net.emits(), cycles = 8, cps = 1.5, channel = "sound").describe())
          displayOpen("sound")
  # 7 ── the live path: the same net, through the speakers, in time.
  - create:
      box: petri_demo_live
      name: 7 — play it live
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 960.0, w: 320.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.simulation.petri.*

          /*
          Boxes 1-6 render *offline* — they mix a wav and hand you a player, which needs no
          audio device and so works in a docs build and in CI. This is the other path: the real
          polyphonic Dirt player, driven by the transport, tempo-synced and interruptible.
          */
          val root = DirtRender.dirtSampleRoot()
          println(
              root?.let { "samples: $it" }
                  ?: "no Dirt-Samples found — set ${DirtRender.ENV_VAR}, or install the SuperCollider quark",
          )

          val net =
              petri(
                  """
              #petri
              !grid 1/8
              !conflict priority

              pulse : 1
              fill  : 0 ^3

              pulse  -[ a @1/8 pri=9 : bd ]-> mid
              mid    -[ b @1/8 pri=9 : hh ]-> pulse
              &mid   -[ build @1/8 pri=3      ]-> fill
              3*fill -[ crash @1/8 pri=1 : sd ]->
          """,
              )
          showPetriNet(net, w = 700.0, h = 360.0)

          /*
          Flip to true to hear it. It is false by default because `audio { }` opens a real
          output device, and this transcript is replayed end to end in CI on machines that have
          none — everything below still compiles either way, which is the point of the flag
          rather than a comment.
          */
          val live = false

          if (live && root != null) {
              val kit = dirtPlayer(library = dirt(root.toString()))
              audio { kit }
              net.emits().playDirt(kit, cps = 1.5)
              println("playing — stop the box to stop the sound")
          } else {
              println("set `live = true` and run again to hear this through the speakers")
          }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_loop }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_polyrhythm }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_structure }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_tokens }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_philosophers }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_playground }
  - execute: { box: petri_demo_live }

""" .trimIndent(), ) - create: box: pitch_roundtrip_clean name: 2 · notate → render → hear it back frame: { x: 520.0, y: 40.0, w: 440.0, h: 100.0 } properties: code: | // The notation, and the ground truth Field already owns because it wrote it. val notation = "60 62 64 65 67 69 71 72" val cycles = 2 val cps = 1.0 val sustain = 0.85 val voice = patVoice(sustain = sustain, decay = 0.03) val audio = patRenderStereo(pat(notation), cycles, cps, voice).mono val reference = patReferenceNotes(notation, cycles, cps, sustain = sustain) // One call: transcribe, score against the notation, draw both on one axis. val heard = showPatTranscriptionOf( audio, reference = reference, minGapSeconds = (1.0 / cps) / 8, minHz = patMidiToHz(59.0), maxHz = patMidiToHz(73.0), label = "notated against recovered", ) display("authored", "pat(\"$notation\") × $cycles cycles at cps $cps") display("recovered", "pat(\"${heard.miniNotation}\") at cps ${"%.3f".format(heard.cps)}") display( "pitch error", heard.notes.joinToString("\n") { "MIDI ${it.midi} ${"%+.1f".format(it.centsOffset)} cents conf ${"%.2f".format(it.confidence)}" }, ) display("summary", heard.describe()) - create: box: pitch_roundtrip_legato name: 3 · a line with no attacks in it frame: { x: 40.0, y: 190.0, w: 440.0, h: 100.0 } properties: code: | /* One oscillator, continuous phase, stepped frequency. The amplitude never moves, so the RMS envelope is flat and there is no attack anywhere except the entry from silence. patRenderStereo CANNOT produce this. It adds one voice per event and gives each its own 3 ms attack ramp, so even at sustain = 1.0 a "legato" Pat render still has one amplitude rise per note — and an energy detector handles it fine. That was measured, and it is why this box uses Dough instead. */ val steps = [60.0, 62.0, 64.0, 65.0, 67.0, 69.0, 71.0, 72.0] val stepSeconds = 0.25 val sr = 48_000 val audio = doughRenderMono( patSteppedSine(steps, stepSeconds), (steps.size * stepSeconds).toFloat(), sr, ) val reference = steps.mapIndexed { i, midi -> PatRefNote( startSample = (i * stepSeconds * sr).toInt(), endSample = ((i + 1) * stepSeconds * sr).toInt(), midi = midi, ) } val scheduled = reference.map { it.startSample } val tolerance = (0.030 * sr).toInt() val frames = patF0Frames(audio, sr, minHz = patMidiToHz(59.0), maxHz = patMidiToHz(73.0)) val energy = patDetectOnsetSamples(audio, sr, stepSeconds) val pitch = patDetectPitchChangeSamples(audio, sr, stepSeconds, frames) val merged = patDetectNoteOnsets(audio, sr, stepSeconds, frames) display( "the counterfactual", """ eight notes, one continuous tone, flat envelope: ${patTallyOnsets(energy, scheduled, tolerance).describe("energy (amplitude envelope)")} ${patTallyOnsets(pitch, scheduled, tolerance).describe("pitch (periodicity) ")} ${patTallyOnsets(merged, scheduled, tolerance).describe("merged (the union) ")} The energy detector is not misconfigured. The evidence it consumes is not in this signal. """ .trimIndent(), ) showPatTranscriptionOf( audio, sampleRate = sr, reference = reference, minGapSeconds = stepSeconds, minHz = patMidiToHz(59.0), maxHz = patMidiToHz(73.0), label = "legato, no attacks — 48 kHz Dough render", ) - create: box: pitch_roundtrip_register name: 4 · POKE THIS — the register is the whole lever frame: { x: 520.0, y: 190.0, w: 440.0, h: 100.0 } properties: code: | // Sixteen notes in half a second: 31 ms each. val notation = "60 62 64 65 67 69 71 72 72 71 69 67 65 64 62 60" val cycles = 2 val cps = 2.0 val sustain = 0.9 val audio = patRenderStereo( pat(notation), cycles, cps, patVoice(sustain = sustain, decay = 0.01), ) .mono val reference = patReferenceNotes(notation, cycles, cps, sustain = sustain) /* ─── CHANGE THIS ONE LINE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── The analysis window is derived from minHz, because YIN needs a frame at least twice the longest period it is asked to consider. So the lowest pitch you admit sets the shortest note you can resolve, and declaring the register truthfully is worth more than any threshold in this package. patMidiToHz(59.0) ≈ 247 Hz → window ≈ 16 ms → these 31 ms notes survive PAT_PITCH_MIN_HZ = 65 Hz → window ≈ 46 ms → longer than the notes Swap the line below for `val minHz = PAT_PITCH_MIN_HZ` and re-run. Measured on exactly this audio, onset recall falls from 0.91 to 0.03, every recovered note disappears, and the verdict below changes from PITCHED to UNRESOLVED — which names the fix rather than just reporting silence. The audio does not change. Only what the detector was promised. */ val minHz = patMidiToHz(59.0) // ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── val window = patPitchFrameSpan(PatSoundDocs.SR, minHz) val heard = showPatTranscriptionOf( audio, reference = reference, minGapSeconds = (1.0 / cps) / 16, minHz = minHz, maxHz = patMidiToHz(73.0), label = "31 ms notes, minHz = ${"%.0f".format(minHz)} Hz", ) display( "resolution", """ minHz ${"%.1f".format(minHz)} Hz → analysis window $window samples (${"%.1f".format(1000.0 * window / PatSoundDocs.SR)} ms) the notes are ${"%.1f".format(1000.0 / cps / 16)} ms long """ .trimIndent(), ) display("verdict", heard.diagnosis.describe()) display("recovered", "pat(\"${heard.miniNotation}\")") - create: box: pitch_roundtrip_refusal name: 5 · a chord, refused rather than guessed at frame: { x: 40.0, y: 340.0, w: 440.0, h: 100.0 } properties: code: | /* Three simultaneous pitches. A monophonic detector's correct output here is a stated inability, not the loudest note. `~` is the only thing mini-notation can say for a span that sounded and was not named, so the refusal lives in the warnings and the verdict. */ val notation = "[60,64,67] ~ [62,65,69] ~" val cycles = 2 val cps = 0.75 val sustain = 0.85 val audio = patRenderStereo( pat(notation), cycles, cps, patVoice(sustain = sustain, decay = 0.03), ) .mono val heard = showPatTranscriptionOf( audio, reference = patReferenceNotes(notation, cycles, cps, sustain = sustain), minGapSeconds = (1.0 / cps) / 4, minHz = patMidiToHz(59.0), maxHz = patMidiToHz(73.0), label = "a triad — outlines with nothing in them", ) display("named", "${heard.notes.size} notes · pat(\"${heard.miniNotation}\")") display("verdict", heard.diagnosis.describe()) display("warnings", heard.warnings.joinToString("\n\n")) display( "how it knows", """ the voicing gate does nearly all of this: three sines in a non-harmonic ratio are not periodic at any single lag, so YIN rejects them frame by frame without consulting a spectrum. The spectrum is then only asked one question — sparse or dense — which is what separates a chord (a few discrete partials) from a snare (a continuum). Compare: a sawtooth is a full harmonic stack on ONE note and is NOT refused, because timbre is not polyphony. """ .trimIndent(), )

before:
name: polytope_canonical_gallery
description: >
  One editable Field box for canonical realization in afield.geometry.polytope. Change the single
  Conway expression string at the top and the box re-evaluates the notation, canonicalizes the
  result, and draws both side by side in the on-canvas Three.js viewer: on the left the raw
  per-operator realization, on the right the canonical form in which every edge is tangent to one
  common midsphere and every face is planar. The printed diagnostics report the tangency-radius
  spread, the tangency-centroid offset and the planarity error before and after, so the picture and
  the numbers agree. Hover a face to highlight it; click it to read its degree, its combinatorial
  symmetry orbit, and its distance from the centre.
operations:
  - create:
      box: polytope_canonical_gallery
      name: "Polytope — Conway expression gallery, canonicalized"
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 450.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          /*
          ---- the one parameter to change -------------------------------------------------
          Conway prefix notation, read right to left, over the seeds T C O I D and the
          operators d a k t g j n z o e s m b. Try "gD", "ktC", "bD", "sD", "dkD", "tI", "eC".
          */
          val expression = "gD"
          // ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          val plain = conway(expression)
          val raw = plain.polyhedron
          val run = raw.canonicalize()
          val solid = run.polyhedron
          val orbits = solid.combinatorialOrbits()

          println(
              """
              $expression = ${plain.summary().primitiveOperations.joinToString(" ")}
              ${solid.topology.elements(0).size} vertices, ${solid.topology.elements(1).size} edges, ${solid.topology.elements(2).size} faces
              before: spread ${"%.3e".format(raw.canonicalDiagnostics().tangencyRadiusSpread)}  planarity ${"%.3e".format(raw.canonicalDiagnostics().maxFacePlanarityError)}
              after:  spread ${"%.3e".format(run.finalDiagnostics.tangencyRadiusSpread)}  planarity ${"%.3e".format(run.finalDiagnostics.maxFacePlanarityError)}  centre ${"%.3e".format(run.finalDiagnostics.tangencyCentroidOffset)}
              ${run.reason} after ${run.iterations} iterations (reciprocal ${run.reciprocalIterations}, relaxation ${run.relaxationIterations}, reseeded ${run.reseeded})
              orbits: ${orbits.summary()}
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )

          val status: (String) -> Unit = { message -> markdown("canonical face", message) }

          // Face colour by polygon degree, so the Archimedean/Catalan structure reads at a glance.
          val hues = mapOf(
              3 to vec(1.00, 0.60, 0.30),
              4 to vec(0.35, 0.77, 1.00),
              5 to vec(0.62, 0.91, 0.42),
              6 to vec(1.00, 0.44, 0.60),
              8 to vec(1.00, 0.88, 0.40),
              10 to vec(0.72, 0.78, 0.86),
          )

          fun PolyhedralObject.shiftedBy(dx: Float): PolyhedralObject {
              val coordinates = realization!!.vertexCoordinates.map { Vec3(it).add(dx, 0f, 0f) }
              return copy(realization = Realization3(coordinates))
          }

          fun PolyhedralObject.panel(label: String, dx: Float, alpha: Double) =
              shiftedBy(dx).toFaceFLines { face, line ->
                  val degree = topology.faceCycle(face.id).size
                  val hue = hues[degree] ?: vec(0.70, 0.74, 0.80)
                  val orbit = orbits.faceClasses.indexOfFirst { face.id in it }
                  val normal = faceNormal(face.id)
                  val centre = faceCentroids[topology.elements(2).indexOfFirst { it.id == face.id }]
                  val depth = (centre.x * normal.x + centre.y * normal.y + centre.z * normal.z).toDouble()

                  line.filled = true
                  line.stroked = true
                  line.thickness = 1.2
                  line.color = vec(hue.x, hue.y, hue.z, alpha)
                  line.hoverColor = vec(0.98, 0.99, 1.00, 0.98)
                  line.onClick = {
                      status(
                          """
                          **$label — face ${face.id.value}**

                          - degree: `$degree`
                          - combinatorial orbit: `$orbit of ${orbits.faceClassCount}`
                          - face-plane distance from centre: `${"%.5f".format(depth)}`
                          """
                              .trimIndent(),
                      )
                  }
              }

          /*
          Left: the per-operator realization the Conway transform produced. Right: its canonical
          representative. Both are centred and scaled by the same rigid gauge, so the difference
          on screen is shape and nothing else.
          */
          val before = raw.normalize(RigidGauge.CANONICAL, reference = raw.realization)
          val faceLines = before.panel("realized", -1.4f, 0.34) + solid.panel("canonical", 1.4f, 0.86)

          threeLines(
              faceLines,
              channel = "polytope",
              name = "canonical-gallery",
              height = 560,
              autoFrame = true,
              editable = false,
          )
          displayOpen("polytope")

          viz("diagnostics", listOf(run.initialDiagnostics, run.finalDiagnostics, orbits))
  - execute:
      box: polytope_canonical_gallery
  - wait:
      millis: 750

before:
name: polytope_conway_demo
description: >
  One editable Field box for the afield.geometry.polytope vertical slice. It marks the two opposite
  square faces of a cube with different height attributes, selects those faces, applies kis only
  there, and sends the resulting polygonal face FLines to Field's on-canvas Three.js viewer.
  Orbit the result, hover a face, or click it to inspect its output id, Conway provenance, source
  elements, and resolved non-uniform parameter. This deliberately compact worked example is
  the starting point for exploring the completed polytope vertical slice.
operations:
  - create:
      box: polytope_selective_kis
      name: "Polytope — selective kis, topology to FLine"
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 80.0, w: 400.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Topology is the source of truth. Coordinates and the FLine viewer only arrive after
          // selection and the abstract Conway operation have decided what the new faces are.
          var source = cube()
          val sourceFaces = source.topology.elements(2)

          // The first pair are the cube's opposite z faces. Attributes do both jobs here: `raise`
          // selects the domain of kis, while `height` is deployed independently over that domain.
          val raisedFaces = sourceFaces.take(2)
          val raisedHeights = listOf(0.22, 0.68)
          for (i in raisedFaces.indices) {
              source = source.withAttributes(
                  raisedFaces[i].id,
                  mapOf("raise" to true, "height" to raisedHeights[i]),
              )
          }

          val result = source.kis(
              selector = ElementSelectors.attributeEquals("raise", true),
              heightScale = ElementParameters.attribute("height"),
          )
          val polyhedron = result.polyhedron
          val topology = polyhedron.topology
          val triangles = polyhedron.triangulate()

          println(
              """
              selective kis on two opposite cube faces
              transform = ${result.summary()}
              triangles = ${triangles.summary()}
              orbit the view; hover and click a face to inspect its lineage
              """
                  .trimIndent(),
          )

          val status: (String) -> Unit = { message -> markdown("face provenance", message) }

          // One FLine per authoritative polygonal face. The face attributes propagated through kis
          // become styling here; no triangle mesh has been smuggled in as the topology model.
          val faceLines = polyhedron.toFaceFLines { face, line ->
              val attributes = polyhedron.attributes[face.id]
              val height = (attributes["height"] as? Number)?.toDouble()
              val lineage = result.lineage(face.id)
              val role = (lineage as? ElementLineage.Derived)?.role ?: "source"
              val sources = result.sourceElements(face.id).joinToString { "rank ${it.rank} / id ${it.id.value}" }

              line.filled = true
              line.stroked = true
              line.thickness = if (height == null) 1.1 else 1.8
              line.color = when {
                  height == null -> vec(0.28, 0.32, 0.38, 0.62)
                  height < 0.4 -> vec(0.30, 0.82, 0.96, 0.78)
                  else -> vec(1.00, 0.62, 0.24, 0.82)
              }
              line.hoverColor = vec(0.96, 0.98, 1.00, 0.98)
              line.onClick = { hit ->
                  val deployed = height?.let { "%.2f".format(it) } ?: "not selected"
                  status(
                      """
                      **output face ${face.id.value}**

                      - role: `$role`
                      - deployed height: `$deployed`
                      - source: $sources
                      - clicked at: `${hit.position}`
                      """
                          .trimIndent(),
                  )
              }
          }

          threeLines(
              faceLines,
              channel = "polytope",
              name = "selective-kis",
              height = 560,
              autoFrame = true,
              editable = false,
          )
          displayOpen("polytope")

          // These are registered polytope value printers. They reduce the larger immutable objects
          // to public data-class summaries, then use Field's normal nested data-class visualizer.
          viz("inspection", listOf(result, triangles))
  - execute:
      box: polytope_selective_kis
  - wait:
      millis: 750

before:
name: popup_prior_inspect
description: >
  One box that asks Field what ranking prior the completion popup currently has for a given receiver
  type, by calling the same object the completion server calls — afield.runtime.completion.CommonMemberPrior — rather
  than describing it. Prints the receiver's @CommonMembers list in declared order with the score each
  position earns, which is one of the two things that place a row in the popup.

  It cannot print the other one — which SECTION the row lands in. Grouping is applied to the rows that
  ranking has already chosen and truncated to (`orderItemsForGroupedDisplay(rankItems(…).slice(0,
  MAX_VISIBLE_ITEMS))`), so it is a permutation within them: it can push a row a long way down the
  visible list, and a prior cannot lift a row out of its own section into an earlier one, but grouping
  never decides whether a row is on screen at all — ranking alone does that. The category answer belongs

before:
name: rectsl_inverse_animation
description: >
  Self-contained demo of RectSL's third, differentiable backend: inverse animation. A RectSL track
  now lowers to an afield.math.functions.Functions.Fn, which autodiff_fn.kt differentiates exactly, so a
  track marked with free parameters can be *solved* instead of authored. Box one declares a rect
  whose position is `amp * trig(rate*t + phase) + centre` in both axes with all six numbers unknown,
  says where the rect must be at three instants, and solves — then renders target / seed / fitted as
  three stacked bands in one image so the miss and its closing are visible side by side (seed misses
  by 7.7 wall metres, the fit by ~5e-15). Box two does the same from RectSL source, using the
  `free-param` word, and prints the track IR as its own algebra. Open or replay this into a fresh
  Field4 and look at box one: the top band is where the rect was asked to go, the middle band is a
  seed that misses every waypoint, and the bottom band is a solved arc threading all three.
operations:
  - create:
      box: rectsl_inverse_fit
      name: RectSL inverse animation
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 60.0, w: 360.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.lang.rectsl.*

          val duration = 4.0

          // A clamped identity in time: RectSL's way of saying "follow the clock".
          fun clock(d: Double): Track<Double> = LinearScalarTrack(listOf(TcbKey(0.0, 0.0), TcbKey(d, d)))

          fun channel(axis: String, rate: Double, op: TrackOp1): Track<Double> = BinaryDoubleTrack(
              BinaryDoubleTrack(
                  MappedDoubleTrack(
                      BinaryDoubleTrack(
                          BinaryDoubleTrack(clock(duration), constantTrack(rate), TrackOp2.MUL),
                          FreeParamTrack("$axis-phase", 0.0),
                          TrackOp2.ADD,
                      ),
                      op,
                  ),
                  FreeParamTrack("$axis-amp", 1.0),
                  TrackOp2.MUL,
              ),
              FreeParamTrack("$axis-centre", 0.0),
              TrackOp2.ADD,
          )

          val seedX = channel("x", 1.1, TrackOp1.COS)
          val seedY = channel("y", 1.1, TrackOp1.SIN)

          // Where the rect must be, and when.
          val waypoints = listOf(
              RectSLFitFigure.Marker(0.4, -6.5, 2.6),
              RectSLFitFigure.Marker(1.8, 0.5, -2.4),
              RectSLFitFigure.Marker(3.4, 6.2, 1.8),
          )
          val window = Functions.Domain(0.0, duration)
          val fitX = seedX.fitParameters(waypoints.map { TrackFitTarget(it.time, it.x) }, window, iterations = 1500)
          val fitY = seedY.fitParameters(waypoints.map { TrackFitTarget(it.time, it.y) }, window, iterations = 1500)

          fun miss(x: Track<Double>, y: Track<Double>): Double = waypoints.maxOf {
              hypot(x.sample(it.time) - it.x, y.sample(it.time) - it.y)
          }

          display(
              "figure",
              RectSLFitFigure.render(
                  bands = listOf(
                      RectSLFitFigure.Band(
                          "target",
                          constantTrack(0.0),
                          constantTrack(0.0),
                          Color4(0.86, 0.88, 0.91),
                          note = "3 waypoints",
                          strobe = false,
                      ),
                      RectSLFitFigure.Band(
                          "seed",
                          seedX,
                          seedY,
                          Color4(1.0, 0.42, 0.28),
                          note = "worst miss %.2fm".format(miss(seedX, seedY)),
                      ),
                      RectSLFitFigure.Band(
                          "fitted",
                          fitX.fitted,

before:
# Generated from solidsl_gallery/metadata.edn by afield.examples.DocumentToTranscript.
name: "solidsl_gallery"
operations:
  - create:
      box: "refusals"
      name: "Solid notation — refusals, and the hybrid build"
      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 280.0, w: 380.0, h: 50.0 }
      properties:
        "autorun": false
        "code": |
          import afield.geometry.solid.manifold.ManifoldLibrary
          import afield.lang.solidsl.*

          /*
          ---- a part that is half CSG and half field -------------------------------------------
          A plate you could machine, unioned with a blob you could not: the fillet where the ball
          meets the post lies on NEITHER of them, so no sequence of unions, intersections and
          differences can produce it. The exact lowering says so instead of guessing.
          */
          val fillet = 0.28

          val machinable =
              cuboid(3.2, 3.2, 0.5) -
                  unionOf(
                      listOf(-1.1 to -1.1, 1.1 to -1.1, -1.1 to 1.1, 1.1 to 1.1).map { (x, y) ->
                          cylinder(2.0, 0.22, segments = 128).at(x, y, 0.0)
                      },
                  )
          val organic = smoothUnion(
              sphere(0.62, segments = 128).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.95),
              cylinder(1.6, 0.28, segments = 128).at(0.0, 0.0, 0.45),
              k = fillet,
          )
          val part = machinable + organic

          // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          run {
              println("---- what this expression refuses, and why ----")
              part.allRefusals().forEach {
                  println("  ${it.node}")
                  println("    ${it.why}")
                  println("    closable: ${it.closable}${if (it.missing.isNotBlank()) " — needs ${it.missing}" else ""}")
              }
              if (part.allRefusals().isEmpty()) println("  (nothing — every node has an exact CSG form)")
              println()

              // The catalogue, and why the last two refusals are a different kind from the first two.
              println("The catalogue, in full — try each of these:")
              listOf<Pair<String, SolidExpr>>(
                      "smoothUnion(a, b, k)" to smoothUnion(sphere(1.0), cuboid(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), k = 0.2),
                      "gyroid()" to gyroid(),

      box: "glsl_backend"

      frame: { x: 80.0, y: 180.0, w: 380.0, h: 50.0 }
      properties:
        "autorun": false
        "code": |
          import afield.lang.solidsl.*

          /*
          ---- a shape that is worth ray-marching ----------------------------------------------
          A twisted star column standing in a bored plate, blended where they meet. Change the
          twist and re-run: the printed shader changes with it, because the shader is emitted
          from the expression rather than written beside it.
          */
          val twist = 140.0
          val blend = 0.18

          val column = Profile.star(6, 0.85, 0.42).extruded(2.4, twistDegrees = twist).at(0.0, 0.0, -1.2)
          val plate = cuboid(3.6, 3.6, 0.5).at(0.0, 0.0, -1.35)
          val scene = smoothUnion(column, plate, k = blend) - cylinder(4.0, 0.28, segments = 64)
          // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

          val emitted = scene.toGlsl()

          println("$emitted")
          println()
          println("A `(Vec3) -> Float` runs on the JVM and nowhere else. An expression tree walks")
          println("into whatever language you like, and this is the third place this one goes:")
          println()
          println(emitted.glsl.lines().take(26).joinToString("\n"))
          println("    ...  (${emitted.glsl.lines().size} lines in total)")
          println()

          /*

          no loops. Any driver re-vectorises it in the first pass, and what it buys is a grammar
          small enough that `SolidSLGlslTest` can parse the shader BACK and run it against the
          Kotlin field. 29 shapes, 58,000 sampled points, worst disagreement 6.3e-15. That is a
          measurement of the backend's fidelity, not a hope that two tree walks agree.
          */
          println(
              "step scale ${emitted.stepScale} — ${if (emitted.notes.isEmpty()) "a true distance field, so sphere tracing is exact" else "the field over-estimates distance somewhere"}",
          )
          emitted.notes.forEach { println("  - $it") }
          println()

          // The simplifier, which only exists because the shape is a value.
          println("---- what the simplifier can do ----")
          val wasteful = differenceOf(
              listOf(scene) + (0 until 40).map { cylinder(3.0, 0.12, segments = 32).at(-8.0 + it * 0.42, 0.0, 0.0) },
          )
          println("40 extra bores, most of them nowhere near the part:")
          println("  ${wasteful.simplificationReport()}")
          println("  Disjointness is decided from symbolic bounds — nothing sampled, nothing built.")
          println()

          /*
          And the rule that is genuinely strange: a blend of radius zero IS a union, and a union
          has an exact CSG form where a smooth blend never will. So simplifying can move an
          expression off the level-set fallback and onto the exact path.
          */
          val noBlend = smoothUnion(column, plate, k = 0.0)
          println("a blend with k = 0:")
          println("  ${noBlend.simplificationReport()}")
          println()

          println("---- the whole raymarch fragment, ready to paste ----")
          println(scene.toRaymarchFragment())

          emitted.notes.forEach { println("  - $it") }
          println()

          // The simplifier, which only exists because the shape is a value.
          println("---- what the simplifier can do ----")
          val wasteful = differenceOf(
              [scene] + (0 until 40).map { cylinder(3.0, 0.12, segments = 32).at(-8.0 + it * 0.42, 0.0, 0.0) },
          )
          println("40 extra bores, most of them nowhere near the part:")
          println("  ${wasteful.simplificationReport()}")
          println("  Disjointness is decided from symbolic bounds — nothing sampled, nothing built.")
          println()

          /*
          And the rule that is genuinely strange: a blend of radius zero IS a union, and a union
          has an exact CSG form where a smooth blend never will. So simplifying can move an
          expression off the level-set fallback and onto the exact path.
          */
          val noBlend = smoothUnion(column, plate, k = 0.0)
          println("a blend with k = 0:")
          println("  ${noBlend.simplificationReport()}")
          println()

          println("---- the whole raymarch fragment, ready to paste ----")
          println(scene.toRaymarchFragment())
  - launch: { box: refusals, property: code }
  - launch: { box: cross_check, property: code }
  - launch: { box: glsl_backend, property: code }
  - await: { wait: pending }

# Generated from sonicpi_pattern_demo/metadata.edn by afield.examples.DocumentToTranscript.
name: "sonicpi_pattern_demo"
operations:
  - create:
      box: "sonicpi-pattern-lower"
      name: "1 — A pattern, lowered to Sonic Pi"
      frame: { x: 60.0, y: 60.0, w: 420.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        "code": |
          /*
          Pat plays Sonic Pi — the program, before you hear it.

          Field's pattern algebra keeps musical structure exact in rational cycle space. Sonic Pi has 66
          synths, 42 FX, 206 samples and a sample-accurate scheduler. This is the join: a pattern is
          lowered to ordinary Sonic Pi source that you can read, paste into a #sonicpi region, and edit.

            public/docs/sonic_pi.md — "Field patterns as a Sonic Pi sequencer"

          Nothing here needs Sonic Pi installed. It is a text transformation.
          */

          /*
          A triplet inside a binary bar — three even hits inside the third quarter. This is exactly where
          a lowering that wrote `sleep 0.333` would start drifting, and it is why the emitter writes
          Rational(1, 3) instead.
          */
          val groove = pat("bd ~ [bd bd bd] bd")

          println(groove.sonicPiSource(cps = 0.5, cycles = 1, name = "groove"))

          // use_bpm makes one Sonic Pi beat exactly one Field cycle, so the sleeps above ARE the pattern's
          // cycle fractions. Nothing about them depends on the tempo — change cps and only use_bpm moves.

          // Atoms resolve against the *installed* vocabulary, in order: a real sample name, then a real
          // synth name, then a note, then the drum-machine aliases.
          println()
          println(SonicPiVocabulary)
          val kit = SonicPiInstruments()
          listOf("bd", "hh", "bd_tek", "tb303", "c4", "60", "nonesuch").forEach {
              println("  %-10s -> %s".format(it, kit.resolve(it) ?: "NOTHING — this atom would be silent"))
          }
  - create:
      box: "sonicpi-pattern-hear"
      name: "2 — Hear it"
      frame: { x: 760.0, y: 60.0, w: 420.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        "code": |
          /*
          Hear it.

          The same lowering, played. Sonic Pi 5 has to be installed; Field starts it itself — owned mode,
          so there is no Sonic Pi window and this box is the buffer. The box stays lit while the music
          runs, and the stop button stops it.

          Turn your volume down before you run this.
          */

          /*
          Three things a layer can carry beyond its pattern: which synth its bare notes play on, an FX
          chain wrapped around its live_loop, and parameters from the pattern algebra. Every FX name and
          every FX opt below is checked against the installed vocabulary when the layer is built — Sonic
          Pi's answer to `with_fx :revreb` is a runtime error on the loop's own thread, minutes in.

          Field's octave numbering puts middle C at c5 = 60, one octave below Sonic Pi's :c4. That is why
          the lowering emits MIDI numbers rather than :symbols — the number the pattern meant survives.
          */
          sonicPiPattern(
              sonicPiLayer("drums", pat("bd ~ [bd bd bd] bd")),
              sonicPiLayer(
                  "hats",
                  pat("[hh hh hh hh]").degradeBy(0.35, salt = 4) with gain(0.35),
                  fx = listOf(sonicPiFx("echo", "phase" to 0.125, "decay" to 2, "mix" to 0.3)),
              ),
              sonicPiLayer(
                  "bass",
                  pat("<e3 g3> ~ e4 ~").every(4) { it.rev() } with cutoff(700.0),
                  synth = "tb303",
                  fx = listOf(sonicPiFx("reverb", "room" to 0.7, "mix" to 0.4)),
              ),
              cps = 0.5,
              cycles = 4,
          )
  - create:
      box: "sonicpi-pattern-live"
      name: "3 — Field's clock, Sonic Pi's instrument"
      frame: { x: 760.0, y: 220.0, w: 420.0, h: 100.0 }
      properties:
        "code": |
          /*
          The other direction: Field's clock is the sequencer, Sonic Pi is the instrument.

          One /run-code per event instead of a live_loop. Slightly less accurate — a UDP hop of jitter per
          note, measured at a few milliseconds — and completely live: edit the pattern below, re-run, and
          the next event goes out changed, with no live_loop to redefine.

          The thing a compiled loop cannot do is on the last line: a continuous signal sampled once per
          note, so the hats breathe.
          */

          (pat("bd*4, [~ cp]*2, hh*8") with gain(sine().range(0.15, 0.5))).sonicPiLive(cps = 0.5)
